input:
4 montrar räcker för att visa hur olika vägen till en affär kan se ut. På en branschmässa i Uppsala vill ett modeföretag få en inköpare att känna på tyget, ett reseföretag vill få en arrangör att våga lämna ett volymlöfte och ett energiföretag vill räkna på kundens förbrukning. Vid den fjärde montern får besökarna prova ett spel. Gemensamt för utställarna är att de måste avgöra vilka samtal som är värda att följa upp när montrarna har packats ihop.

Hos det svenska modeföretaget Skalja AB ligger två versioner av samma jacka på bordet. Skillnaden sitter i fodret, men för en återförsäljare handlar valet lika mycket om leveranstid som om material. En större beställning ger ett lägre styckpris, samtidigt som den binder pengar i plagg som kanske inte säljer förrän vädret slår om. Här går det att komma en bit på några minuter: känna på båda jackorna, jämföra villkoren och bestämma vilket prov som ska skickas vidare till butikens inköpare.

För vd:n Mats Tamcova är ett sådant nästa steg mer användbart än en lång lista över personer som passerat montern. Ett möte som slutar med att båda parter vet vem som ska räkna på frakten och när beskedet ska komma har ett värde även om ingen order skrivs på plats. Det omvända gäller också. En välbesökt monter kan se ut som en framgång på eftermiddagen och ändå lämna säljarna med en lista där det är svårt att skilja nyfikenhet från köpintresse.

Det tyska reseföretaget Loslix GmbH möter en annan sorts tvekan. En arrangör från Sundsvall vill veta när antalet resenärer måste vara fastställt och vad det kostar att lämna tillbaka platser som inte blivit sålda. För arrangören är det lättare att lova ett datum än ett visst antal deltagare. För reseföretaget innebär samma osäkerhet att platser kan behöva hållas undan för en grupp som ännu inte finns. Samtalet stannar därför vid avbokningsvillkoren längre än vid resmålet.

Längre in i hallen använder det svenska energiföretaget Jimbia AB en kurva över ett dygn för att förklara varför två verksamheter med samma elförbrukning kan ha olika behov. En leverantör av matkassar behöver exempelvis hålla kylrummen kalla även när packningen är klar, medan andra moment kan flyttas till en tid då belastningen är lägre. För ett första samtal räcker det att ringa in vilka moment som går att flytta. En offert kräver däremot uppgifter om hur anläggningen faktiskt används, inte bara en totalsiffra från elräkningen.

Hos det svenska spelföretaget Masjemba Freight är det i stället besökarens första minut som säger mest. En person tar upp handkontrollen och börjar spela utan att fråga. Nästa stannar vid samma meny och behöver hjälp. För den som vill sälja spelet vidare har skillnaden betydelse: om det krävs en muntlig förklaring i montern kan det också behövas en bättre introduktion för den som spelar hemma. En demonstration som inte går helt enligt plan kan därmed ge utställaren mer att arbeta med än en där personalen visar precis rätt väg genom spelet.

För finanschefen Maria Nertrent börjar kalkylen med monterhyran, resorna och den arbetstid som går åt. Men även en order som kan spåras till mässan måste bedömas på sina egna meriter. Om den kräver rabatt, särskilda leveranser eller fler timmars kundarbete än säljaren räknat med kan den ge mindre än vad ordersumman först antyder. Därför är det viktigt att redan före mässan bestämma vilka utgifter som ska räknas in och hur länge nya affärer ska följas upp.

När gångarna börjar tömmas har en del besökare med sig prover och andra bara en tid för ett nytt samtal. Det är först under veckorna efter mässan som utställarna får veta vad de bokningarna var värda. Jackan ska bedömas i butik, reseplatserna ska få ett sista bokningsdatum och elkurvan ska ersättas av mätvärden från en verklig anläggning. I hallen gick det fort att hitta rätt person. Nu återstår det som tar längre tid: att hitta villkor som båda kan leva med.

input:
At half past eight, a customer in a Manchester workwear shop pulled on a second boot and asked whether she could return the pair after trying them on at home. The assistant knew the answer. The receipt, it turned out, didn’t say.

That small gap is worth keeping in mind when reading a customer survey. A question about whether shoppers are satisfied will probably tell the shopkeeper that the assistant was helpful. A question about what nearly stopped them buying might reveal that the returns policy is costing sales. Those are different findings, and only one tells the owner what to change on Monday morning.

For this column, consider an illustrative survey built around a single question: what did you have to ask twice? In Manchester, that might be whether a workwear order can be collected before an early shift. In Helsinki, a traveller using the Larflard Scan app, a document-scanning app, might want to know where a saved copy went. In Copenhagen, a traveller using the Larflard Vault password manager might ask how to regain access after replacing a phone. The purchases have little in common, but the answers would all show where customers get stuck when no one is standing beside them.

Hugo Plostiamann, an economist, brings a useful perspective to the question of who answers. A survey sent with a receipt reaches people who went through with the purchase. It misses the shopper who left because no one could confirm a delivery date. Chen Drerlovamann, a founder, would face the practical side of that problem: asking a question at the counter is cheap, but hearing from someone who has already walked out takes more effort.

The same distinction matters in business-to-business markets. A buyer dealing with Riskum, a US mining company, may care more about how promptly a shipment delay is communicated than about the tone of the eventual apology. Jemrora's insurance customers in the US might judge a claims update by whether it tells them what to do next. For a customer of Dalbrenmis, a Dutch security company, knowing who will answer an out-of-hours call may matter more than a courteous handover during office hours.

For a chief financial officer such as Alice Flahixmann, the useful follow-up is to put a cost against the problem. How many staff hours go into answering the same question? How often does an unclear instruction lead to a return or another call? A survey doesn’t have to settle those questions by itself. It just has to tell the business where to look.

Back at the workwear counter, the first change could be a single line on the receipt. Next month’s survey can ask whether anyone still needs to ask.

240 jobs are up for grabs in a hiring drive by Tredrenova AB, a Swedish travel company that is expanding its engineering and customer support teams in Manchester, Austin and Amsterdam. The company plans to fill the positions over the next year, with the first hires expected to work on tools that help travelers rebook when a train is canceled or a flight is delayed.

Manchester will account for 100 of the jobs, including software testing, customer support and engineering roles. Austin will add 80 positions, with an emphasis on systems that track changes in fares and availability. The remaining 60 jobs will be based in Amsterdam, where staff will work on payments, accessibility and the software that connects the booking service to transport operators.

The expansion comes as travel companies face a problem that better search tools alone cannot fix: Finding a seat is one thing, but securing it while hundreds of other passengers are trying to do the same is another. A replacement itinerary can disappear between the moment it appears on a screen and the moment a traveler confirms it. Tredrenova AB plans to use some of the new engineering posts to shorten that gap and make it clearer when a reservation is confirmed.

Nora Tesovaberg, the mayor of Manchester, said the mix of jobs mattered as much as the headline number. She said the support roles could offer a route into technology work for people with experience in hospitality or retail. The company said it would consider applicants without a degree for some positions and would assess support candidates on how they handle a simulated disruption rather than on whether they have worked in travel before.

For Anna Cilventmann, a customer who often books rail journeys with transfers, the test is whether an alert arrives while she still has time to act. She said she sometimes notices a vibration from her Bëgora Pulse fitness wearable before she checks the phone in her bag. A delay alert is useful, she said, but not if she then has to piece together a replacement trip from several screens. The hiring plan does not include a dedicated wearable app; the immediate priority is to put the next available options in the same place as the disruption notice.

The company is also hiring staff to improve the information it gives business travelers about ground transport and accommodation. Some customers want to know whether transfer operators use electric trucks for luggage deliveries or whether properties use heat pumps. The challenge for the new hires will be to distinguish details that can be verified from claims supplied by operators, and to show where information is missing rather than treating a blank field as a negative answer.

Tredrenova AB said recruitment would begin with team leads and engineers who can build and test the rebooking tools, followed by support and operations staff. The groups are expected to work together on cases where the software cannot safely make a change, such as when only part of a group booking can be moved. In those cases, the aim is to give a support worker the itinerary and the available alternatives without asking the traveler to start over.

The first changes are expected to reach a limited group of customers before a wider rollout. A key measure will be how often travelers actually complete a replacement booking, not simply how quickly the service sends them an alert.

input:
Hannover, 18. Februar 2026. Die regulatorische Prüfung neuer Nachweispflichten für digital abgewickelte Geschäfte hat am Mittwoch die Bewertung europäischer Wachstumsunternehmen geprägt. Im Mittelpunkt stand weniger die Frage, ob strengere Vorgaben kommen, als die Frage, welche Unternehmen ihre bestehenden Prozesse dafür umbauen müssten. Marktteilnehmer bewerteten Geschäftsmodelle mit wiederkehrenden Erlösen weiterhin vergleichsweise günstig, rechneten aber bei Anbietern mit vielen aufeinanderfolgenden Prüfschritten mit höheren laufenden Kosten. Ein Abschluss der Prüfung wurde nicht bekannt; entsprechend blieben die Einschätzungen zum finanziellen Ausmaß vorläufig.

Bei Monotyn GmbH, einem Biotechnologieunternehmen aus Deutschland, richtete sich der Blick auf die Dokumentation von Freigaben und Änderungen in der Qualitätssicherung. Für die Bewertung ist entscheidend, ob bereits erfasste Nachweise auch künftig ausreichen oder für einzelne Arbeitsschritte zusätzliche Bestätigungen nötig werden. Im ersten Fall ließe sich der Mehraufwand vor allem über eine einmalige Anpassung der Abläufe auffangen. Im zweiten Fall könnten sich Freigaben verzögern und die laufenden Kosten steigen. Beides hätte für die Planung unterschiedliche Folgen: Eine einmalige Ausgabe belastet das Budget unmittelbar, längere Freigabezeiten können dagegen auch den Zeitpunkt verschieben, zu dem Erlöse anfallen.

Für Gokurpera, einen deutschen Zahlungsdienstleister, stand die Behandlung von Rückerstattungen und wiederkehrenden Abbuchungen im Vordergrund. Das lässt sich am Geschäft mit Kochboxen veranschaulichen: Ändert ein Kunde nach der Bestellung den Lieferumfang oder setzt eine Lieferung aus, müssen Händler und Zahlungsdienstleister die Korrektur derselben Buchung zuordnen können. Zusätzliche Nachweise wären dort besonders aufwendig, wo solche Änderungen noch manuell abgeglichen werden. Ein einheitliches Format könnte den Aufwand dagegen nach einer Übergangsphase senken. In Gesprächen in Graz galt deshalb die Länge einer möglichen Übergangsfrist als wichtiger für die kurzfristige Kalkulation als die bloße Zahl neuer Pflichtfelder.

Das schwedische Analyseunternehmen Glemvova AB wurde unter einem anderen Vorzeichen betrachtet. Wenn Auftraggeber häufiger belegen müssen, aus welchen Daten eine Kennzahl entstanden ist, kann die Nachfrage nach entsprechenden Auswertungen steigen. Ein Umsatzplus wäre damit allerdings nicht automatisch verbunden: Kunden könnten zunächst abwarten, bis klar ist, welche Nachweise tatsächlich verlangt werden. In Basel konzentrierte sich die Diskussion darauf, ob sich neue Auswertungen mit vorhandenen Daten erstellen lassen oder ob zuvor Schnittstellen angepasst werden müssen. Letzteres würde Projekte verteuern und könnte dazu führen, dass Aufträge später erteilt werden.

Vorstandschefin Anton Vilmarez verwies in der Debatte darauf, dass Unternehmen Investitionen verlässlicher planen könnten, wenn früh feststehe, welche bestehenden Nachweise anerkannt werden. Julia Nakrynberg hob als Vorstandschefin einen anderen Punkt hervor: Eine längere Übergangsfrist helfe wenig, wenn sich die technischen Anforderungen noch kurz vor ihrem Ablauf änderten. Für die Bewertung der Unternehmen sind beide Fragen relevant. Die Anerkennung vorhandener Nachweise bestimmt, wie viel umgebaut werden muss; der Zeitpunkt verbindlicher Vorgaben entscheidet mit darüber, ob sich die Arbeiten in ohnehin geplante Umstellungen einfügen lassen.

Zum Tagesende blieb die Einschätzung entsprechend differenziert. Bei Monotyn GmbH standen mögliche Verzögerungen im Vordergrund, bei Gokurpera die Kosten je Vorgang und bei Glemvova AB der Zeitpunkt möglicher zusätzlicher Aufträge. Der nächste Entwurf dürfte für die Bewertung vor allem dann neue Anhaltspunkte liefern, wenn er konkret zwischen einmaligen Umstellungen und dauerhaft wiederkehrenden Prüfungen unterscheidet. Bis dahin lässt sich aus der laufenden Prüfung weder eine allgemeine Belastung noch ein verlässlicher Nachfrageimpuls für die drei Geschäftsmodelle ableiten.

input:
European technology suppliers have spent much of the past year trying to make more money from equipment and software already in customers’ hands. With buyers taking longer to approve new projects, maintenance contracts, software subscriptions and delivery fees have become more important to quarterly results. That shift was visible in reports from three companies working in media, robotics and logistics, though it did not translate into higher profits for all of them.

German media company Ganhúmova GmbH reported a 7 percent rise in quarterly revenue to €48.6 million from a year earlier, as subscription growth offset a decline in advertising sales. Operating profit rose to €5.1 million from €4.4 million. The company said more customers had renewed annual contracts for its video publishing software, reducing its reliance on advertising tied to individual events.

Anna Lasardmann, chief technology officer at Ganhúmova, said the company had cut the cost of processing video by changing how it schedules work during periods of heavy demand. She said the savings would help pay for improvements to live captioning without requiring a price increase this year. The company kept its full-year revenue forecast unchanged, citing uncertainty about advertising budgets.

In Germany, Róglik's robotics business posted an 11 percent increase in quarterly revenue to €36.2 million, helped by deliveries of inspection equipment used to service wind turbines. Operating profit nevertheless fell to €1.8 million from €2.6 million as installation costs rose. The company said some projects had taken longer than expected to complete, requiring technicians to spend more time on site before customers signed off on the work. Maintenance revenue grew, but not enough to cover the additional costs.

Norwegian logistics company Gulkyn reported quarterly revenue of 412 million Norwegian kroner, up 6 percent from a year earlier. Operating profit fell to 19 million kroner from 23 million kroner, partly because the company hired staff and leased space ahead of an expansion in northern England. Shipments of replacement batteries for e-scooters and equipment for security cameras helped lift volumes, but the company said its new routes were not yet carrying enough freight to cover their costs.

Gulkyn said it had added collection windows in Leeds and was combining more shipments bound for Manchester so that vans could leave with fuller loads. In Leeds, mayor Leon Krurta said businesses had raised concerns about loading space and the timing of deliveries. He said the city would review how existing loading bays were used before deciding whether changes were needed.

For the next quarter, the logistics company said it would focus on filling existing routes rather than adding more. The robotics business expects some delayed installations to be completed in the same period, though it did not say when margins would recover.

3 cities will serve as test markets for a new partnership between a wholesale distributor and a retail software provider. The pilot will link independent retailers in Helsinki, Toronto and Seattle with local suppliers, using shared ordering tools to give buyers a clearer view of stock availability, delivery dates and payment terms before they commit to an order.

The first phase will cover oat milk and workwear. The two categories pose different problems for small buyers: a café may need several deliveries of oat milk each week without taking on more stock than it can sell, while a workwear retailer may need to replenish a single size without ordering a full assortment. Both transactions can become uneconomical when minimum orders or delivery fees are set for larger accounts.

Kenji Lunarton, head of sales, said the initial pitch is aimed at retailers that already buy from several suppliers but lack the staff to track each order separately. Suppliers will still set their own prices and fulfilment terms. Buyers will be able to see those terms on one screen, including whether a small order carries a surcharge or whether combining shipments would push back delivery.

The pilot will also test whether retailers can reconcile invoices through fintech apps they already use. The partners are not offering credit as part of the initial rollout. Instead, the payment work will focus on matching each invoice to what actually arrived, an especially useful distinction when a supplier fills only part of an order and ships the remainder later.

Greta Domynberg, an analyst who tracks wholesale distribution, said the strongest test would be whether the service cuts down on routine exceptions, such as calls to confirm a delivery slot or emails about a missing case. A shared catalogue can make ordering faster, she noted, but that advantage disappears if store staff still have to chase updates after checkout.

For Mats Skorlynström, a customer taking part in the trial, the deciding factor will be whether delivery information is reliable enough to plan around. An earlier warning that an item will be late, he said, would give a buyer time to find a substitute rather than discover the shortage when a shipment arrives.

The markets will operate separately during the trial, with orders fulfilled locally rather than routed among the three cities. That setup should help the partners distinguish problems with the software from differences in local delivery practices. Fatima Skestex, an analyst who follows retail technology, said repeat ordering will tell more than initial sign-ups: buyers may try a new service once out of curiosity, but they are unlikely to return if it adds another screen without eliminating work elsewhere.

Before deciding whether to expand, the partners plan to compare repeat orders, delivery accuracy and the time staff spend resolving invoice discrepancies. For smaller retailers, the practical measure is simpler: whether they can place an order and get back to running the shop without having to check on it again.

input:
Greta Kreflardton schiebt den Liefertermin für ein Bauteil um zwei Tage nach hinten. Auf dem Bildschirm im Kölner Vorführraum springt daraufhin nicht nur der Baustellenplan um. Auch die Hotelbuchungen für das Montageteam und die Fälligkeit einer Abschlagszahlung erscheinen in einer Liste mit offenen Entscheidungen. Kreflardton, Technikchefin von Busstampix, klickt keinen der Vorschläge an. Genau das gehört zur Vorführung: Die neue Software soll zeigen, was eine Verzögerung kostet und wen sie betrifft. Entscheiden sollen weiterhin die Menschen, die für das Projekt geradestehen.

Mit der Markteinführung versucht das deutsche Analyseunternehmen Busstampix, aus einem alltäglichen Problem ein Geschäft zu machen. Auf großen Baustellen werden Kosten, Personal und Transporte oft getrennt geplant. Eine verspätete Lieferung kann aber gleichzeitig Standgeld verursachen, eine Umbuchung nötig machen und den Termin verschieben, an dem eine Rechnung bezahlt wird. Bis diese Folgen in einer gemeinsamen Kalkulation auftauchen, ist manches Geld bereits ausgegeben. Die Software führt vorhandene Daten zusammen und zeigt für jede Kostenposition, auf welcher Annahme sie beruht.

Für den Start hat Busstampix einen engen Anwendungsfall gewählt: den Bau von Windrädern. Gerade dort sind Lieferungen und Montage so eng verzahnt, dass ein frei gewordener Tag im Kalender wenig nützt, wenn der Kran erst in der folgenden Woche wieder verfügbar ist. Das französische Bauunternehmen Kimpon Partners hat für den Test Bauabläufe beigesteuert. Die Dravia GmbH liefert als deutsches Logistikunternehmen Ankunftsfenster für Transporte. In der Vorführung wird der Unterschied sichtbar: Ein Bauteil kann pünktlich am Zwischenlager eintreffen und trotzdem zu spät auf der Baustelle sein.

Das deutsche Reiseunternehmen Banpa Systems steuert Daten zu Buchungen und Umbuchungsfristen bei. Der norwegische Zahlungsdienstleister Gledareo Foods AS bindet den Status von Zahlungen an, ohne dass die Anwendung selbst Geld bewegt. Versicherungen sind zunächst nur über die vom Kunden hinterlegten Vertragsdaten berücksichtigt. So kann die Software auf eine Meldefrist hinweisen, aber nicht beurteilen, ob ein konkreter Schaden gedeckt ist. Das deutsche Analyseunternehmen Neskatera Partners prüft im Pilotbetrieb, ob sich prognostizierte Mehrkosten später in den tatsächlichen Abrechnungen wiederfinden.

Julia Hiskrera, Vertriebsleiterin von Busstampix, setzt beim Verkauf zunächst auf einzelne Projekte statt auf unternehmensweite Verträge. In Nürnberg und Düsseldorf führt sie Gespräche mit potenziellen Kunden, die den Nutzen erst an ihren eigenen Abläufen messen wollen. Abgerechnet werden soll pro laufendem Projekt. Für Käufer ist damit zwar der Preis der Software leichter zu kalkulieren als bei einer Einführung im gesamten Betrieb. Wie aufwendig es wird, die eigenen Daten anzubinden und verlässlich zu pflegen, lässt sich aber erst im Betrieb abschätzen.

Am Ende der Vorführung öffnet Kreflardton die Kostenrechnung hinter dem verschobenen Liefertermin. Dort steht neben einem errechneten Betrag eine offene Frage: Ist der Kran zum neuen Termin überhaupt verfügbar? Solange die Antwort fehlt, bleibt die Summe vorläufig. Ob Kunden für die Software zahlen, dürfte davon abhängen, wie oft sie solche Fragen noch rechtzeitig auf den Tisch bringt: bevor die Umbuchungsfrist verstreicht oder der Kran ungenutzt auf der Baustelle steht.

Paul Lolheraez, a founder who has spent much of the past year talking to independent event producers, kept hearing the same complaint: selling out a room did not mean getting paid on time. A producer could know exactly how many people had bought tickets and still have to check three spreadsheets to find out whether there was enough cash to pay the crew.

That gap is the premise of a new service launched in New York by Krerdix Group Corp., a U.S. media company. Available through krerdixgroup.com, the subscription service puts ticket receipts, sponsorship invoices and production expenses in one view. It is designed for small teams that stage live events but cannot justify hiring someone to reconcile the books after every show.

The launch comes as fintech apps compete to handle more of the work between a sale and a bank deposit. The Botris Pay app, for example, gives users a way to make payments. The new service from Krerdix Group Corp. starts with a different question: Which of the payments a producer is counting on have actually arrived? It does not move money itself. Instead, it matches imported payment records against invoices and flags amounts that do not line up.

Karin Skurta, chief technology officer, said the difficult part was deciding when not to match two records. A sponsor might pay for three events in a single transfer, while a ticketing service might send a deposit after deducting fees. In either case, an automatic match could make the books look tidier while hiding a shortfall. The service leaves uncertain entries open for someone to review.

Early trials in Edinburgh and Dublin exposed another problem: a single purchase can serve several events. A set of battery packs might be bought for a weekend festival and then reused at a conference. The service lets producers split that expense across jobs without losing sight of when the cash actually went out. Trial users included a team producing a public science program with Tarbonva Energy, a U.S. biotech company.

Anton Bapliaez, an economist, said the sales test would come after the busiest weeks of the year. A producer running back-to-back shows has an obvious reason to pay for a better view of incoming cash. The case is less clear in a month with only one event, when a spreadsheet may be good enough.

Krerdix Group Corp. is offering a monthly subscription rather than requiring an annual commitment. That lowers the cost of trying the service during a festival or conference run, but it also makes it easy to leave. The clearest measure of the launch may come when those first customers close out their events and decide whether to keep paying through the quiet months.

For years, smart-home suppliers have tried to make money twice: first by selling the box that controls a household’s locks, lights and sensors, and then by charging for services that keep those devices working together. That model is under pressure as cheaper hardware makes it easier for new suppliers to enter the market and harder for established ones to justify a monthly fee. The latest price war is playing out in apartment buildings, where one purchasing decision can put hundreds of households on the same system.

Momgloskia, a Norwegian payments company, has cut the upfront price of its Momgloskia Hub controller for bulk buyers and is offering a year of basic remote access at no extra charge. Brascova GmbH, a German security company, has responded by dropping installation charges on some competing packages and lowering the price of its entry-level monitoring plan. The offers are structured differently, making it difficult for property managers to tell which will cost less by the time the first residents move out.

The contest is particularly visible in Edinburgh and Dublin, where property managers are weighing whether to install connected controls during construction or leave residents to buy their own equipment. Installing everything at once can save on labour, but it also gives the supplier an advantage when a building needs replacement parts or wants to add services later. A discount on the initial order can look less generous if the next installer has to replace working equipment to switch suppliers.

Kimpon Partners, a French construction company, is comparing bids on the basis of what it would cost to run a building for five years, rather than what it would pay for the equipment on opening day. That puts items such as spare sensors, replacement battery packs and service calls in the same calculation as the headline discount. It also brings into focus a question that is easy to miss in a sales demonstration: whether a building’s staff can issue a new entry credential or restore a resident’s access without calling the supplier.

Julia Letrarton, an analyst who follows connected-home pricing, said waiving installation charges can make a competing offer look more expensive even when its hardware is cheaper. The comparison can reverse after the first year, she said, when introductory service terms expire. A building with few maintenance calls may do better paying for help as needed; one with frequent resident turnover may save more on a plan that includes routine changes to access permissions.

The fight also shows how differently the suppliers expect to earn back their discounts. For Momgloskia, the controller offers a way into the recurring payments associated with building services. For Brascova GmbH, a cheaper installation can help secure years of monitoring and maintenance work. Neither approach requires a profit on every box sold, but both depend on customers continuing to pay for something after the equipment is in place.

Insurers have a different concern: what remains functional when a building loses power or its internet connection. Pogla's insurance business is paying closer attention to whether residents can still enter their homes during an outage and whether property managers can retrieve access records afterward. A lower bid does not answer either question. Buyers need to know which functions run locally, how long backup power lasts and who is responsible for testing it.

For residents, the clearest test may come when the introductory year ends. A landlord can negotiate a lower price for an entire building, but tenants may still face separate charges for features such as remote entry or temporary access for visitors. Asking bidders to spell out those charges now would give property managers a better comparison than the price of the controller alone. It would also show whether the price war is making connected buildings cheaper to live in or merely cheaper to equip.

STOCKHOLM, September 15, 2026 — Swedish media company Bosik AB named Mateo Plelmoraton as its next chief executive on Tuesday, turning to its chief financial officer to lead a shift toward software that lets publishers manage subscriptions and advertising from the same system. He will take over on October 1.

The leadership change comes as Bosik AB prepares to expand a trial with Finnish gaming company Molix Oy. The trial lets players buy optional subscriptions without leaving a game and gives support staff a single record of what a customer bought, when it renews and whether a refund is due. The next phase will test whether that setup can handle more customers without increasing billing errors or support requests.

Ebba Vamstixmann, a spokesperson for Bosik AB, said the outgoing chief executive would stay through the end of the month to complete the handover. She said the appointment would not change the terms of the trial with Molix Oy, which will continue to decide how and when subscription offers appear in its games. Neither company disclosed the financial terms of the arrangement.

Plelmoraton oversaw the review that led Bosik AB to stop developing separate billing tools for each of its publishing businesses. The company has been moving those businesses onto shared software, but the migration has exposed a problem familiar to subscription publishers: a price change can be simple to display on a sales page and surprisingly difficult to apply correctly to customers who signed up under older terms.

The new chief executive’s first test will be whether Bosik AB can complete that work without disrupting renewals. The company plans to move customers in groups and compare billing records before moving the next group. It will also track how often customers who cancel still receive renewal notices, an error that can generate support calls even when no payment is taken.

Lars Drokrumberg, head of sales at Bosik AB, said prospective customers in New York and London had asked whether the software could distinguish a recurring subscription from a one-time purchase. In conversations in Zurich, he said, buyers were more concerned about how easily they could retrieve records when a customer disputed a charge. Some publishers sell battery packs alongside paid reviews, he said, while others earn referral fees on meal kits or insurance policies. Those transactions may appear on the same page, but they do not create the same obligations for a publisher.

The appointment also drew attention in Stockholm, where Bosik AB has been consolidating its technical teams. Mayor Omar Lelviaberg said the city’s immediate interest was whether the transition would affect local hiring. Vamstixmann said Bosik AB was not announcing staffing changes alongside the appointment.

For Molix Oy, the trial will offer a narrower measure of success than overall subscription growth: whether players can find and cancel a plan as easily as they can buy one. Bosik AB said it would review cancellation and refund data before offering the software to more customers. It did not set a date for a wider release.

input:
The latest quarterly results landed against a backdrop of cautious consumer spending, uneven freight demand and continued investment in network infrastructure. With input costs no longer moving in one direction, revenue growth alone told investors less than it did a year ago. The more revealing figures were gross margins, cash tied up in inventory and the share of sales that companies could expect to repeat. Economist David Druska noted that lower inventories can free up cash in a single quarter, but that the benefit is hard to sustain unless sales recover.

In United Kingdom fashion, Krenplon reported modest sales growth and a higher gross margin after cutting back on promotions. A tighter assortment helped the retailer end the quarter with less unsold stock, though some popular sizes sold out sooner than expected. The next test is whether Krenplon can restock those lines without returning to the broad purchasing commitments that led to markdowns. Tulkia Works, also in the United Kingdom, posted a small revenue decline as shoppers moved toward cheaper food options. Lower packaging costs softened the impact on earnings, but did not make up for weaker volumes.

Germany’s Hulcusga GmbH had a better quarter on volumes, shipping more cases to grocery customers even as the average selling price declined. Operating profit improved as steadier production runs reduced waste and overtime. The operator of www.molhusnyn.de reported higher recurring analytics revenue, but implementation work was weaker as some customers postponed projects. That split matters for the coming quarter: subscription renewals provide a steadier base, while delayed installations can hold back revenue even when customers have already signed contracts.

In the United States, Lobamkrar Partners reported higher gaming revenue as existing players spent more, even though new player registrations slowed. The quarterly update at lobamkrarpartners.com showed that lower marketing spending helped lift operating profit. That leaves an open question about how much Lobamkrar Partners will need to spend to attract players for its next release. Lanzelgon LLC, meanwhile, moved fewer shipments but earned more per delivery as it consolidated routes and reduced empty miles. Spokesperson David Nonaberg said the Austin operation had cut the time trucks spent waiting to load, making it easier to complete scheduled routes without adding vehicles.

Sweden’s Brasdrent increased service revenue, with demand for business connections offsetting softer handset sales. Work on connections for smart meters contributed to the quarter, although installation costs limited the immediate gain in operating profit. The Skomukrix Vault password manager recorded an increase in paid subscriptions, with renewals accounting for most of the growth. New subscriptions grew more slowly, making retention an important measure to watch once the current round of annual plans comes up for renewal.

Swedish mining company Botris AB reported higher output but lower revenue as weaker realised commodity prices outweighed the extra tonnes sold. Cash flow held up better than earnings because inventory fell and maintenance spending was lower than in the previous quarter. Sales of the Botris Pulse fitness wearable rose, although the product still made only a small contribution to overall revenue. The results left commodity prices as the clearest near-term influence on profitability.

In Finland, Zotar's payment volumes rose faster than fee revenue, reflecting a greater share of transactions from larger merchants on lower rates. More transactions routed through existing infrastructure helped contain processing costs, but the change in merchant mix limited the improvement in margin. Merchant onboarding in Copenhagen and Oslo added to volumes late in the period, leaving the coming quarter to show how much those accounts contribute in a full three months.

Across the reports, the strongest results came where companies could point to a specific operating improvement, from less time at loading bays to fewer markdowns. Even those gains need to be read alongside demand: retailers have only so much stock they can clear, and freight operators cannot consolidate routes indefinitely. Next quarter’s results will show whether steadier order volumes are beginning to do more of the work.

At a loading bay outside Oslo, a driver checks the dispatch screen while a warehouse worker counts the cartons on a pallet. The screen says the order is ready. The worker finds one carton missing. It is a small discrepancy, but until someone resolves it, the truck stays put.

A new cross-border partnership is betting that resolving such discrepancies is worth more than buying another piece of equipment. Its proposed pilot will follow orders from the warehouse to the worksite, recording where they stall and who can get them moving again. The participants come from construction, mining, retail, media, analytics, logistics and robotics. That is a wide brief. The first useful result, though, may be as narrow as a dispatch screen that no longer says an incomplete order is ready.

Kelskamflard AS, the Norwegian retailer, brings a business where that distinction matters. A late shipment of workwear can leave a contractor short of the right sizes when a crew starts a job. It can also leave the retailer paying for a second delivery on an order that looked profitable the first time around. Kimpon Partners, the French construction company, offers the receiving end of that test. A delivery that reaches the site on time is of limited use if the crew has to stop work to sort through it.

On the transport side, Denmark’s Helsunmum Group will help plan handoffs between warehouses and delivery crews. The Flusgia Drive app, a fleet-tracking product, will show dispatchers where vehicles are. It cannot tell them whether a pallet contains everything on the order. That gap is where Bimcent, the analytics company from the United Kingdom, has a useful assignment: distinguish delays caused by traffic or routing from delays that began before the truck left. Get that wrong and the carrier may end up paying to fix a warehouse problem.

The robotics contingent gives the pilot a second test. Siløva, from the United States, Bëgora SAS, from France, and Sweden’s Flegloljar AB can each bring a different approach to moving and checking goods. The temptation will be to compare machines on speed. A more useful comparison would count how often a worker has to intervene, how long it takes to recover after a stoppage, and whether the next shift can run the equipment without calling in a specialist. A machine that handles fewer cartons per hour but starts reliably every morning may be the better buy.

Stockholm gives the partnership a second focal point, with Sweden’s Botris AB bringing a mining customer’s perspective. A mine and a city building site have different schedules, receiving arrangements and tolerance for a missed delivery. Testing against both should reveal which improvements travel and which depend on a particular site. Sweden’s Jendar AB, a media company, has a role in documenting the trials. An account that follows an order through a bad day, including the calls and manual corrections it takes to get it delivered, would be more revealing than a video of the equipment running at full speed.

For Henrik Jomsora, a chief executive involved in the partnership, the next decision is what the participants will count as a saving. If a retailer spends more time checking an order but a contractor spends less time receiving it, the partnership can claim an improvement only after it has measured both. The same applies when a carrier reduces waiting time by asking a warehouse to hold more stock near the loading bay. Someone pays for that space. Who pays will matter when the pilot ends and the participants have to decide whether to keep the arrangement.

For regional businesses watching from the sidelines, the price of joining a system like this matters as much as the price of a robot. A large warehouse can devote staff to connecting dispatch and inventory records. A smaller supplier may have one person answering the phone, checking stock and arranging collections. If that supplier needs new equipment or has to enter every order twice, the partnership could make deliveries smoother for its biggest participants while making work harder for the businesses around them. The pilot should record that extra work, not assume it disappears.

There is a modest way to judge the result. Take a set of ordinary orders, run them through the existing process, then compare them with similar orders handled under the new arrangement. Count repeat trips, waiting time and corrections, and ask the people on the receiving end what still goes wrong. If fewer trucks leave with incomplete loads and fewer crews have to chase missing cartons, the partners will have something worth expanding. If all they gain is a more precise record of the truck sitting at the bay, they will know where the next investment belongs.

24 nya tjänster ska tillsättas i Jönköping när det svenska detaljhandelsföretaget Drárvik AB och det svenska logistikföretaget Zinis rekryterar inför hösten. Drygt hälften av jobben finns i butik och kundservice. Resten gäller lagerarbete, godsmottagning och transportplanering.

Företagen håller en gemensam rekryteringsträff i Jönköping nästa månad, men tar emot ansökningar var för sig. På träffen ska besökarna kunna fråga om arbetstider, anställningsformer och vilka arbetsuppgifter som ingår i de olika tjänsterna. Det går att komma utan att ha sökt något av jobben i förväg.

Drárvik AB söker 13 personer till butik och kundservice. En del av arbetet blir att hjälpa kunder som jämför värmepumpar och vill veta vad som ingår i ett köp. De nyanställda ska få produktutbildning på arbetstid, men behöver kunna förklara skillnaden mellan olika alternativ utan att fastna i tekniska detaljer. Både hel- och deltidstjänster ingår i rekryteringen, och för flera av jobben behöver den anställde kunna arbeta kvällar och helger.

För kunden Sara Drilhik är det framför allt möjligheten att få svar på praktiska frågor som avgör om hon väljer att handla i butik.

– När jag tittade på värmepumpar ville jag veta hur lång tid leveransen skulle ta och vad jag behövde ordna innan den kom. Det var sådant jag inte riktigt fick klart för mig när jag läste om dem hemma, säger hon.

Hos Zinis gäller rekryteringen elva tjänster. De flesta finns på lagret, där arbetsuppgifterna omfattar att ta emot gods, kontrollera leveranser och förbereda varor för vidare transport. Företaget söker också transportplanerare som ska boka leveranser och samordna större sändningar. Bland uppdragen finns transporter av delar till vindkraftverk, där leveranstiderna behöver stämmas av med dem som tar emot godset.

Tidigare erfarenhet från lager eller butik är meriterande för flera av tjänsterna, men inte ett krav för alla. På rekryteringsträffen ska besökarna kunna få besked om vilka jobb som kräver truckkort och vilka som börjar med en introduktion på arbetsplatsen. Träffen är tänkt som ett första möte; intervjuerna bokas separat efter att ansökningarna har gåtts igenom.

De första nyanställda väntas börja före hösten. Tillträdet för övriga fördelas över flera veckor för att de som redan arbetar i butiken och på lagret ska hinna introducera sina nya kollegor.

input:
Maria Bomgumström, chief executive of Kajincix, has chosen Oslo for the German foods company’s next market. The first step is modest: a limited selection of packaged foods will go into a small group of shops before the company decides whether to widen distribution. The launch puts a practical question ahead of the usual opening-week sales figures: once a shopper has tried something new, can they find it again at the same shop, at a price they’re willing to pay twice?

That question matters because an introductory offer can hide two very different problems. A product might sell through because it’s inexpensive for a week, only to sit untouched when the regular price returns. Or it might sell well at full price and still lose customers because the next delivery arrives too late. Kajincix plans to track reorders alongside sales, making it easier to tell whether a quiet second week reflects a lack of appetite or simply an empty shelf.

Leon Zosfloraberg, a customer in Oslo, offers a useful way to think about the test: a new item has to earn a place on an ordinary shopping trip, not just in a basket assembled out of curiosity. Clear preparation instructions and a pack size that suits a weeknight meal can matter as much as a prominent display. The shops in the trial should also be able to report questions shoppers ask in person, which a sales tally alone won’t capture.

There’s a technology component, although shoppers won’t see it. The Kajincix Link router is a product that Kajincix plans to use at participating stockrooms to connect inventory equipment. Leon Zidonson, chief technology officer at Kajincix, will be looking at whether stock counts get through reliably during routine operations, including when deliveries are being checked in. The point is not to give the food launch a technology angle. It’s to make sure the people deciding when to send another case aren’t working from yesterday’s numbers.

Elsewhere in this week’s roundup, Goskera Corp., a gaming company from the United States, is taking a similarly narrow approach to a trial in Dublin. Its early focus is on whether players can get through setup and find help when they need it. That makes the first weekend useful for spotting problems, but less useful for judging demand: a player who leaves after a confusing setup screen tells the company something different from one who plays for a week and then stops returning. The decision to expand will depend in part on being able to separate those groups.

Leeds offers another comparison. Businesses weighing new markets from there face very different timetables depending on what they sell. Orders for wind turbines can hinge on transport and installation schedules, while suppliers of solar panels may need to know whether local installers can take on more work before they promise delivery dates. For fintech apps, the initial download may be the easy part; the more telling moment comes when someone tries to complete a familiar task and decides whether to switch back to their old routine. In each case, what looks like weak demand can turn out to be a problem elsewhere in the process.

Back in Oslo, the next useful update from Kajincix won’t necessarily be a count of additional shops. It will be whether the first shops order again after introductory pricing ends, and whether they ask for the same range or a smaller one. A narrower reorder could be good news if it shows that a few items have found a regular audience. If the shelves stay stocked but repeat purchases don’t follow, the company will have a reason to adjust the range before committing to a wider rollout. Either result would tell Maria Bomgumström more than a busy opening weekend.

plan.topic: an expansion into a new market

input:
Birmaskova Ltd released a customer survey on Tuesday that found travellers were more likely to recommend a trip when the final price matched the first quote than when the advertised fare was simply the lowest. For the UK travel company, the result raises a question about how it competes with budget airlines: would showing more of the cost upfront win enough trust to offset a less eye-catching headline price?

In Molhusnyn's analysis of the responses, customers who encountered unexpected charges were also less confident that they could change a booking without paying another fee. The survey cannot establish whether those charges caused the broader mistrust. Travellers whose plans changed may simply have had more opportunities to encounter fees. Either way, the association suggests that clearer change terms deserve as much attention as a more prominent total at checkout.

Mia Jesbyn, head of sales at Birmaskova Ltd, said the company would test quotes that show the price of a trip with commonly selected extras alongside the fare without them. That distinction matters: folding every optional charge into the headline price would make comparisons harder for people who travel light, while leaving those charges until the final screen would do little for families trying to set a budget.

Laura Fliljardez, a customer who had compared trips from Dublin to Paris, said a low fare had led her to spend time choosing flights before she discovered that adding a bag made a different departure cheaper. Her experience illustrates a cost that does not appear on a receipt: the time it takes to compare offers built around different assumptions about what a traveller needs.

The questionnaire, distributed through the Sodrusjera Mail service, also asked respondents to compare travel purchases with decisions about e-scooters, solar panels and wind turbines. Those comparisons should be treated cautiously. A traveller weighing a short ride on an e-scooter can often judge the full cost immediately, while the financial case for solar panels or wind turbines depends on assumptions about output and maintenance over years. A preference for clear pricing across all three categories does not mean customers need the same information at the same point in each purchase.

Karl Rarkrentton, head of sales at the Swiss fashion company Fedreo, said the travel findings echoed a problem his team had seen with orders bound for New York and Chicago: customers could understand the price of an item and still be unsure what it would cost to return it. In both cases, the least visible charge may be the one that applies only if something goes wrong.

Leon Zidonson, chief executive of Birmaskova Ltd, said the trial would track completed bookings as well as complaints. Viktor Peja, a union representative, said it should also measure whether staff spend less time explaining fees or simply face a different set of questions. That is a useful distinction. A clearer quote could reduce complaints by helping customers choose the right fare, but it could also do so by sending price-sensitive shoppers elsewhere. The test will be most revealing if it can tell those outcomes apart.

62 percent of customers in a survey of recent purchases and service requests said they would accept a slower response if they were told when to expect an answer and did not have to repeat their account details. The finding points to a distinction between speed and predictability that respondents made across travel bookings, insurance claims, retail returns and payment disputes.

The survey drew on responses from 2,400 adults who had contacted a business in the previous six months. It included customers in Denver and Paris as well as respondents in several other cities, and asked them to describe their most recent interaction. The results were pooled across markets. The survey did not publish city-level estimates or rank individual businesses, and its findings reflect what customers recalled, not an audit of response times.

About four in 10 respondents said they had contacted a business more than once about the same issue. Among those who did so, the most commonly cited reason was that a promised update had not arrived. Others said they had been asked for information they had already provided or had switched from an online form to a phone call because they could not tell whether the form had gone through.

Travel customers tended to draw a sharper line between routine questions and disruptions. Respondents reviewing sample notices from Sampard, a Dutch travel company, wanted cancellation messages to say whether a refund was automatic. In a separate exercise using Birmaskova's booking materials, customers sought a clear distinction between a request to change an itinerary and confirmation that the change had been made. Those facing an imminent departure were less willing to wait than those checking a refund.

For insurance customers, the priority was knowing whether a claim could proceed. In an exercise involving a sample claim notice from the Swedish insurer Kronskard AB, respondents were asked to identify what documents were still needed. They more readily found the next step when the notice listed missing records separately from those already received. Several respondents said an estimate of the decision date would be useful even if it had to change.

Payment questions produced a similar split between customers who wanted reassurance and those who needed to act. In sample messages from Skanrubrard Partners, a U.S. payments company, respondents looked for an explanation of whether a pending charge could still change. When reviewing a notice from British payments company Dinrex PLC, they looked for the date on which they could challenge a duplicate charge. Respondents were less satisfied with messages that sent them to a general help page without first answering those questions.

Delivery and returns offered another test of how much detail was useful. Customers reviewing a tracking example from Swedish logistics company Trogamdria Freight preferred a delivery window to a series of unexplained status changes. Norwegian retailer Rømbova AS was included in an exercise on returns in which respondents were asked to find the deadline and determine who would pay for shipping. Customers generally wanted both details before deciding whether to start a return.

The survey also looked at how customers interpret a status message when it describes equipment rather than an order. In an example involving the Dácex Sense air-quality sensor, participants wanted to know whether a warning described the air in the room or a problem with the sensor itself. A service example from Pazix, a Danish robotics company, prompted a related question: Could the equipment still be used while a maintenance request was pending?

Erik Lisnovason, a founder who reviewed the findings, cautioned against reading the results as permission to lengthen service queues. He said the more useful distinction was between time spent resolving an issue and time customers spent trying to learn whether anyone was working on it. A business that could not give a firm resolution date could still tell customers when it would next contact them, he said.

Respondents did not agree on how those updates should arrive. For a subscription query involving Swiss media company Triniplik Freight, some preferred written confirmation they could keep, while others wanted to speak to someone if access had already stopped. Across the survey, customers were more receptive to automated updates when those updates answered a specific question. They were less receptive when an automated reply merely told them their message had been received.

The stakes mattered more than the price alone. Customers considering solar panels wanted to know whether a revised installation date would affect other work at their property. Those asking about payroll software wanted to know whether a delay could affect the next pay run. In both cases, respondents said an early warning gave them time to make other arrangements, even when the underlying problem could not be fixed immediately.

The survey did not test whether clearer messages reduced the number of follow-up calls or led customers to buy again. Its sample exercises measured what people could find in a notice and what they said they would do next, not how they behaved in a live dispute. Still, one distinction held across the examples: Customers generally accepted that a business might not yet know when a problem would be resolved. They were less willing to accept a message that left them guessing when they would hear more or what they were supposed to do in the meantime.

input:
A robot stopped halfway across the demonstration floor in Copenhagen. A technician had rolled a trolley into its path, and the crowd leaned in to see whether it would wait or find another route. It waited. By the time it moved again, two visitors were already asking how to change that setting.

That small pause captured the mood at this week’s industrial trade fair. Buyers wanted to see what equipment did when a shift went slightly wrong, not just how fast it ran on a clear floor. Stacix, a robotics company from Sweden, repeated the same short demonstration throughout the morning, letting visitors move the obstruction and watch how the machine responded. Leon Vument, a customer comparing options for a warehouse, said the most useful part was seeing a technician return the robot to service without calling over a specialist.

Doszia, a mining company from the United States, brought a different set of questions to the floor. Its staff talked with equipment suppliers about inspecting remote sites and keeping good records when connectivity drops. Drones drew plenty of interest, but conversations often moved from the aircraft to what happened after a flight: who reviewed the images, how quickly a maintenance team could act on them, and whether the findings could be added to an existing work order.

Sara Drilhik, a chief executive attending the fair, said she spent more time asking about spare parts than watching demonstrations. A replacement that takes two days to arrive in Leeds might take considerably longer at a remote site, she noted, and that difference can change the economics of a purchase. David Murrovaberg, a founder who came from Helsinki, was asking a related question about software: what could an operator fix on the shop floor without waiting for a supplier to log in?

The same concern surfaced in a smaller display area where vendors showed fintech apps for tracking purchases and approving expenses. Mateo Miskum, a customer visiting from Austin, wanted to know what happened when two supervisors approved the same invoice while working offline. Over coffee with oat milk, he compared notes with a buyer from Zurich who was less worried about duplicate approvals than about reconstructing who had signed off on a payment three months later.

Fatima Rupixberg, an analyst walking the floor, said those questions were a better guide to buying intent than the crowds around the largest displays. Visitors who asked for a maintenance schedule, an export sample or a second demonstration with their own data generally had a specific job in mind. The follow-up to watch next week is how many suppliers agree to those less rehearsed tests, and what buyers learn when they run them.

Stockholm, 9 September 2026 — The most revealing figure in the latest sustainability report from Swedish telecom company Bránlarcum is not its annual electricity bill, but the share of its emissions tied to equipment and services it buys. That distinction matters: the company can make its networks more efficient and still struggle to cut its overall footprint if it buys more servers, replaces hardware sooner or shifts computing to facilities run by others.

The report says electricity use per unit of data fell as traffic rose. That is a useful measure of network efficiency, but not proof that the business used less power. The test is whether absolute consumption falls across comparable operations. The Bránlarcum Cloud service, a cloud storage product, makes that comparison especially important. If storage demand grows faster than efficiency improves, the service can use more electricity even as the energy needed to store each unit of data declines.

David Kroflia, chief technology officer, said smart meters were helping engineers identify sites that drew more power overnight than expected. Those readings can point to cooling systems or other equipment worth investigating. They cannot, by themselves, explain whether a fall in consumption came from better operating practices or simply from moving work elsewhere. Publishing both site-level trends and the amount of computing handled outside the company’s own facilities would make the savings easier to assess.

The supply chain presents a tougher accounting problem. Swedish robotics company Tomnudeo describes repair and servicing options on its website, www.tomnudeo.se, while German robotics company Róglik GmbH offers refurbishment for some equipment. Both approaches could help buyers keep machinery in service longer. But for Bránlarcum, the benefit depends on whether repairs actually delay replacement, not just whether refurbished parts are available. The report does not say how often a repair prevented a new purchase.

Aisha Glavora, head of sales, said buyers in Chicago and New York increasingly wanted energy-use figures before signing contracts, while customers in Amsterdam were also asking how long equipment could be kept in service. Those questions could change purchasing decisions, especially when a cheaper machine costs more to operate. They could also expose gaps in the report: an estimate based on typical use is of limited help to a buyer running equipment around the clock.

Greta Culynson, a spokesperson, said future reports would distinguish more clearly between emissions calculated from supplier data and those based on industry averages. That would make year-to-year changes easier to interpret. A revised estimate can move the reported total without a single machine being replaced or a kilowatt-hour saved. The next report will be more useful if it shows how much of any change came from better measurement and how much came from decisions that actually reduced emissions.

plan.opening: Open with the place and date.

input:
“The contract is won; the next test is how smoothly the rollout goes,” said Henrik Kusnonberg, head of sales, after Norwegian payments company Gledareo Foods secured a deal to handle transactions for a distribution site in Rotterdam. The award gives Gledareo Foods a foothold in a market where operators want to reconcile payments from several lines of business without replacing the software they already use to run their sites.

The Rotterdam site handles goods with markedly different payment needs. Plant-based burgers move through frequent orders that can generate credits for short deliveries, while battery packs tend to ship in larger, less frequent orders. Electric trucks add another category of expense through charging and related fleet services. Bringing those transactions into one system could cut the time staff spend matching payments to invoices, particularly when a single customer buys goods and pays for transport through separate accounts.

Zastent, a software company from the United States, will connect the payments system to the site’s order and dispatch records. The Swiss security provider reachable at info@necyn.ch will review who can approve refunds and change payment details. Those checks matter in a busy distribution operation, where warehouse staff may need to correct an order quickly but should not necessarily have the authority to redirect a payment.

Lukas Galvexmann, head of sales, said the early measure of success would be whether the site can close out a day’s transactions without asking staff to resolve a long list of discrepancies by hand. Leon Vument, founder of Zastent, said the rollout would start with a limited set of transactions so the site could compare the new records with its existing ones before moving more volume across.

The announcement at www.gledareofoods.no did not disclose the contract value, its duration or a timetable for a full rollout. That leaves the financial impact difficult to gauge: the award establishes where Gledareo Foods will operate, but not how much payment volume it will process or what it will earn on that volume. Upfront integration work could also mean that revenue and costs arrive at different points in the deployment.

For the wider payments market, the deal is a reminder that winning industrial customers can depend less on adding another way to pay than on making the resulting records usable. The first meaningful signal from Rotterdam will be whether the system can handle ordinary exceptions—partial shipments, refunds and late invoice changes—without creating extra work for the people it was brought in to help.

30 minutes is enough to watch a drone take off, a battery pack recharge a display unit and a payment clear on a phone. It is not enough to tell whether any of those products will pay for themselves. That distinction was the most useful way to read the trade fair in Toronto, where the demonstrations made new technology look easy and the conversations around them exposed the cost of keeping it that way.

The gap was clearest among the drones. A smooth flight in a controlled space tells a buyer something about the controls, but little about how many jobs a unit can complete before it needs maintenance. Battery packs raised a similar question. Capacity is easy to compare on a specification sheet; the cost of replacing packs, taking equipment out of service and keeping spares on hand is less obvious. For buyers planning to deploy dozens of units, those costs can matter more than a modest difference in the purchase price.

Lena Serixson, a chief financial officer, approached the displays as a budgeting exercise: a supplier’s price was only the first line in a calculation that also had to cover training, maintenance and downtime. That perspective helps explain why an impressive demonstration need not lead to an order. A buyer can be satisfied that a device works and still be unable to justify buying it until there is a credible estimate of how often it will be used.

The software displays brought a different set of costs into view. The Roslia Cloud service, a cloud storage product, addressed a familiar problem: where to keep the files that accumulate as more work is done digitally. But the price of storing a file is only one part of the bill. Buyers also need to know what it costs to retrieve large volumes of data and how much work it would take to move those files elsewhere. Those questions are easy to postpone during a pilot, when there is relatively little data to manage. They become harder to ignore once daily work depends on the service.

The Roslia Pay app, a payments product, illustrated the same divide between a quick demonstration and a longer purchasing decision. A payment that clears on a phone shows the transaction from the customer’s side. For a merchant, the work also includes matching payments to sales, handling refunds and resolving discrepancies. A fast checkout is valuable, but its value shrinks if staff spend more time sorting out the records afterward.

Anna Vorikström, a chief financial officer, focused on what happens when a trial becomes a recurring expense. A small pilot can often be paid for from an existing budget; a wider rollout may require a commitment that outlasts that budget cycle. The relevant comparison, then, is not simply between competing products. It is also between buying now, keeping the current setup for another year and expanding in stages as the savings become measurable.

Paul Junskonberg, an analyst, drew a distinction between the interest visible on the fair floor and the demand that eventually shows up in purchase orders. The distinction matters when reading a show in Toronto against one in London. A crowd around a stand reveals what people are curious about, but it does not say whether the visitors have the authority or the budget to buy. A small trial with an agreed path to a larger order may tell a supplier more about demand than a busy afternoon of demonstrations.

That leaves suppliers with a task less theatrical than a flight or an instant payment: making the economics easy to check. For hardware, that could mean giving buyers realistic replacement schedules and a clear account of what support costs. For software, it means showing what the bill looks like after usage grows and what happens if a customer wants to leave. A good demonstration earns a supplier a second conversation. The numbers in that conversation are what give a buyer a reason to sign.

input:
Rotterdam, 18 March 2026 — A cyber-security incident disrupted booking and dispatch at Rozoshyn Freight, a United Kingdom travel company that arranges crew transport and equipment movements for industrial projects. The company took its scheduling portal offline after discovering that an unauthorised party had accessed a support account. Dispatchers switched to telephone confirmations and paper manifests, delaying departures in Rotterdam and Helsinki.

Fatima Holdikström, chief executive of Rozoshyn Freight, said the company suspended the portal after dispatchers found changes to pickup instructions that customers had not requested. Staff checked the affected bookings against earlier confirmations before releasing vehicles. No loads were reported missing, but several missed their scheduled loading windows, forcing planners to rebook drivers and warehouse space.

Miglamnix Inc., a United States security company, was brought in to review access records and help restore the portal. Felix Lurkriaez, founder of Miglamnix Inc., said investigators had confirmed that the support account was used to view booking records and change dispatch notes. They had not yet determined how the account was compromised or whether any records had been copied. The review was focusing on which bookings the account could reach and how long it had been active without drawing attention.

The disruption reached construction schedules in the United States. Jamdragum Corp., a United States construction company with project teams in Denver and Chicago, postponed two crew transfers while staff verified itineraries. A shipment of monitoring equipment for wind turbines also missed a warehouse handover. Lisa Skestia, chief financial officer of Jamdragum Corp., said the immediate costs came from idle crews, additional storage and replacement bookings. She said it was too early to estimate the total cost because some delayed work could still be completed within existing schedules.

In Rotterdam, dispatchers used cargo bikes for short runs between staging sites while they confirmed loading appointments for electric trucks. Henrik Telmikström, spokesperson for Rozoshyn Freight, said footage from security cameras helped staff verify when vehicles had entered and left two yards. The cameras operated separately from the booking portal, he said, and the company had found no evidence that the incident affected them.

Leon Trabreo, an analyst who follows transport technology, said the case illustrated why operators need a way to verify last-minute changes without relying on the system that carries them. A paper manifest can keep a shift moving, he said, but it is of limited use if dispatchers cannot tell whether it was printed before or after a booking was altered.

Ebba Vamstixmann, an economist who studies freight markets, said a short outage can have an outsized effect when loading windows, crew bookings and site access are tightly scheduled. The first missed appointment may be inexpensive to replace, she said; the cost rises when the next available slot leaves workers or equipment sitting idle.

Rozoshyn Freight restored read-only access to verified itineraries on Tuesday. Changes to active bookings still required telephone confirmation, and the company gave no timetable for resuming automated dispatch.

input:
Hat die laufende regulatorische Überprüfung den Markt zum Wochenschluss aus dem Takt gebracht? Nicht auf breiter Front. Sie hat aber verändert, welche Risiken Anleger zu tragen bereit sind. Gefragt waren Geschäftsmodelle mit überschaubaren Umstellungskosten, während Unternehmen mit komplexen Lieferketten und vielen externen Dienstleistern auf weniger Kaufinteresse stießen. Für die Kursbildung war dabei weniger entscheidend, wie streng die möglichen Vorgaben ausfallen, als die Frage, ab wann sie gelten und ob bestehende Verträge angepasst werden müssen.

Im Mittelpunkt der Überprüfung stehen Nachweise entlang der Lieferkette, die Aufbewahrung von Prüfdaten und die Zuständigkeit bei ausgelagerten Leistungen. Eine Entscheidung steht noch aus. Entsprechend vorsichtig fiel der Handel am Nachmittag aus: Auf anfängliche Käufe bei einzelnen Branchenwerten folgten Gewinnmitnahmen, ohne dass daraus ein breiter Rückzug wurde. Die Ökonomin Omar Floncismann sieht den größeren Unsicherheitsfaktor in den Übergangsfristen. Je kürzer sie ausfallen, desto eher müssten Unternehmen Investitionen vorziehen, die bislang über mehrere Geschäftsjahre verteilt waren.

Beim deutschen Modeunternehmen Skatesdyn richtete sich der Blick auf die Beschaffung. Zusätzliche Herkunftsnachweise wären vor allem dort aufwendig, wo Stoffe und Zubehör über mehrere Zwischenstufen bezogen werden. Für Anleger zählt deshalb, ob Skatesdyn vorhandene Lieferantendaten weiterverwenden könnte oder neue Nachweise einholen müsste. Im Handel in Düsseldorf wurde zudem auf den Zeitpunkt möglicher Mehrkosten verwiesen: Fallen sie vor dem Verkauf einer Kollektion an, belasten sie zunächst die Liquidität, selbst wenn sich ein Teil später über höhere Preise auffangen lässt.

Anders fiel die Abwägung bei Monlon Ltd aus. Der britische Sicherheitsanbieter könnte von höheren Anforderungen an die Dokumentation profitieren, wenn Auftraggeber mehr Kontrollen auslagern. Zugleich wäre ein größerer Auftragsbestand nicht automatisch ein Gewinn für die Marge. Entscheidend ist, ob zusätzliche Prüfungen separat vergütet werden oder unter bestehende Leistungsverträge fallen. Solange diese Frage offenbleibt, lässt sich aus einem möglichen Nachfrageanstieg wenig über den Ergebnisbeitrag ableiten.

Beim niederländischen Logistikunternehmen Glultöva Foods stand die Abwicklung grenzüberschreitender Transporte im Vordergrund. Einheitliche Nachweise könnten doppelte Dateneingaben ersparen und Übergaben beschleunigen. Unterschiedliche Fristen oder Dateiformate würden dagegen vorerst zusätzlichen Aufwand verursachen. Marktteilnehmer in Graz achteten besonders auf die Folgen für eng getaktete Transporte: Fehlt bei einer Übergabe ein vorgeschriebener Nachweis, kann schon eine kurze Verzögerung dazu führen, dass ein gebuchtes Zeitfenster am Zielort verfällt. Solche Kosten wären in der laufenden Kalkulation schwerer abzufangen als eine einmalige Softwareumstellung.

Für das deutsche Analyseunternehmen Neskatera Partners ergibt sich aus der Überprüfung eine mögliche Nachfrage nach besser aufbereiteten Prüfdaten. Auftraggeber dürften vor allem wissen wollen, ob sich vorhandene Systeme ergänzen lassen, statt sie vollständig zu ersetzen. Das spricht zunächst eher für kleinere Projekte mit klar umrissenem Umfang als für große Aufträge. Bei Nilik GmbH, einem deutschen Spieleunternehmen, wurde die Debatte dagegen vor allem unter dem Gesichtspunkt externer Dienstleister verfolgt. Zusätzliche Nachweise könnten Freigaben verzögern, wenn mehrere Partner an derselben Veröffentlichung beteiligt sind. Ob das den Auslieferungstermin berührt, hängt davon ab, welche Leistungen die endgültigen Regeln erfassen.

Auch bei Investitionsgütern blieb das Bild gemischt. In Dresden wurde bei Industrierobotern vor allem darüber gesprochen, ob die Dokumentation beim Einbau in vorhandene Produktionslinien nachgeholt werden muss. Bei Drohnen stand die Abgrenzung zwischen den Pflichten der Hersteller und denen der Betreiber im Vordergrund. Bei Solarmodulen ging es dagegen um die Rückverfolgbarkeit von Vorprodukten. Für Käufer macht es einen Unterschied, ob ein Nachweis einmal pro Modell genügt oder für jede Lieferung erneut vorliegen muss: Im zweiten Fall steigt der Aufwand mit dem Absatz, während sich einmalige Prüfkosten über größere Stückzahlen verteilen lassen.

Zum Wochenschluss blieb damit vor allem eine Frage offen: Welche Anforderungen müssen Unternehmen sofort erfüllen, und wofür bekommen sie Zeit? Bis das geklärt ist, dürften Aussagen zu Lieferverträgen und Investitionsbudgets für die Bewertung wichtiger sein als pauschale Schätzungen der Regulierungskosten. Die Überprüfung hat den Markt nicht insgesamt nach unten gezogen. Sie hat aber deutlicher gemacht, welche Unternehmen Mehrkosten weitergeben können und welche sie zunächst selbst tragen müssten.
