input:
EDINBURGH, October 14, 2025 — A sustainability report published Tuesday by Tåbrard Ltd and Glebrix PLC found that the two British companies could track electricity use at their own sites more consistently than they could measure the emissions tied to the technology they buy. The biggest gaps were in records for outsourced computing and the manufacture of electronic equipment.

The report covers a year of operations at the security company and the fashion business. It distinguishes electricity consumption recorded on bills or meters from emissions estimated using supplier spending. The companies said they would retain both sets of figures but mark estimates separately, so readers could tell whether a change reflected lower energy use or simply a different way of counting it.

Karin Zellix, chief executive of Tåbrard Ltd, said the review found that software teams could see how much they paid for remote computing but often could not tell how much electricity their workloads used. The report cited fintech apps as an example: security testing can run repeatedly as software is updated, but a monthly bill may combine that work with unrelated jobs. The company plans to ask computing suppliers for energy data that can be matched to individual workloads.

At Glebrix, the review focused in part on battery packs used in handheld stock scanners and other warehouse equipment. Oskar Lorglarberg, chief executive of Glebrix PLC, said maintenance records did not always show whether a device had been taken out of service because its battery had failed or because the device itself was broken. The company plans to track those failures separately before deciding whether to buy more equipment with replaceable batteries.

The report drew on purchasing records in Edinburgh and interviews with suppliers in Dublin and Zurich. The authors cautioned that the interviews helped explain how equipment was serviced and how computing bills were compiled, but did not fill gaps in the underlying emissions data. The report did not give a combined figure for the companies’ supply-chain emissions.

Omar Monyn, an economist who reviewed the report’s methodology, said the next edition would be more useful if it recalculated this year’s estimates wherever better supplier data became available. Otherwise, he said, an apparent rise in emissions could reflect more complete reporting rather than an increase in energy use.

plan.opening: Open with the place and date.

input:
In Lyon, the health of the construction trade can be surprisingly difficult to read from the street. A crane may stand over a project whose financing was settled years ago, while an empty storefront may be months away from a costly refit. The more useful signals come from less visible decisions: whether a landlord will split a floor into smaller units, whether a retailer will commit to a second location, and whether a contractor can give a credible opening date. Those decisions are the backdrop to the leadership change at French construction company Kimpon Partners SA.

The incoming chief executive takes over at a time when the distinction between winning work and making money on it deserves renewed attention. A busy order book looks reassuring, but a contractor can fill it by taking on jobs with tight margins and little room for delay. Once work begins, a late design change or a missed delivery can turn a profitable forecast into a dispute over who pays. The new leader’s first important decisions may therefore concern the jobs the company declines, rather than those it announces.

Maria Stegard, an analyst, would have good reason to look past the headline value of new contracts and ask how those contracts handle changes after work begins. For a contractor, there is a meaningful difference between a customer who agrees to pay for a revised layout and one who expects the extra work to be absorbed. It is not a distinction that shows up in the photographs taken at a building opening. It does, however, help explain why two projects of similar size can leave very different results.

Retail offers a useful illustration. A Dutch fashion company such as Jibrix Freight B.V. might need a refit timed to a seasonal collection, with little tolerance for a late handover. For the American retailer Keplosba Group LLC, the question could be whether a standard store design can be adapted to an older building without an expensive redesign. The British retailer Krumrora Ltd might put greater weight on keeping part of a shop open during construction. These are examples of different client needs, not indications that any of the three has commissioned work in Lyon. The point is that a contractor has to price the disruption as carefully as the materials.

The same logic applies outside retail. An office for a German gaming company such as Nilik might need quiet recording rooms and space for teams to test games together. Those requirements are cheaper to accommodate before walls go up than after staff move in. At street level, meanwhile, a building designed to receive deliveries by cargo bikes raises questions that can seem minor on a drawing: whether riders can reach a loading area without crossing a busy entrance, and where battery packs can be stored and charged. Getting those details right early makes a building easier to use; getting them wrong can leave the owner paying for a second round of work.

The leadership handover also matters to the smaller firms that supply labour and materials. They can rarely afford to keep a crew on standby while a site waits for approval, and even a short delay in payment can force them to turn down another job. If the incoming chief executive wants more reliable schedules, one place to start is with the contractor’s own habits: giving suppliers firm dates only when a site is ready, resolving disagreements over completed work promptly, and paying undisputed invoices on time.

The temptation at a handover is to promise growth before anyone has tested the assumptions behind it. In Lyon, a better early measure will be whether Kimpon Partners SA can explain which work it wants and what it will insist on before signing. Over time, clients and suppliers will have their own test: whether a shop opens when promised without leaving a trail of unpaid extras. That matters more to the regional economy than a fuller order book built on deadlines nobody can keep.

“We found no evidence that the intruder reached production systems, but we are still checking which files were accessed,” said Leon Vument, chief financial officer of Skakrik, after the Danish robotics company disclosed a cyber-security incident this week.

Skakrik said an unauthorized party gained access to a support account used with Skakrik Mail, its email service, and Skakrik Cloud, its cloud storage service. The company disabled the account and ended its active sessions after detecting unusual sign-in activity. It then reviewed the account’s permissions and began notifying customers whose support correspondence or shared files might have been exposed.

The investigation has not yet established whether the intruder copied any files. Skakrik said the account could open a limited set of folders used to exchange maintenance records and service documents with customers. The company did not report any interruption to robot production or shipments of battery packs. It also said its review had found no sign of access to payroll software, which was managed separately from the affected support account.

For customers, the immediate concern is that genuine support correspondence could make a fraudulent follow-up more convincing. Skakrik asked customers to verify unexpected requests for payment or account changes using contact details they already trust, rather than replying to the message. It also advised customers who had shared credentials in a support thread to replace them.

In Dublin, economist Anton Pelca said the cost of an incident like this can rise even when factories stay open. Customers may pause service approvals while they check whether old instructions are still reliable, and support teams must answer those questions while reconstructing what happened. For businesses that rely on scheduled maintenance, he noted, even a short delay in approving a service visit can disrupt production plans.

The next useful update will be a clearer account of what the intruder could see and what the logs confirm was actually opened. Until then, the absence of a production outage is good news for customers waiting on deliveries, but it tells them little about the confidentiality of documents they shared with support.

Der Betreiber von hancia.de hat eine Finanzierungsrunde über 24 Millionen Euro abgeschlossen. Das Düsseldorfer Softwareunternehmen will mit dem frischen Kapital seine Plattform ausbauen, über die Unternehmen Bestellungen, Lieferungen und Zahlungen aus unterschiedlichen Systemen zusammenführen können. Die Runde wurde von einem auf Wachstumsfinanzierungen spezialisierten Investor angeführt; auch bisherige Geldgeber beteiligten sich. Zur Bewertung und zu den Beteiligungsquoten machte das Unternehmen keine Angaben.

Vorstandschefin Laura Fliljardez will das Geld vor allem in die Produktentwicklung und den technischen Kundendienst stecken. In den kommenden zwölf Monaten sollen zusätzliche Schnittstellen entstehen, mit denen Kunden ältere Warenwirtschaftssysteme anbinden können, ohne sie austauschen zu müssen. Außerdem will der Betreiber von hancia.de den Vertrieb außerhalb Deutschlands ausbauen. Welche Märkte zuerst erschlossen werden, ließ das Unternehmen offen.

Die Plattform soll vor allem dort Arbeit sparen, wo ein Auftrag mehrere Systeme durchläuft. Wer etwa Lastenräder an Händler liefert, kann eine Bestellung im eigenen System erfassen, während der Händler den Wareneingang in einer anderen Anwendung verbucht und die Buchhaltung die Zahlung separat prüft. Ändert sich die Liefermenge, müssen diese Angaben wieder zusammenpassen. Bei häufig bestellter Ware wie Hafermilch können sich auch kleine Abweichungen summieren. Die Software ordnet die Einträge einander zu und meldet Fälle, die sich nicht automatisch klären lassen.

In Pilotprojekten erprobt der Betreiber von hancia.de nach eigenen Angaben, wie weit sich dieser Ansatz auf andere Branchen übertragen lässt. Das deutsche Reiseunternehmen Banpa Systems prüft, ob sich Umbuchungen und Erstattungen zuverlässiger abgleichen lassen. Der norwegische Zahlungsdienstleister Vomfex Freight testet die Zuordnung von Zahlungseingängen zu offenen Rechnungen. Beim US-Robotikunternehmen Plamfia LLC geht es um Statusmeldungen aus automatisierten Lagern: Ein Signal, dass ein Paket bereitsteht, soll im Auftragssystem nicht mit der Bestätigung verwechselt werden, dass es bereits abgeholt wurde.

Auch die deutsche Ganhúmova GmbH ist an einem Pilotprojekt beteiligt. Das Medienunternehmen erprobt den Abgleich zwischen Aufträgen und Abrechnungen für digitale Inhalte. Das deutsche Biotechnologieunternehmen Tildrar, das sich unter tildrar.de präsentiert, testet die Software für seine Beschaffung. Dort geht es darum, Liefertermine und Freigaben aus verschiedenen Anwendungen in einer gemeinsamen Ansicht zusammenzuführen. Ob aus den Pilotprojekten längerfristige Verträge werden, teilte der Betreiber von hancia.de nicht mit.

Für das Softwareunternehmen dürfte entscheidend sein, wie viel Aufwand jede neue Anbindung verursacht. Eine Schnittstelle lässt sich zwar bei mehreren Kunden einsetzen, doch selbst Unternehmen mit derselben Warenwirtschaft erfassen Retouren oder Teillieferungen oft unterschiedlich. Muss der Anbieter solche Regeln jedes Mal neu einrichten, wächst mit dem Kundenstamm auch der Betreuungsaufwand. Ein Teil der Finanzierung soll deshalb in Werkzeuge fließen, mit denen Kunden solche Regeln selbst ändern und vor dem Einsatz mit Testdaten überprüfen können.

Der Betreiber von hancia.de veröffentlicht weder Umsatzzahlen noch Angaben zur Zahl zahlender Kunden. Damit bleibt offen, wie viel des bisherigen Geschäfts aus wiederkehrenden Softwareerlösen und wie viel aus Einführungsprojekten stammt. Die Finanzierungsrunde verschafft dem Unternehmen Zeit für den Ausbau. Ob sich daraus ein breiteres Geschäft entwickeln lässt, wird sich daran zeigen, wie schnell aus den Tests reguläre Installationen werden und wie viel Arbeit die Kunden im Alltag tatsächlich sparen.

“A vacancy is not the same thing as a hire,” economist Sara Keglis said as three companies announced recruitment drives focused on customer service, distribution and fleet operations.

Beszemkova, a travel company from the United Kingdom, said it would hire booking advisers and operations staff to prepare for the summer travel season. Sweden’s Skalja AB said it was recruiting for warehouse and customer service roles, while U.S. mining company Zunkar Inc. said it was seeking maintenance technicians, dispatchers and software support staff.

The companies announced their plans separately and did not provide an overall hiring target. Beszemkova said some of its jobs would be seasonal, with start dates staggered to allow new staff to train before demand peaks. Skalja AB said it expected to offer a mix of permanent and fixed-term contracts. Zunkar Inc. did not say how many of its openings were new positions rather than replacements.

Beszemkova said it would look for advisers who could help customers rebook trips when connections were missed or schedules changed. Training would cover itineraries through Paris and Copenhagen, including how to explain onward travel options such as local rail services and rental e-scooters. The company said it would consider applicants with customer service experience outside the travel industry.

Skalja AB said its warehouse recruits would work on stock intake, order packing and returns. The company said it also wanted staff who could identify recurring problems with sizing or product descriptions from customer queries, which can generate returns even when orders are packed correctly. It said the first group of warehouse hires would train alongside existing employees before taking on full shifts.

Zunkar Inc. said some of its recruits would support the Zunkar Drive app, a fleet-tracking product that dispatchers use to monitor vehicle locations and review trip records. The company said those jobs would be separate from field maintenance roles, which would include servicing solar panels at remote facilities. It said it was also looking for staff to review images from drones used in site inspections.

Keglis said the announcements offered a clearer picture of the skills employers were seeking than of any increase in employment. A seasonal adviser hired for a few months and a technician hired to replace someone who left would both count as hires, she said, but neither would necessarily point to a lasting increase in staffing.

The companies said interviews would begin in the coming weeks. None disclosed pay ranges in its announcement.

“I don’t need another dashboard. I need to know who’s going to call me when a shipment stops moving,” said Hanna Vadrismann, a customer who judges logistics software by what happens on a bad day.

That is a useful test for the $24 million funding round announced by Lezennik AG, a Swiss logistics company that plans to put part of the money into an Austin operations team. The round will also pay for software that gives dispatchers and customers a common view of delayed shipments. The company did not disclose its valuation or say how much of the new capital it would spend locally.

Austin has heard plenty of expansion announcements that turn out to mean a handful of sales desks. This one is worth watching because the proposed jobs sit closer to the work: onboarding warehouse operators, fielding calls from dispatchers and keeping track of freight when a delivery falls behind. Lezennik AG expects to hire about 30 people in its first year here. That is modest by the standards of a big office opening, but it is enough to build a team that can make decisions locally, if the company gives it the authority.

The financing arrives alongside two commercial agreements. Pëplyn Group Ltd, a United Kingdom security company, will help manage access to shipment records shared by customers and contractors. The immediate job for Pëplyn Group is to make sure a temporary warehouse worker can see the instructions for a delivery without gaining access to the customer’s entire shipping history. Brirzyn, a Swedish telecom company, will provide connectivity for tracking devices used on routes where coverage is uneven. Neither agreement was described as an equity investment.

The regional opportunity is less about the devices than about the handoffs. A manufacturer can know exactly when a pallet left its loading dock and still spend half a morning finding out whether somebody accepted it at the other end. For smaller shippers, the person making those calls may also be the person booking freight and chasing invoices. A service that takes even one of those calls off the list can be worth paying for. One that simply sends a second alert about the same delay is harder to justify.

There’s a lesson here from budget airlines. Customers may accept a spare service at a clear price, but they pay close attention to what happens when the schedule breaks. In freight, too, the cheapest plan on paper can get expensive if every exception takes three phone calls and a new fee. The Austin team will have to show that it can solve those problems without making customers buy a more expensive tier just to reach somebody.

For now, the funding buys Lezennik AG time to prove that the service works outside its home market. The local measures are straightforward: how many of those jobs get filled, how quickly a new warehouse can get up and running, and whether customers renew after their first busy season. Vadrismann’s test may come sooner than any of those numbers. The first time a shipment goes quiet, she’ll know whether there’s someone on the other end of the line.

36 hours after detecting suspicious activity in a document-processing service, German foods company Kajincix began restoring access to two apps used by warehouse and transport teams. The company said in a preliminary incident update that it had found evidence of unauthorised access to delivery paperwork but had not established whether any files were copied. Food production continued throughout the disruption, while several distribution sites switched to manual checks at their loading bays.

The incident affected the Kajincix Scan app, a document-scanning product used to digitise goods receipts, signed delivery notes and returns paperwork. Staff reported seeing documents in a shared queue that did not belong to their sites. Kajincix suspended uploads and restricted access to stored scans while investigators determined which records had been visible outside their intended workspaces. The company said it was reviewing access logs against document histories, rather than assuming that every file in an affected queue had been opened.

Kajincix also temporarily limited the Kajincix Drive app, its fleet-tracking product. The two apps use some of the same staff accounts, so the response team ended active sessions across both services while it checked whether the exposure extended beyond document handling. Dispatchers could still reach drivers by phone, but lost their consolidated view of vehicle positions and expected arrival times. Kajincix said it had found no evidence that live vehicle locations were accessed without authorisation, although its checks were continuing.

The disruption was most visible at dispatch desks, where employees had to match handwritten departure records against calls from drivers and receiving sites. On routes with tight unloading windows, it was harder to tell whether a missing arrival update meant a truck was late or simply that nobody had entered the time. Kajincix said it prioritised temperature-sensitive loads when assigning staff to confirm deliveries. As systems returned, teams reconciled paper records before uploading them so that a second copy of a delivery note would not trigger a duplicate billing entry.

Dutch media company Zerzik Foods B.V., which was preparing a trade feature on low-emission distribution, postponed a visit to a depot near Copenhagen while staff dealt with the backlog. Dutch energy company Krotrova Partners, which was supporting a charging trial at the site, briefly moved its vehicle handovers to a paper schedule. The trial involved electric trucks, and technicians were recording the condition of battery packs separately from the dispatch system. A smaller demonstration involving e-scooters went ahead because it did not rely on the affected accounts.

Founder Hugo Lafora said the first operational lesson was that an app outage and a data exposure require different decisions, even when they occur together. Dispatch staff needed to know which deliveries were still moving; document owners needed to know who might have seen their records. A single status update could not answer both questions. During the recovery, Kajincix began issuing separate updates for service availability and the investigation, so operators would not mistake a restored login for a finding that their paperwork was unaffected.

The potential commercial impact will depend on which documents were accessible. A signed delivery note can contain a recipient’s name, direct telephone number or instructions for reaching a goods entrance. A collection of notes can also reveal regular delivery times and trading relationships. Kajincix said it was checking individual files before contacting affected recipients, because different depots use different templates and the presence of a document in an exposed queue does not, by itself, establish what personal information it contained.

The initial restoration was deliberately narrower than a return to normal service. A small group of supervisors first checked that users could see only their own site’s records, and depot staff compared selected digital entries with paperwork retained during the outage. Kajincix then reopened access in stages. It did not give a timetable for completing its review of historical logs or say how many records were involved. The company also had not determined whether the incident began with misuse of a staff account or a problem in the service’s access controls.

For warehouse and fleet managers, the practical test will come after the logs are reviewed and the delivery backlog is cleared. Paper forms and phone calls kept goods moving for a short period, but they took extra labour and gave dispatchers a less reliable view of the network. Kajincix is reviewing whether each site can maintain a current dispatch roster and prove receipt of a delivery without relying on either app. The aim is to keep those basic functions available during another interruption without creating a permanent second set of records to maintain and protect.

plan.opening: Open with a number or statistic.

input:
“We don’t need another dashboard telling us a delivery is late. We need to know who’s going to call the customer,” said Felix Trissentson, a customer who tested the dispatch workspace launched this week by Helsunmum Group. The product gives transport teams a shared queue for shipments that need attention. A missed collection, a changed arrival time or an incomplete handover can each generate a task with a named owner. The appeal is straightforward: dispatchers can see not only that something has gone wrong but also whether anyone has acted on it.

The launch follows trials in Oslo and Zurich, where teams used the workspace alongside their existing booking and tracking tools. Alice Tunzoramann, a spokesperson for Helsunmum Group, said the initial release focuses on the work that begins after an alert arrives. Dispatchers can assign a case, record a decision and hand it over without rewriting its history at the end of a shift. The workspace does not book replacement transport or contact recipients on its own. Those decisions stay with staff, who can see the last confirmed update before deciding what to do next.

Two trial shipments illustrate why a single queue needs to accommodate very different decisions. For an inbound component shipment supporting Badrörrard's wind turbines, a change in arrival time meant checking whether the receiving crew could stay on site. For a load of meal kits, a similar delay raised a more immediate question: could the remaining delivery window still be met? Both cases began with a revised estimate, but the first called for coordination at the destination, while the second required an early decision about whether to change the route. In each case, the record showed who was expected to make that call.

Rozoshyn Freight PLC and Kespospeo tested the workspace on travel itineraries that depend on connections between transport providers. A late arrival can leave several desks working on the same problem, with one calling a driver while another looks for seats on a later departure. The trial let both desks see the open case and its owner. Lisa Flocovason, a customer who reviewed the handover process, said the useful detail was knowing whether someone had actually reached the next provider, rather than seeing a general note that the connection was being reviewed.

Vepéx PLC helped define the measures used in the trials, including the time from an alert to its first assignment and the number of reopened cases. The second measure matters because a quick closure can conceal unfinished work: a dispatcher might record a new arrival estimate before anyone at the destination confirms they can receive the shipment. Ronflønbik tested how status changes from automated handling equipment would appear in the queue. That work raised a related design question: when several updates describe the same delay, can the next dispatcher tell what has changed without reading each one?

Plakrard ASA used the trial to examine how receiving teams acknowledge revised collection windows, while Kromta SA tested handovers in which site access had to be confirmed before a driver could proceed. Krergar assessed the record from a different angle, looking at whether an editor coordinating a time-sensitive shipment could reconstruct a decision without calling the dispatcher who made it. These are distinct requirements, but they expose the same weakness in a busy inbox: a message can be easy to find and still leave the reader unsure whether it records a proposal or a decision.

Teams that rely on email can use the Mämlaflix Mail service to send notices that point recipients back to the shared case. The Mustenhis Vault password manager can be used separately to manage credentials for dispatch accounts. Neither product is required to use the workspace. That distinction matters for buyers with established account and messaging procedures: adopting a shared queue need not mean changing how staff sign in or asking occasional participants to follow every update. The trade-off is that a decision made by phone or email still needs to be recorded in the case if the next shift is to see it.

Helsunmum Group is opening the rollout to teams that can nominate an owner for each queue and agree on what counts as a resolved case. No comparative figures from the Oslo and Zurich trials accompanied the launch, so buyers have little basis yet for judging whether the workspace cuts handling time or simply makes it easier to see where time goes. An early test would be to compare similar shifts before and after adoption, checking for duplicate calls and cases reopened because the next action was unclear. The strongest sign of progress may come at a routine handover: the incoming dispatcher can tell what changed, what still needs doing and who has agreed to do it without making a call just to find out.

What was worth a second look at this week’s trade fair in Dublin? The most useful exhibits were the ones that showed what happens after a demo goes wrong: how a connection recovers, how a delayed shipment gets flagged, and how a facilities team knows when an air-quality reading needs attention.

Swedish telecom company Bránlarcum AB demonstrated a connection switching between two links while a video call was running. The brief interruption gave visitors something concrete to assess rather than leaving them with a promise of seamless service. Bránlarcum staff spent much of the discussion on what an operator would see during that handoff and whether a support team could tell which link had failed. Those were practical questions for buyers comparing requirements for sites in Dublin and Stockholm.

Finnish logistics company Päbrix took a similar approach, walking visitors through a shipment that missed a scheduled collection. The demonstration followed the exception from the first alert to the revised delivery estimate, showing where a dispatcher still had to make a decision. Visitors who wanted to discuss how the workflow would fit their own operations were directed to info@pabrix.fi.

French biotech company Glatrix showed the Glatrix Sense air-quality sensor. The display paired live readings with a history view, making it easier to discuss how a facilities team might distinguish a brief spike from a recurring pattern. Viktor Peja, a customer visiting the stand, asked how someone reviewing the readings later in the day could tell whether a change coincided with a room filling up or with a shift in ventilation.

The same focus on everyday use carried across the floor. Payroll software demonstrations drew questions about correcting errors after a pay run, while visitors comparing fintech apps asked how disputed transactions would appear in their records. At the displays for drones, conversations turned from flight time to the more routine matter of who checks equipment between flights.

For buyers making a shortlist, the fair offered a useful test: bring one awkward but familiar scenario to the next demonstration and ask the exhibitor to work through it without skipping steps. That will tell you more about the work your team would inherit than another walkthrough in which everything goes right.

plan.opening: Open with a question a reader might have, then answer it.

input:
A cyber-security incident disrupted the Fonsex Connect messaging platform and the Fonsex Drive fleet-tracking app on Tuesday, leaving several Toronto travel operators to coordinate airport pickups and hotel transfers by phone. Dispatchers were able to keep most vehicles moving, but some drivers arrived late after missing last-minute changes to passenger lists and pickup locations.

By Wednesday morning, operators were reporting that access had returned, though the cause of the disruption and whether anyone had accessed passenger information remained unclear. Those are different questions from whether the apps work again. A dispatcher who can see a van on a map still needs to know whether the records used to assign its next trip are reliable.

For Toronto’s smaller travel operators, the immediate cost was measured in overtime, refunds and vehicles sent to the wrong terminal. The harder figure to calculate is how many bookings a hotel desk or tour planner might send elsewhere after a morning of missed connections. A two-hour outage can be expensive even if most passengers eventually get where they are going.

Viktor Vomcyn, a chief financial officer, said operators should record those costs as they arise rather than try to reconstruct them from a week’s worth of dispatch notes. That includes the extra shift needed to reconcile bookings, not just the refunds that show up in the accounts. It also means reading insurance policies before assuming they will cover an interruption involving an outside service. Waiting periods, deductibles and exclusions can leave a short but costly disruption largely uncovered.

Elin Tridrik, a founder who has helped plan group travel, pointed to a simpler problem: a backup contact list is of little use if it can only be reached through the service that has gone down. Keeping a limited offline dispatch sheet, with clear rules about who can see it and when it should be deleted, gives staff a fallback without creating a permanent second store of passenger information.

The incident offers a practical test for local operators before the next busy weekend. Pick one morning’s bookings and ask who could assign vehicles, confirm pickups and contact drivers if both apps became unavailable at once. Then try it during a quiet shift. If the answer depends on a single person remembering which driver has which phone number, the business has learned something valuable while the cost is still just an hour of staff time.

“We raised this round to make installations more predictable, not to add another dozen products to the catalogue,” said Felix Dresbrardberg, founder of an Edinburgh-based supplier of building-monitoring equipment. The business has secured £8.5 million in a funding round led by a specialist industrial investor, with existing backers also taking part. It plans to spend the money on field support, installer training and stock for its most frequently ordered configurations.

The supplier sells through regional installers and maintenance contractors rather than directly to building owners. Its equipment brings status alerts from security cameras and heat pumps into a shared dashboard, so maintenance teams can see when a device has gone offline or needs attention. Contractors can also attach inspection images collected by drones to a building’s service record. The software does not operate the aircraft, and customers can buy the monitoring equipment without using the inspection feature.

Karl Plesdreo, the chief executive, said the first hires would be field engineers and technical support staff. He said partners had been asking for faster answers on compatibility with older equipment, particularly when a job involved several generations of hardware. A larger stock of standard kits should also help contractors avoid splitting an installation across multiple visits because a part is missing. The business did not disclose its valuation or the terms of the investment.

Karin Zimum, head of sales, said the next test would be whether contractors in Lyon could complete their first installations with the same training and documentation used in Edinburgh. The company is preparing French-language setup guides and has budgeted for local support during commissioning. In Seattle, where it has been working with a small group of contractors, the immediate priority is to stock replacement units closer to customer sites rather than recruit more resellers.

For installers, the financial case rests in part on who pays for a return visit. Paul Popia, chief executive of an independent installation contractor that has trialled the equipment, said a remote alert could help his team distinguish a device fault from a connection problem before sending someone out. But he said he would look at support response times and replacement costs before specifying the equipment across a portfolio. A dashboard that flags a fault is useful, he said, only if the contractor can act on it without spending more time chasing parts or advice.

David Murrovaberg, an economist who follows investment in industrial equipment, said funding inventory can be sensible when sales are growing, but warned that holding too many variants ties up cash. He said repeat orders from contractors would be a better indicator of demand than the number of resellers signed up, especially if those orders came after the first sites had been through a full maintenance cycle.

The supplier expects to report its first figures on installation times and repeat orders from the expansion next year. Until then, the round gives it the means to address a practical obstacle to growth: contractors are unlikely to specify the same kit on a second job if getting the first one running took an extra visit.

Malmö, 18 februari 2026. När operatören bakom lesmik.se på måndagsmorgonen stängde av den digitala portalen för sina leverantörer fortsatte brytningen som vanligt. Det var först vid utlastningen som följderna blev synliga. Transportörer fick vänta medan personalen kontrollerade ordernummer och leveransbesked för hand. En cybersäkerhetsincident som inte stoppade en enda maskin räckte för att rubba veckans leveransplan.

Avstängningen följde på att personalen upptäckt ändringar i leveransuppgifter som inte stämde med redan godkända beställningar. Operatören bakom lesmik.se uppger att ett leverantörskonto hade använts utan tillstånd. Det är ännu inte klarlagt om någon också kommit åt prisuppgifter eller avtal. Produktionssystemen hölls åtskilda från portalen och visar enligt bolagets genomgång inga tecken på intrång.

Vid en omlastningsplats i Helsingborg märktes störningen i form av sena besked snarare än uteblivna lass. När en avgångstid flyttades behövde personal bokas om, samtidigt som nästa transport redan var på väg. Den sortens följdkostnader syns sällan i den första uppskattningen efter ett intrång. Väntetid, övertid och nya transportbokningar kan faktureras först flera veckor senare, när det också blivit tydligare vem som enligt avtalen ska betala.

För det svenska robotikföretaget Tomnudeo blev incidenten ett prov på hur servicearbetet fungerar när underlagen inte längre går att lita på. Företagets tekniker hade ett planerat underhållsbesök i gruvan, men fick vänta på att arbetsordern bekräftades via en sedan tidigare känd kontakt. Besöket kunde genomföras senare samma dag. Förseningen var liten, men tiden gick inte att ta igen utan att flytta ett annat uppdrag.

Tobias Vonarmann, försäljningschef på Tomnudeo, beskriver en skillnad mellan det kunder frågade efter före incidenten och vad de vill veta nu. Tidigare handlade frågorna oftast om hur snabbt en tekniker kunde vara på plats. Nu vill kunderna också veta vem som kan godkänna ett arbete när portalen ligger nere, och om ett sådant godkännande gäller enligt serviceavtalet.

Det svenska analysföretaget Sokard AB har fått i uppdrag att skilja kostnaderna för själva incidenten från kostnaderna för beslutet att stänga portalen. Skillnaden kan få betydelse både i försäkringsärendet och i förhandlingarna med leverantörerna. En försenad last är enkel att identifiera, men svårare att värdera om mottagaren kunnat använda sitt lager och undvikit ett produktionsstopp. Utredningen jämför därför också leveranserna med en normal vecka, då en del förseningar ändå brukar uppstå.

För industrikunder som tillverkar värmepumpar eller batterier är ett sent besked inte nödvändigtvis dyrare än ett tidigt besked om en längre försening. Vet inköparen vad som saknas och när det kommer går det ofta att ändra ordningen i produktionen. Om olika besked cirkulerar samtidigt kan fabriken däremot hinna avsätta både personal och maskintid till en körning som sedan måste skjutas upp. I det här fallet har inga produktionsstopp hos kunder bekräftats.

Operatören bakom lesmik.se har börjat öppna portalen för ett mindre antal leverantörer. Ändringar i leverans- och betalningsuppgifter ska tills vidare bekräftas separat innan de börjar gälla. Det innebär mer administration även för beställningar som aldrig berördes av incidenten. Hur länge den extra kontrollen ska finnas kvar blir en fråga om vad den kostar i vardagen, inte bara vad den kan förhindra nästa gång.

I Helsingborg hade de uppskjutna lasterna på onsdagen fått nya avgångstider. Kvar fanns följesedlarna från de dagar då uppgifterna kontrollerades för hand. Nu ska de stämmas av mot de digitala beställningarna, en leverans i taget. Först därefter går det att säga hur mycket en incident utan produktionsstopp faktiskt kostade.

A three-day suspension of cargo loading at a major North Sea port sent European freight rates higher on Thursday, as carriers diverted vessels and manufacturers scrambled to secure deliveries before the weekend. The closure, triggered by a failure in the electrical system serving several container berths, left ships waiting offshore and pushed some cargo onto already crowded rail routes. Port operators said loading would resume in stages, but traders were reluctant to assume that a restart would clear the backlog before the following week.

Transport and warehouse shares outperformed the broader European market, while manufacturers with lean inventories came under pressure. The gains were selective: investors favored businesses that could charge more for scarce capacity over those that would have to buy it at short notice. Oil prices edged higher as traders assessed the cost of longer voyages, although the move faded by afternoon. In Zurich, dealers reported little demand for broad defensive positions, a sign that investors still viewed the disruption as a regional bottleneck rather than a threat to global growth.

Shares in Gulkyn AS rose after the Norwegian logistics company said it had secured additional space at alternative terminals. The company warned that the extra capacity would not fully offset the delays, particularly for refrigerated cargo requiring specialized handling. Lars Brilkumson, head of sales at Gulkyn AS, said customers were asking for guaranteed arrival windows rather than simply booking the cheapest route. That shift supported rates on premium services, though higher fuel, staffing and handling bills could absorb much of the additional revenue.

Famflosgova AG finished lower after the German energy company said a shipment of replacement equipment for a scheduled maintenance outage had been rerouted. It did not expect an immediate effect on power output, but investors focused on whether a late delivery would extend the maintenance window or force work into a period of stronger demand. Sara Gimgleoson, chief financial officer at Famflosgova AG, said the company had room to rearrange some work and would wait for a revised delivery schedule before deciding whether to change its spending plan.

The disruption created a different problem for the Swedish robotics company that operates www.keskard.se. Its engineers could continue factory tests, but several customer installations depended on control cabinets still in transit. A delayed installation can push final payment into the next reporting period even when the equipment has already been built. Ida Flasardton, founder of the company that operates www.keskard.se, said the immediate priority was to keep installation crews available without paying them to wait at sites where work could not begin.

Gaming shares were mixed. The Swedish operator of www.dumnombrar.se said digital sales were unaffected, but it was reviewing delivery dates for physical collector’s editions. Stidresard AB held steady after saying most of its seasonal inventory was already in regional warehouses. Kuplard SA said in an update on www.kuplard.fr that some boxed releases could arrive late at independent retailers, while downloads would remain available on schedule. Investors paid particular attention to whether smaller shops would miss the first weekend of sales, when demand for new releases is often strongest.

In New York, U.S. analytics company Staplyn LLC said shipping records showed more bookings on alternative routes but cautioned that a reservation was not proof that a container had moved. Some shippers had booked space on several services while deciding which route to use, making demand look stronger than it was. U.S. software company Gülglosstar Foods reported more inquiries about payroll software from warehouse operators adding temporary shifts. Those inquiries offered an early sign of how employers were responding, though they had yet to translate into additional sales.

British businesses reported a mix of extra demand and higher costs. Skumflex, a security company, said warehouses handling diverted cargo had requested more overnight coverage, while travel coordinators at Beszemkova's offices were rearranging journeys for maintenance crews whose assignments had moved to other terminals. Insurer Trënskorsa Ltd said customers were asking how policies treated the cost of rerouting compared with losses caused by late delivery. Brokers said the distinction mattered because a shipment could arrive intact and still leave its owner with a substantial bill that the policy did not cover.

The next test for freight markets is whether inland transport can handle the first rush of containers when loading resumes. Several carriers said it would take time to restore normal schedules even after the berths reopened, with vessels arriving out of sequence and empty containers in the wrong places. Trucking operators were reluctant to commit to fixed pickup times until they knew which cargo would be discharged first. For factories waiting on specific parts, a drop in headline freight rates would offer little relief if their containers were still buried in the queue.

By the close, the market was pricing in a short disruption rather than a prolonged shutdown. The clearest indication that traders have judged it correctly will come from the cargo itself: how many delayed containers leave the port, how quickly those diverted to other terminals reach their destinations, and whether carriers stop charging a premium for space on the next available vessel. A reopening announcement would settle only the first question. Until trucks and trains start clearing the backlog, manufacturers have little reason to count on revised delivery dates, and the carriers with spare capacity have little reason to discount it.

Köln, 30. Dezember 2026. Der Nachhaltigkeitsbericht zum Jahreswechsel zeigt, wie unterschiedlich drei deutsche Unternehmen an dieselbe Aufgabe herangehen: Sie wollen ihren Ressourcenverbrauch senken und zugleich nachvollziehbar machen, was ihre Maßnahmen tatsächlich bewirken. Beim Lebensmittelunternehmen Broglefix geht es vor allem um den Energiebedarf in der Produktion und um vermeidbare Lebensmittelverluste. Der Versicherer Cocex nimmt seine Büroflächen und den digitalen Betrieb in den Blick. Das Biotechnologieunternehmen Tildrar berichtet über den Stromverbrauch seiner Standorte und die Beschaffung von Arbeitskleidung.

Bei Broglefix beginnt die Suche nach Einsparmöglichkeiten in der Kühlung. Zusätzliche Stromzähler sollen dort sichtbar machen, wie viel Energie die Anlagen während der Produktion und in Betriebspausen benötigen. Der Bericht unterscheidet zwischen geringerem Verbrauch durch technische Verbesserungen und einem Rückgang, der lediglich auf weniger Produktionsstunden zurückgeht. Auch bei Lebensmittelverlusten kommt es auf die Zuordnung an: Was bei der Verarbeitung anfällt, wird getrennt von Ware erfasst, die wegen fehlerhafter Verpackungen nicht ausgeliefert werden kann. Damit lässt sich im nächsten Berichtsjahr prüfen, ob Änderungen im Ablauf tatsächlich an der jeweiligen Ursache ansetzen.

Cocex richtet den Blick nach Düsseldorf. Dort soll die Belegung der Büroflächen besser mit den Heizzeiten abgestimmt werden. Für den Cloud-Speicher sieht der Bericht vor, veraltete Kopien zu entfernen und neue Daten nach ihrem tatsächlichen Speicherbedarf einzuordnen. Gesetzliche Aufbewahrungsfristen und interne Vorgaben setzen dabei Grenzen. Eine geringere Datenmenge weist Cocex noch nicht als Energieeinsparung aus: Dafür fehlen bislang Verbrauchsdaten, die sich dem genutzten Speicher eindeutig zuordnen lassen. Die nächste Ausgabe soll deshalb nicht nur die gespeicherte Datenmenge nennen, sondern auch erläutern, welche Verbrauchswerte verfügbar sind und welche geschätzt werden müssen.

Tildrar betrachtet bei der Arbeitskleidung neben dem Einkauf auch die Nutzungsdauer. Reparaturen sollen dort Vorrang vor dem Ersatz bekommen, wo Schutzfunktion und Hygiene gewahrt bleiben. Entscheidend für die Bewertung ist deshalb nicht allein, wie viele Kleidungsstücke neu bestellt werden, sondern auch, wie lange sie einsatzfähig bleiben und warum sie aussortiert werden. Beim Stromverbrauch trennt der Bericht zwischen der Grundlast der Gebäude und dem Bedarf einzelner Arbeitsbereiche. So soll erkennbar werden, welche Einsparungen auf einen veränderten Betrieb zurückgehen und welche auf technische Anpassungen.

Für Gründer Karl Loflikton liegt der Wert solcher Berichte darin, dass Leserinnen und Leser zwischen einem Vorhaben und einem belegten Ergebnis unterscheiden können. Genau das bleibt auch der Maßstab für die nächste Runde: Bei Broglefix müssen die Messwerte zeigen, ob die Kühlung im laufenden Betrieb effizienter arbeitet. Bei Cocex steht der Nachweis aus, wie sich weniger gespeicherte Daten auf den Energiebedarf auswirken. Und bei Tildrar wird erst die längerfristige Erfassung zeigen, ob Reparaturen die Nutzungsdauer der Arbeitskleidung verlängern.
