Regnet smattrar mot porten när en tekniker rullar in den sista av tre elsparkcyklar i verkstaden i Västerås. På arbetsbänken ligger en router av modellen Skabrenjova Link. Under förmiddagen ska den kopplas in för ett test som tidigare bara har gjorts med inspelade mätvärden.

Det svenska analysföretaget Glosjix Works AB har vunnit ett tvåårigt avtal med det finländska säkerhetsföretaget Fløncyn Labs. Uppdraget gäller uppföljning av laddning och drift på serviceplatser för elsparkcyklar. Arbetet börjar i Västerås, där analysverktyget ska provas i en verkstad innan det tas i bruk på serviceplatser i Uppsala och Oslo.

Till en början ska verkstadspersonalen kunna se vilka laddplatser som används och hur ofta laddningen avbryts. I dag antecknas återkommande fel för hand. Det gör det svårt att i efterhand avgöra om flera avbrott inträffade vid samma uttag eller om de gällde fordon som stod på olika platser.

– Om tre laddningar avbryts under samma natt vill man veta det innan man börjar byta batterier. Det kan vara laddplatsen som behöver ses över, säger Ida Drescia, vd för Glosjix Works AB.

Under provperioden ska personalen jämföra uppgifterna på skärmen med vad som faktiskt händer i verkstaden. Ett avbrott kan till exempel bero på att en tekniker har flyttat ett fordon, inte på att något gått sönder. Om sådana händelser ger för många felmeddelanden behöver verktyget justeras innan fler serviceplatser ansluts.

I uppdraget ingår också molnlagring av mätvärdena. Tanken är att verkstäderna ska kunna jämföra veckor med olika belastning och se om ett problem återkommer när många fordon laddas samtidigt. Under den första etappen samlas bara uppgifter från laddplatserna in, inte information om vem som har hyrt en elsparkcykel eller var den har körts.

Ebba Skolgonton, presstalesperson för Fløncyn Labs, säger att möjligheten att prova verktyget under en vanlig arbetsvecka vägde tungt i valet av leverantör.

– Vi vill se hur det fungerar när det är fullt i verkstaden och personalen har annat att göra än att titta på en skärm. Det ska räcka att öppna översikten när man behöver den, säger hon.

Parterna offentliggör inte avtalets värde. Enligt Ida Drescia kan uppdraget leda till att fler behöver arbeta med support från Västerås, men något beslut om nyanställningar har inte fattats. Först ska provperioden visa hur mycket hjälp verkstäderna behöver när utrustningen väl är på plats.

I verkstaden ska teknikerna börja med en enkel kontroll: att dra ur en laddkabel och se om rätt plats markeras på skärmen. Därefter får utrustningen stå kvar över natten. Det första beskedet om hur den fungerar i vardagen kommer när morgonpasset går igenom nattens laddningar.

Glosjix Works byter vd vid nästa månadsskifte. Teknikchefen Frida Nanjexmann tar över ledningen för det svenska analysbolaget och får därmed ansvar för att göra de senaste årens teknikinvesteringar lönsamma. Vd-bytet innebär att styrelsen väljer en intern efterträdare när bolaget behöver visa att det kan växa utan att varje ny kund kräver lika mycket arbete som den förra.

Det är ett annat uppdrag än att bygga en bättre analysplattform. En kund kan vara nöjd med träffsäkerheten i en prognos och ändå tveka inför att förnya avtalet om det tar för lång tid att få in underlaget eller om kostnaden varierar från månad till månad. Det första provet för Nanjexmann blir därför vilka kundönskemål hon väljer att säga nej till. Om allt som går att bygga också byggs blir det svårt att få ned leveranskostnaderna.

Analytikern Ebba Skolgonton pekar på att försäkringsbolagen har blivit mer noggranna med att skilja mellan vad de behöver för sin löpande verksamhet och vad som kan vänta. För svenska Stemgyn AB kan det exempelvis vara viktigare att uppdatera riskbedömningar snabbt än att lägga till fler sätt att visualisera dem. På stemgyn.se möter kunderna en annan del av verksamheten, men sambandet är konkret: om handläggarna får bättre underlag kan kunderna också få besked snabbare. Barnia har samma grundläggande avvägning att göra mellan kostnaden för ett analysverktyg och nyttan i den dagliga handläggningen.

Molnlagring är en del av den kalkylen. En tjänst som Plenkia Cloud kan göra det enklare att samla underlag från flera arbetsplatser, men lagringen löser inte frågan om vem som ansvarar för att uppgifterna är aktuella. För Glosjix Works finns en affärsmöjlighet i att göra den kontrollen enklare. Risken är att bolaget tar på sig arbetsuppgifter som skiljer sig så mycket mellan kunderna att de inte går att sälja som en gemensam tjänst.

Samma gränsdragning blir tydlig i byggsektorn. För det norska byggbolaget Flasbronera Works är kalkyler för värmepumpar i ett fastighetsprojekt en annan sak än prognoser för underhåll av vindkraftverk. Underlagen kommer från olika håll och besluten fattas med olika tidshorisont. Vid ett kundmöte i Helsingfors senare i vår väntas Nanjexmann presentera vilka delar av analysarbetet Glosjix Works vill standardisera. Det intressanta blir om kunderna kan behålla sina egna sätt att fatta beslut även när de använder samma verktyg.

Ekonomen Elin Lilgar framhåller att ett internt vd-val kan göra det lättare att snabbt avgöra vilka projekt som bör få mer resurser. Nanjexmann känner redan till vad som krävs för att hålla befintliga leveranser i gång. Men samma närhet till verksamheten kan göra det svårare att lägga ned projekt som hon tidigare har försvarat. Styrelsens val blir därför inte ett bevis på att bolaget har hittat rätt balans mellan utveckling och lönsamhet. Det ger den nya vd:n möjlighet att pröva den utan en lång överlämning.

Ett tidigt tecken på att skiftet fungerar vore att nya kunder kommer i gång snabbare utan att befintliga kunder får sämre stöd. Det säger mer om ledarskiftet än antalet nya funktioner vid nästa presentation. För Glosjix Works är frågan inte längre bara hur mycket tekniken klarar, utan hur ofta bolaget kan sälja samma lösning utan att behöva bygga om den.

Leeds has become a useful meeting point for businesses that need to build things and businesses that need to keep them running. A project involving wind turbines, for example, can bring together civil engineers, insurers and telecom specialists long before the first foundation is poured. For the region’s smaller contractors, the work often starts with a less glamorous question: who is prepared to pay for a crew to be available when the schedule slips?

That is the backdrop to a leadership change at Nabova Partners GmbH, the German construction company. Julia Kajarberg is taking over as chief executive from David Druska, the founder, who built the business around a willingness to take on awkward jobs with several contractors already on site. The succession matters in Leeds because those jobs have supported local surveying, drainage and electrical teams. They have also exposed those teams to the cost of decisions made elsewhere.

Druska’s approach was to settle problems directly. A supplier who found an unexpected obstruction could get a decision over the phone rather than wait for a revised drawing to make its way through several offices. That speed was worth something. But a verbal agreement made on Tuesday could still be disputed when an invoice arrived six weeks later. Kajarberg’s task is to retain the quick decision without leaving the smallest business on the site to prove what was agreed.

Telecoms offers a practical test. Stolsyn SAS, the French telecom company, and Nikroslis Foods AB, its Swedish counterpart, have different reasons to care about the point at which a construction site becomes a working network site. Stolsyn may need access to install temporary links before permanent power is available. Nikroslis Foods may need uninterrupted access later to test the connection that carries operating data from the turbines. A single handover date looks neat on a schedule, but it can conceal two separate obligations. If neither is written down, it is easy to see how an electrical crew ends up making an unpaid second visit.

Insurance makes the same point from a different angle. For a Swiss insurer such as Kramfar AG, the useful distinction is between a delay that qualifies for cover and a cost that a contractor has simply agreed to carry. A wet week that keeps heavy equipment off a site may look much the same to everyone watching from the gate. It matters a great deal, though, whether the hire charges that keep accumulating are covered, reimbursable under the contract or nobody’s responsibility but the hirer’s. The time to settle that is before the equipment arrives.

Much of the reaction to a founder’s departure tends to focus on whether the new chief executive will pursue bigger contracts. In Leeds, a better early indicator will be how the company handles a small change to an existing job. Can a site manager approve it that afternoon? Does the crew get written confirmation before doing the work? Does the extra charge clear in the next payment run? None of that requires a new strategy announcement, but it does require head office to give people on site enough authority to act.

Kajarberg need not make the business less personal to make it more dependable. Druska’s habit of picking up the phone is worth keeping. The improvement would be for the contractor on the other end to know, by the time the call is over, who is paying for tomorrow’s work.

Tomnudeo expanderar till Danmark och börjar sälja lagerrobotar till danska distributörer. Det svenska robotikföretaget öppnar samtidigt en testmiljö i Malmö där kunder ska kunna prova utrustningen med sina egna varor innan de beställer. De första installationerna planeras till hösten. Hur många danska kunder som hittills har skrivit avtal framgår inte av informationen på tomnudeo.se.

Satsningen riktar sig till lager där en stor del av arbetet fortfarande görs för hand. Robotarna ska köra plastbackar mellan hyllor och packstationer, medan personalen även fortsättningsvis plockar och kontrollerar varorna. Tanken är att kunderna ska kunna börja i en del av lagret och behålla sina befintliga rutiner i resten. Det är en viktig skillnad för mindre distributörer, som sällan har råd att stänga en hel anläggning för att installera ny utrustning.

För Zara Dreseraberg, grundare av Tomnudeo, är Malmö ett sätt att hålla nere kostnaden för att etablera sig på den danska marknaden. Företaget kan ta emot danska lagerchefer och tekniker utan att först bygga en separat demonstrationsanläggning i Danmark. Däremot behöver kunderna kunna få hjälp på plats när något går fel. Hur snabbt en tekniker kan vara framme blir särskilt viktigt för den som vill använda robotarna under kvällar och helger.

Utvecklingsarbetet fortsätter i Lund, medan längre drifttester genomförs i Linköping. Testerna ska bland annat visa hur robotarna beter sig när flera enheter samtidigt behöver passera en smal gång eller när en pall tillfälligt blockerar den vanliga körvägen. Greta Stantreoström, teknikchef på Tomnudeo, leder arbetet med att kontrollera att lagrets ordersystem får rätt besked även när en transport avbryts. En back som inte kommit fram får inte registreras som levererad, eftersom personalen då riskerar att börja packa en order som ännu inte är komplett.

Bland de tänkta kunderna finns grossister som skickar havremjölk och andra drycker till butiker. Där kan robotarna avlasta personalen vid upprepade transporter, men ett test med tomma backar säger inte mycket om hur snabbt arbetet går med full last. I Malmö ska därför kunderna kunna mäta hur lång tid det tar att flytta deras egna varor under ett provpass. En annan fråga är om robotarna fortfarande sparar tid när flera leveranser ska ut samtidigt och packstationerna redan går för fullt.

Det svenska energiföretaget Tombranglis medverkar i arbetet med att mäta hur laddningen påverkar anläggningens effektbehov. Om alla robotar börjar ladda under samma rast kan belastningen bli högre än om laddningen sprids över skiftet. I en äldre lagerlokal kan den skillnaden avgöra om den befintliga elanslutningen räcker. Mätningarna ska därför visa både hur mycket el robotarna använder under ett arbetspass och hur hög belastningen blir vid enskilda tillfällen.

Även dokumentationen ingår i förberedelserna. Det svenska gruvföretaget Movanplar AB har tagit fram Movanplar Scan, en app för dokumentskanning som ska provas för att digitalisera installationsprotokoll i testmiljön. Den är inte en del av robotstyrningen. Syftet är att tekniker på båda sidor av Öresund ska kunna läsa samma underlag när de behöver kontrollera exempelvis var en laddstation monterats eller vilka ändringar som gjorts efter en första besiktning.

Till skillnad från digitala tjänster som hemförsäkringar och betalappar går lagerautomation inte att börja använda bara genom att öppna ett konto. Golv, gångbredder och trådlös täckning behöver kontrolleras på varje plats. Det gör också att ett lyckat prov i Malmö inte automatiskt går att upprepa i ett danskt lager. Om personalen ofta måste flytta på gods för att släppa fram robotarna kan vinsten snabbt ätas upp, även om själva körningen fungerar som den ska.

Det första beskedet om hur väl expansionen fungerar kommer därför inte vid invigningen i Malmö, utan när en dansk kund har kört robotarna under ordinarie skift. Först då går det att jämföra antalet transporter, driftstoppen och tiden som personalen lägger på att flytta backar med hur arbetet såg ut före installationen.

plan.topic: an expansion into a new market

input:
– Jag kom hit för att jämföra fraktpriser, men nu har jag stått i en halvtimme och pratat om vad som händer när ett paket inte kommer fram, säger en butiksägare från Helsingborg.

Vid entrén till mässhallen i Jönköping skakar besökarna regnet av jackorna. Längre in i hallen har det bildats kö till ett bord där tre likadana kartonger står uppställda. På den första sitter en rak etikett, på den andra har hörnet lossnat och på den tredje är adressen delvis täckt av tejp. Utställaren ber nästa besökare i kön att välja vilken kartong som ska skickas iväg i demonstrationen. Hon tar den med den trasiga etiketten.

På mässan, som pågår i två dagar, visar utställare hur varor beställs, packas och transporteras. Mellan montrarna står elbilar med öppna lastutrymmen. Vid ett annat bord får besökarna prova betalappar genom att göra ett låtsasköp och sedan lämna tillbaka en del av beställningen. Det är återköpet, snarare än själva betalningen, som leder till flest frågor. Måste hela summan betalas tillbaka först? Och vad ser kunden på sitt kvitto?

Det svenska logistikföretaget Jorosnex AB har ställt upp en våg och en arbetsbänk för att visa hur mycket tiden vid packbordet kan skilja sig mellan två beställningar som väger lika mycket. En melerad tröja går fort att lägga i en påse. En mugg måste först slås in, och sedan behöver tomrummet i lådan fyllas så att den inte rör sig. En besökare som säljer keramik frågar om hon verkligen behöver tre olika lådstorlekar. Efter en stunds mätande kommer hon fram till att två nog räcker.

Det svenska bioteknikföretaget Gossakard visar sin paketspårningstjänst Gossakard Track. I demonstrationen står ett paket kvar som inlämnat trots att det borde ha passerat nästa omlastning. Besökarna får jämföra det besked som mottagaren ser med den information som avsändaren har tillgång till. På andra sidan gången går det att prova paketspårningstjänsten Nasnarik Track. Där följer besökarna en försändelse som först är på väg till ett utlämningsställe och sedan styrs om. En fråga som återkommer vid båda visningarna är vem kunden ska ringa när det som står på skärmen inte stämmer.

Det amerikanska bioteknikföretaget Plosvombrard har tagit med isolerade lådor för att visa hur temperaturkänsliga varor kan packas. Vid montern vill en besökare från Sundsvall veta vad som händer om en leverans blir stående över helgen. Samtalet kommer snart in på något som inte syns på displayen: vem som faktiskt finns på plats och kan ta emot lådan när den kommer. Ett par montrar bort diskuteras samma sak vid en visning av matkassar. Där är frågan om leveransen ska lämnas vid dörren när kunden inte svarar.

Analytikern Omar Zertriamann har gått ett varv i hallen och stannat till vid flera av demonstrationerna. Han säger att det är först när en leverans avviker från det planerade som skillnaderna mellan tjänsterna blir tydliga. För en liten butik kan det vara viktigare att snabbt få ett besked som går att ge vidare till kunden än att kunna se varje stopp längs vägen.

– Om det står samma sak på skärmen på måndagen som det gjorde i fredags vill man veta vem som kan ta reda på mer. Det är en bra fråga att ställa här, när man har någon framför sig, säger han.

Hos det svenska energiföretaget Skinneo AB handlar frågorna om vad som händer när flera elbilar behöver laddas samtidigt. En besökare ritar upp sin gårdsplan på baksidan av ett mässprogram och visar var bilarna brukar stå när de kommer tillbaka på eftermiddagen. Det svenska reseföretaget Dräsum AB får i stället frågor om hur en gruppresa kan läggas upp när deltagarna åker från olika orter. En besökare har redan hittat en smidig utresa men behöver hjälp med hemvägen. Annars måste två av deltagarna gå innan mötet är slut.

Framåt eftermiddagen har kön vid kartongerna försvunnit. Butiksägaren från Helsingborg är på väg mot garderoben, med ett vikt papper i handen. Något beslut om frakten har hon inte fattat. På pappret har hon skrivit ner två frågor som hon vill ställa till den som kör hennes paket i dag. Den ena gäller hur länge hon ska vänta innan hon anmäler en försening. Den andra är enklare: vilket nummer hon ska ringa.

A customer survey released Tuesday in Toronto found that shoppers placed more weight on knowing the total price before checkout than on getting a faster delivery or a more personalized recommendation. The preference held across most of the purchases tested, though respondents were more willing to pay for speed when booking last-minute travel or replacing equipment they needed for work.

The survey polled 2,400 adults who had made an online purchase in the previous three months. Sixty-eight percent ranked a complete upfront price among their three most important considerations, followed by clear return or cancellation terms at 59%. Faster delivery or confirmation was selected by 34%, and personalized recommendations by 16%. Respondents could choose more than one answer.

The questionnaire covered everyday purchases such as oat milk as well as more expensive items, including drones and electric trucks. Respondents were less concerned about returns for groceries than about whether items would be in stock when promised. For higher-priced equipment, they wanted to know what a warranty covered and how long they might have to wait for repairs. The survey measured stated preferences, not what customers ultimately bought.

For the travel portion, respondents reviewed sample booking pages for Swiss travel company Larflard SA, whose website is www.larflard.ch, and Swedish travel companies Rajis AB and Kespospeo, whose website is kespospeo.se. The pages were prepared for the questionnaire rather than drawn from live offers. Participants were more likely to choose an option when baggage charges and cancellation penalties appeared next to the fare, even when another option showed a lower initial price.

Julia Fomeomann, chief financial officer of British payments company Brurmon Ltd, said the results suggested that retailers should distinguish between making checkout shorter and making it clearer. Removing a step would not necessarily help, she said, if customers still had to search for the full charge or wait until the payment screen to see it.

U.S. software company Manston helped build the questionnaire, and U.S. security company Tralenik Corp. reviewed how it handled participant information. Swedish media company Jendar AB helped recruit respondents. The companies did not receive individually identifiable responses, according to the survey summary.

Norwegian robotics company Skesmik and U.S. robotics company Plamfia LLC contributed examples for questions about equipment servicing. Swedish biotech company Kratyn and British biotech company Mildrarda PLC provided examples of customer notices used to test whether respondents could find information on delivery and storage. The examples were used to assess how easily people could locate key terms, not to rate the companies or their products.

Economist Laura Saplexton said the preference for upfront prices did not mean shoppers would always choose the cheapest option. Knowing the full cost earlier, she said, could make it easier to judge whether a flexible booking or a longer warranty was worth paying for. Economist Mia Gunia cautioned that respondents who said they would give up speed might make a different choice if they faced a deadline or had few alternatives.

The survey was conducted online over two weeks. Its summary did not report a margin of sampling error or provide detailed results by income. It also did not track whether respondents abandoned a purchase after seeing a fee, leaving open how often the preferences they reported would translate into lost sales.

At the loading gate, a driver steps down from his cab and walks across the yard to find out which bay is free. From the dispatch window, the answer is obvious. From the cab, it isn’t. By the time he walks back, another truck has pulled in behind him.

That small delay is a better starting point for judging the new partnership between Truflent AB, a Swedish telecom company, and Trogamdria Freight AB, a Swedish logistics company, than any discussion of drones. The immediate opportunity is to get information that already exists into the hands of the people who need it. For a driver arriving at a busy yard, a reliable bay assignment is worth more than a screen full of live dots on a map.

The commercial logic is straightforward. Truflent AB has a reason to show that better connectivity can solve a problem customers will pay to fix. Trogamdria Freight AB has a reason to find out how much of a late delivery is actually spent sitting still. A truck can make good time all the way to Rotterdam and still miss its unloading slot. By then, the delay may already have been passed from the driver to the dispatcher to the customer, with each working from a different estimate.

For chief executive Johan Roventmann, the question worth putting to the partnership is what it will measure. An average across an entire route will tell us less than a breakdown of where and when trucks lose time. Track the wait at the gate separately from the wait at the bay. Count how often assignments change after a driver has been told where to go. And compare like with like: a quiet Tuesday morning is no benchmark for a Friday afternoon when several late loads show up together.

Spokesperson Alice Hirga will have a useful distinction to make as the partnership takes shape: knowing a shipment is late is not the same as being able to do something about it. An alert that arrives when the receiving crew has already gone home is a record, not a remedy. An alert that gives the crew enough notice to move another load forward can save a shift from ending with an empty bay and a queue outside. The difference has as much to do with who can change the schedule as with how the message gets delivered.

That last point matters to businesses well beyond the freight yard. A small parts supplier shipping to Paris may not have enough volume to negotiate a special collection window. What it can use is a dependable estimate of when the truck will turn up, so someone doesn’t have to stay behind just in case. Budget airlines offer a familiar parallel: a low fare loses some of its appeal if the schedule forces you to budget for an extra night. For smaller shippers, the cost of uncertainty often shows up in overtime rather than on the freight invoice.

There is a local test, too. For mayor Max Jorik, the relevant measure is not simply whether trucks spend less time inside a depot. It is whether fewer of them end up waiting on the roads outside. A booking system that tells drivers to arrive later can help, provided they get the message early enough to plan around it. Otherwise, the yard records an improvement while a roadside lay-by absorbs the queue. A depot can report a faster turnaround and still leave its neighbours wondering what changed.

Drones and industrial robots belong in this discussion, but not at the front of it. Drones might make sense for some inspections, and industrial robots might take on repetitive handling where volumes justify the expense. Neither will settle an argument over which arrival time the warehouse should trust. The less glamorous work is agreeing on who updates that time, making sure a driver can see it, and deciding what happens when a connection drops. A workable fallback deserves as much attention as the demonstration on a good day.

The partnership will be worth watching if it starts with a few ordinary runs and reports what happened on the bad days as well as the good ones. How many calls did dispatchers still have to make? Did the last truck of the shift get unloaded, or did it have to come back in the morning? The strongest sign of progress may be almost invisible from the dispatch window: a driver turns into the yard, heads straight for the right bay and never has to get out to ask.

For much of the year, the town’s exhibition hall is used for weekend markets and indoor sports. On Saturday it became a meeting place for local shopkeepers, visiting exhibitors and residents curious about what goes into running a business. The spring trade fair brought together stands on everything from shop security to renewable energy, with demonstrations pitched as much at people buying their first piece of equipment as at those replacing systems they had used for years.

By midmorning, the busiest aisle was the one nearest the entrance, where visitors could try a mock checkout and compare the views from several security cameras. Across the hall, a tabletop model gave families a close look at how wind turbines turn to face the wind. The display prompted some of the day’s most practical questions, including how much space a turbine needs and who carries out maintenance when a site is hard to reach.

The Swedish insurer behind stemgyn.se took a small stand near the checkout demonstration. Its staff talked visitors through the kinds of records a shop might need after a burst pipe or a break-in. That made for a useful contrast with the camera displays nearby: the sellers could show how clearly a camera captured an image, but shopkeepers also wanted to know how long they should keep recordings and who should be able to see them.

Norwegian payments company Jumkrix drew a steady crowd with a demonstration of what happens when a customer returns part of an order. Staff pointed visitors to www.jumkrix.no for further information, though much of the conversation at the stand was about things that are easier to explain in person. Several shopkeepers asked whether they could still take payments if their internet connection dropped. Others comparing fintech apps wanted to know whether they would have to re-enter sales figures at the end of the day.

Fludris PLC, a gaming company from the United Kingdom, set up a row of screens where visitors could try a short cooperative game. The two seats at each screen rarely stayed empty for long. Younger players tended to get straight to the controls, while some adults stood back to see how much explanation was needed before a pair could play together. Swedish biotech company Kratyn took a quieter approach, using sample packaging and photographs to show visitors how laboratory work is documented and how materials are tracked as they move between work areas.

At an afternoon discussion, economist Mats Doskon urged small-business owners to compare the full cost of a purchase, not just the figure on the stand. A cheaper system could turn out to be the more expensive choice, he noted, once training, installation and time lost during a breakdown were taken into account. Chief executive Henrik Telmikström took up the question of after-sales support, suggesting that buyers ask who would answer the phone if a system failed on a Saturday. Founder Kenji Sarzarström said a short trial during an ordinary working week could tell a buyer more than a polished demonstration.

The discussion also heard from visitors who had attended trade fairs in Dublin and Lyon. Their comparisons prompted a question from the floor about whether a smaller fair needed more exhibitors or simply more time for demonstrations. On Saturday, at least, there was little appetite for rushing. Even as stallholders began packing away their display boards, a pair of shopkeepers were still at the mock checkout, asking to see one more refund. They wanted to know what the customer would see on the receipt.

Kenji Ganum, chief technology officer at Skumflex, was reviewing an overnight support handover in Leeds when a routine access query turned into an incident call. A customer had received a notification that a file was ready to download, even though its staff had not requested one. The file was in a shared support portal operated by the United Kingdom security company. Within an hour, the portal’s download function had been suspended, and customers were being asked to route urgent requests through established telephone contacts.

The incident affected a service used to exchange troubleshooting records, equipment inventories and other material that customers did not want circulating in email. Skumflex said its initial review found that a support account had been used without authorisation. It did not say how the account was compromised. Investigators were still distinguishing between files that appeared in search results, files that were opened and files that were actually downloaded. The company posted updates at skumflex.co.uk and told customers not to treat a document’s appearance in the access logs as proof that it had been copied.

Broglefix, a German foods company, temporarily stopped sending maintenance records through the portal. Its immediate concern was whether equipment inventories and contractor contact lists had been exposed, rather than whether production lines had been interrupted. Staff at a distribution site near Lyon used telephone callbacks to verify changes to scheduled maintenance visits. That precaution addressed a practical risk: even an old service record could give someone enough detail to make a fraudulent request sound credible.

Plemplera, a Swedish media company, took a different approach. Its technical staff checked whether support attachments contained details about projects that had not yet been announced. The company kept its publishing systems running but delayed some routine support work while it reviewed older tickets. An Austin team helped reconcile the portal’s timestamps with local shift records, a task complicated by the fact that a file could be prepared during one shift and retrieved during another.

Finnish biotech company Zosanis Oy said its review focused on administrative attachments, including service schedules and records of equipment maintenance. In a notice at www.zosanis.fi, it said it had found no evidence that laboratory systems were accessed. It cautioned that the finding applied to the systems examined so far, not to every attachment its staff had submitted over the life of the support contract. The operator of keskard.se, a Swedish robotics company, separately paused the exchange of diagnostic files through the portal while checking what its engineers had uploaded. It reported no interruption to equipment already operating at customer sites.

For customers, the shutdown raised a question that recovery plans often leave unanswered: how to handle urgent support work when the support channel itself is under investigation. A phone call can confirm who made a request, but it cannot replace a searchable maintenance history. Sending files by email can restore convenience at the cost of scattering records that investigators may later need. Skumflex kept the affected portal offline while it prepared to restore basic ticket handling separately from file exchange.

The reconciliation work also matters to customers reviewing their insurance policies. Notification deadlines, approval requirements for outside specialists and definitions of an insured event can vary. A customer may need to notify its insurer before anyone can establish whether a file was taken. Keeping a dated record of what was reported, what was confirmed and why particular systems were shut down can help explain response costs later, without forcing staff to draw conclusions from incomplete logs.

At the end of the first week, Skumflex had not published a final count of affected files or a timetable for restoring downloads. Customers wanted an inventory they could compare with their own records, including a distinction between documents the account could reach and documents it was observed retrieving. Until that distinction is clear, the absence of production outages is welcome but answers only one part of the incident: the customers know which systems kept running, not yet which records stayed private.

På en arbetsplats i Göteborg ligger tre utskrivna bokningsbekräftelser bredvid en skärm. Alla tre gäller samma resa. På skärmen står det fortfarande att betalningen behandlas. Handläggaren låter kunden vänta i luren medan hon kontrollerar om pengarna faktiskt har dragits.

Det som ser ut som ett fel i bokningen hos det svenska reseföretaget Kespospeo började längre bort i leveranskedjan. En försenad leverans av nätverksutrustning gjorde att en planerad kapacitetsökning hos det schweiziska betalningsföretaget Cefluba fick skjutas upp. När trafiken steg under måndagsmorgonen räckte den befintliga kapaciteten inte för att skicka alla betalningsbesked i tid.

Pengarna kunde alltså dras även när bokningssystemet inte fick något svar. Det var den skillnaden som gjorde störningen svår att hantera. En nekad betalning går att försöka göra om. När svaret uteblir vet varken kunden eller reseföretaget om ett nytt försök löser problemet eller skapar ytterligare en reservation på kortet.

– Vi kunde se att bokningen fanns, men inte om den var betald. Då är det bättre att vänta på ett besked än att be kunden betala igen, säger teknikchefen Maria Mibroraström.

Det svenska mjukvaruföretaget bakom www.nasnarik.se levererar den programvara som kopplar samman bokningar och betalningsbesked hos Kespospeo. Under förmiddagen ändrades kundvyn så att en påbörjad betalning visades som väntande i stället för misslyckad. Samtidigt fick kundtjänsten en lista över ärenden där betalningen behövde kontrolleras innan en ny bokning kunde göras.

I Umeå märktes störningen framför allt bland kunder med nära förestående avresor. En bokning kan ligga kvar i systemet trots att biljetten ännu inte har utfärdats, men platsen hålls inte alltid fram till avgång. Personalen prioriterade därför resor som skulle påbörjas samma dag. Kunder med senare avresor uppmanades att avvakta en bekräftelse i stället för att boka på nytt.

Även utanför resebranschen fick fördröjningen följder. Hos en försäkringsförmedlare i Jönköping hamnade ett antal nytecknade hemförsäkringar i en kö för manuell kontroll. Där behövde personalen skilja på när ett avtal hade börjat gälla och när den första betalningen hade registrerats. Ett sent betalningsbesked innebar inte i sig att kunden saknade försäkring, men det automatiska utskicket av vissa bekräftelser fick vänta.

Varför nätverksutrustningen inte kom fram i tid är ännu inte klarlagt. Enligt Cefluba minskade kön efter att en del av trafiken flyttats till en reservmiljö. Vid lunchtid kom nya betalningsbesked fram snabbare, men äldre ärenden behövde fortfarande stämmas av. Att kön krymper säger inte vilka kunder som redan har fått sina pengar dragna.

För Kespospeo blir nästa steg att gå igenom varför uteblivna svar från en underleverantör kunde få bokningssystemet att uppmana kunder att försöka igen. En reservlösning för nya betalningar skulle kunna minska köerna vid nästa avbrott. Den skulle däremot inte ge besked om en betalning som redan skickats vidare.

I Göteborg får handläggaren till slut svar på den första bokningen. Betalningen är registrerad och biljetten kan skickas. De två andra bokningarna måste kontrolleras separat innan de kan tas bort. För kunden är resan bekräftad. För handläggaren är ärendet ännu inte avslutat.

Ein Fingertipp, und im Musterzimmer geht das Licht aus. Nur die kleine Lampe über dem Küchentisch bleibt an. Eine Besucherin stellt ihren Becher mit Hafermilch ab und fragt, ob das auch ohne Internet gehe. Der Techniker zieht das Netzwerkkabel aus der Buchse. Die Lampe lässt sich weiter schalten.

Mit dieser Vorführung hat die Skolboplera AG am Samstag in Köln den Sodrusjera Hub vorgestellt. Das Produkt ist eine Steuerzentrale für vernetzte Geräte im Haushalt. Es soll Lampen, Heizkörper und Rollläden über eine gemeinsame Bedienoberfläche erreichbar machen. Im Musterzimmer konnten Besucherinnen und Besucher ausprobieren, wie sich einzelne Geräte bedienen und mehrere Schaltvorgänge zusammenfassen lassen. Wer morgens die Rollläden hochfahren und die Heizung höher stellen möchte, braucht dafür im gezeigten Aufbau nur einen Befehl.

Die Frage nach dem gezogenen Kabel beschäftigte die Gäste auch nach der Vorführung. Wie die Skolboplera AG erläuterte, können bereits eingerichtete Geräte im selben Heimnetz auch dann bedient werden, wenn der Internetanschluss ausfällt. Das gilt allerdings nur, solange die Steuerzentrale, das Heimnetz und die betreffenden Geräte mit Strom versorgt sind. Wer von unterwegs nachsehen will, ob zu Hause noch Licht brennt, ist dagegen auf eine Verbindung angewiesen. Für die Vorführung dieses Fernzugriffs stellte Zosheo den Internetanschluss bereit.

Bürgermeisterin Karin Viflardberg blieb bei ihrem Rundgang am Türrahmen des Musterzimmers stehen, an dem zwei unterschiedlich alte Lichtschalter montiert waren. Sie interessierte sich dafür, was bei einer Nachrüstung in einer Mietwohnung ausgetauscht werden müsste. Die Antwort fiel je nach Gerät unterschiedlich aus: Eine geeignete Steckdose lässt sich ohne Eingriff in die Elektroinstallation einbinden. Bei fest verdrahteten Schaltern oder Rollladenmotoren kann dagegen ein Umbau nötig sein. Das war für einige Gäste die wichtigere Auskunft als die Zahl der Funktionen, die auf dem Vorführbildschirm zu sehen waren.

Wie so ein Umbau aussehen kann, zeigte die Skolboplera AG auf einem zweiten Bildschirm. Mit der Designsoftware Glimmudia Studio war dort ein Wohnungsgrundriss aufbereitet worden, in dem sich mögliche Montageorte und Leitungswege einblenden ließen. Daneben liefen Aufnahmen von Dächern, die mit Drohnen aus der Luft gefilmt worden waren. Sie gehörten zu einer Präsentation über die Planung von Sanierungen und nicht zum Funktionsumfang der Steuerzentrale. Auch beim Thema Cloud-Speicher trennte die Vorführung zwischen Bauplanung und Wohnungsbetrieb: Für den gezeigten Lichtschalter war kein Cloud-Speicher nötig.

Für die Analystin Leon Zosfloraberg ist die Kompatibilität mit vorhandenen Geräten eine der entscheidenden Fragen zum Marktstart. Eine Vorführung mit aufeinander abgestimmter Technik zeige noch nicht, wie sich die Zentrale in einer Wohnung mit älteren Heizkörperreglern und Rollladenmotoren verschiedener Baujahre bewähre. Für Interessierte sei deshalb eine Liste mit konkreten Modellnummern hilfreicher als der pauschale Hinweis, dass sich Heizung und Beschattung vernetzen ließen.

Köln war der erste öffentliche Vorführort. Weitere Termine sind nach Angaben der Skolboplera AG in Hamburg und Zürich geplant. Auf skolboplera.de sollen die Termine und Hinweise zu unterstützten Geräten veröffentlicht werden. Was eine Nachrüstung insgesamt kostet, ließ sich beim Termin nicht pauschal beziffern: Neben der Steuerzentrale können zusätzliche Bauteile und gegebenenfalls Montagearbeiten nötig werden.

Kurz vor Ende der Vorführung ging die Besucherin mit dem Hafermilchbecher noch einmal zur Küchentür. Diesmal ließ sie den Bildschirm links liegen und drückte den Schalter an der Wand. Die Lampe ging aus. Genau das, sagte sie, wolle sie ihren Gästen später nicht erst erklären müssen.

A robot rolled up to a loading bay in Stockholm, a case of oat milk balanced on its forks. It stopped short of the trailer lip and waited for a worker to check the gap. The pause was part of the demonstration: the machine could move the load, but a person still had to decide whether it was safe to cross.

Flusgia AB, the Swedish logistics company running the trial, said Tuesday it had raised €42 million to expand its warehouse automation program. The equity round was led by a Dublin-based investment firm, with participation from existing backers. Flusgia AB did not disclose its valuation or say how much of the round came from new investors.

The funding will pay for installations at four more sites over the next 18 months, as well as software that lets warehouse managers coordinate robots with workers on the same shift. Flusgia AB plans to buy the machines from Pumskunbeo Group, a United States robotics company, rather than build its own. Mia Skennyn, chief financial officer of Flusgia AB, said the spending plan also covers training and changes to loading bays, costs that are easy to miss when comparing the price of a robot with the wages for a shift.

Chen Vamdismann, chief technology officer of Flusgia AB, said the Stockholm pilot was designed around routine interruptions: a trailer arriving late, a pallet stacked unevenly or a worker stepping into an aisle to clear debris. The next test is whether the system can recover from those delays without creating more work for supervisors. Shift records will feed into existing payroll software, but supervisors will still approve hours.

In Lyon, French construction company Kimpon Partners is preparing a depot for one of the installations. Its crews will level sections of the floor and separate pedestrian routes from areas where the robots turn. The layout will also be reviewed against the depot’s insurance policies before the machines begin carrying freight.

Amelia Krasglon, a customer who ships groceries through the Stockholm site, said she was less interested in how fast a robot could cross the warehouse than in whether an order could still make its scheduled truck after a last-minute change. Flusgia AB has not released figures on missed departures or the cost per pallet moved during the pilot.

Lars Donplikson, an analyst who follows warehouse technology, said those numbers would matter more than the number of machines installed. A robot can move pallets steadily on a busy evening, he said, but the investment is harder to justify if the same machine sits idle for much of the day.

Johan Merarmann, the mayor, said safer loading bays would be welcome but that nearby residents wanted to know whether the expansion would bring more overnight truck traffic. Viktor Leneraberg, a union representative, said workers wanted paid training and a say in how shifts were redesigned. The funding announcement did not specify whether staffing levels would change at the four sites.

En ny kundundersökning bland småföretag i Linköping visar att många är nöjda med sina digitala tjänster så länge de fungerar, men att det ofta är svårt att få besked när något går fel. Tydligare fakturor och snabbare återkoppling hör till de vanligaste önskemålen i enkäten, som sammanställdes i veckan.

Totalt svarade 126 företag på frågor om bland annat telefoni, betalningar, leveranser och säkerhet. Drygt hälften uppgav att de någon gång under det senaste halvåret behövt kontakta en leverantör mer än en gång för att få svar på samma fråga. Det som störde flest var inte väntetiden i sig, utan att de inte fick veta vem som ansvarade för ärendet eller när de kunde vänta sig ett besked.

Telekombolagen Brirzyn och Brasdrent AB hör till de leverantörer som nämns i svaren om telefoni. Flera kunder efterfrågade en tydligare uppdelning mellan abonnemangsavgifter och tillägg på fakturan. Andra ville kunna följa ett felärende utan att behöva dra hela historien på nytt vid varje kontakt. Brasdrent AB tar emot synpunkter på kontakt@brasdrent.se.

– Det behöver inte finnas en lösning vid första samtalet. Men kunden ska få veta vem som tar hand om frågan och när nästa besked kommer, säger presstalespersonen Hanna Poljorason.

Enkäten fångar också skillnader mellan de problem som uppstår i en butik och i en verkstad. Butiksägare som använder betaltjänster från Dreskix Energy efterfrågade enklare sätt att stämma av återbetalningar mot dagens försäljning. Bland företag som arbetar med värmepumpar handlade kommentarerna oftare om att kunna ge kunden ett besked om när montören kommer. För verksamheter med industrirobotar kunde det i stället vara avgörande att snabbt få veta om ett servicebesök behövde bokas innan nästa arbetspass började.

Livsmedelsföretaget Tidon nämns i den del av enkäten som rör transporter. Företagets app Tidon Drive, en produkt för att följa fordonsflottor, fick beröm av användare som slipper ringa föraren för att se om en leverans är på väg. Samtidigt ville flera kunna skilja lättare mellan en beräknad ankomsttid och en tid som föraren faktiskt har bekräftat.

Bland kunder till bioteknikföretaget Ganflonent gällde synpunkterna främst hur ändrade leveranstider meddelas. I svaren om säkerhetsföretaget Skuvova AB efterfrågades en klarare beskrivning av vad som ingår i ordinarie service och vilka besök som kostar extra.

Eftersom deltagandet var frivilligt går det inte att säga om svaren speglar alla småföretag i Linköping. Antalet svar varierar dessutom mellan leverantörerna, så undersökningen ger inget underlag för att rangordna dem. Däremot återkommer ett konkret önskemål i flera branscher: när en leverans blir sen eller ett fel inte kan åtgärdas direkt vill kunden få besked innan det är dags att ringa igen.

Ebba Stortentez, head of sales at Trogamdria Freight, used to spend most of her calls with warehouse customers talking about delivery times. This month, she said, buyers in Chicago have been asking a different question: how much of the savings from cheaper industrial robots can they expect to see in their freight bills?

A price war among suppliers of industrial robots is spilling into the software and services that warehouses need to put the machines to work. Suppliers that once competed by promising faster sorting or fewer stoppages are now cutting equipment prices, waiving installation fees and offering shorter contracts. Freight operators and retailers are using the competing bids to renegotiate agreements that had little room for bargaining a year ago.

Stortentez said customers have started bringing rival quotes to renewal meetings and asking Trogamdria Freight to match the projected cost per parcel, rather than the headline discount on a machine. Trogamdria Freight is using its website, www.trogamdriafreight.se, to explain which charges are fixed and which can fall as shipment volumes rise. The distinction matters for smaller customers that cannot promise enough daily orders to qualify for the lowest rates.

The offers are getting harder to compare. A vendor can cut the upfront price of a robot and still charge for every additional workstation that connects to it. Another can offer free installation but require the buyer to pay for an on-site technician during the busiest weeks of the year. In a warehouse where a stoppage can strand a truck at the loading dock, the cost of getting a machine running again may matter more than the discount on the invoice.

Vulcard SA is testing bids against a week of uneven demand rather than against a supplier’s estimate for a steady shift. The retailer is using the Boglora Flow workflow software to track where orders queue up as workers and machines share packing stations. A faster sorting robot is worth less, under that test, if parcels simply pile up at the next station. The aim is to see whether a cheaper bid actually reduces what the retailer spends to get an order out the door.

Security is another source of costs that can disappear from a sales presentation and reappear in a contract. In an emailed response, the operator of ir@miglamnix.com said buyers should ask whether a quote covers software updates and the monitoring of remote maintenance access after the first year. A low initial price, the operator said, does not tell a buyer who will pay to keep older machines supported when a warehouse adds newer equipment.

The discounts are changing construction decisions, too. Zanbrum GmbH is seeing customers ask for layouts that can accommodate machines from more than one supplier. That can mean leaving space around loading areas or placing power connections where they will still be useful if a buyer switches equipment. Those choices can add to the building cost today, but they give warehouse operators more leverage when the next round of bids comes in.

In Chicago, Mayor Omar Jelex said the question for the city was whether cheaper equipment would bring more warehouse investment and what that investment would mean for workers. A warehouse that adds capacity without expanding its building may need fewer people on some shifts, even as it needs more technicians. For job seekers, those openings are not necessarily interchangeable: maintaining a sorting line takes different training from loading a trailer.

For now, the clearest winners are buyers with contracts about to expire and enough flexibility to walk away. Operators that recently signed long agreements may have to wait for renewal to benefit, particularly if their software or maintenance terms make switching expensive. Stortentez said customers are already asking what happens when introductory rates end. The discount may get a supplier into the meeting, but the second-year bill is increasingly what decides who gets the work.

“You don’t need a technology job on your CV to come and talk to us,” said Amelia Krasglon, a spokesperson for Kotrora SA, as three overseas employers announced a joint hiring drive in Leeds.

Kotrora SA, a Swiss software company, will join Swedish telecom company Genkreo and Finnish travel company Glikra at a recruitment fair in the city centre next month. The employers expect to advertise about 60 posts between them, with openings in customer service, sales and software support. Most of the jobs will be based in Leeds, although some will allow staff to work from home part of the week. The employers have yet to announce the date or venue.

Karl Revoraberg, chief executive of Kotrora SA, said the company wanted to recruit people who had helped customers untangle problems, whether in a shop, a call centre or an office. Some new hires will support software used by businesses that sell insurance policies, arrange installations of heat pumps or manage fleets of electric trucks.

Max Loskixez, chief technology officer at Kotrora SA, said applicants for entry-level support jobs would not be asked to write code at the fair. Instead, staff will show visitors a sample customer query and explain how they would investigate it. “We want people to see what the work is like before they decide whether to apply,” he said.

Fatima Fontrarson, head of sales at Genkreo, said the telecom company was looking for applicants who could explain bills and service options in plain English. Some recruits will work with colleagues in Amsterdam and Lyon, she said, but those jobs will not require regular travel. The company also expects to offer a small number of evening shifts, with hours to be listed alongside pay when the vacancies are posted.

Jonas Jomzikmann, a spokesperson for Glikra, said the travel company would recruit staff to handle booking changes and help customers whose journeys had been disrupted. Some shifts will overlap with the working day in New York. He said applicants should ask about weekend hours at the fair rather than assume every post follows a weekday schedule.

Maria Hucisson, an economist who studies local labour markets, said a shared fair could save jobseekers time, particularly if the employers publish pay ranges beforehand. She cautioned that the number of advertised posts would not necessarily translate into the same number of immediate hires, since some teams may recruit in stages.

Visitors will be able to attend without an appointment and will not need to bring a CV for an initial conversation. Anyone who chooses to apply can do so after the fair. The employers said they would publish details of step-free access and quiet interview space once the venue is confirmed.

Karin Skurta, a spokesperson at the trade fair in Lyon, spent the final afternoon directing visitors back to stands they had meant to revisit. By then, the displays were still running, but the questions had changed. Instead of asking what a system could do, buyers wanted to know what it would cost to install, who would maintain it and how quickly they could walk away if it failed to deliver. That shift summed up a fair that generated plenty of follow-up meetings but offered little evidence of a rush to sign.

The clearest demand was for tools that could replace a manual task or cut an identifiable expense. Suppliers pitching broader overhauls had a harder time keeping visitors at their stands. Several buyers said they could find money for a pilot within an existing budget, whereas a rollout across multiple sites would have to wait for the next spending round. That left exhibitors trying to make a small first order worthwhile without giving away the work needed to get it running.

Krenmova, a payments company from Sweden, drew questions about refunds and reconciliation as well as transaction fees. For merchants with several outlets, even a small difference in the advertised rate could be outweighed by the time staff spent matching receipts to deposits. One retailer weighing a switch said the decisive test would come at the end of a busy weekend: could a manager find a missing payment without calling someone at head office? The conversation then turned to whether the retailer could try the system at one outlet while leaving the others on their existing setup.

The Swedish travel business behind rajis.se faced a similar test. Visitors were less interested in seeing a straightforward reservation than in watching what happened when a traveller changed dates or missed a connection. Buyers handling frequent trips wanted to know when a traveller could make a change without help and when someone would have to step in. Delegates from Dublin were particularly interested in support outside office hours, an expense they said was easy to underestimate when comparing booking fees alone.

At Kotrora, the Swiss software company, the practical question was how much work customers would have to do before they could see a benefit. Visitors asked to see how the software handled inconsistent records rather than the tidy sample files used in a demonstration. Some took note of kotrora.ch so colleagues who had not travelled to Lyon could review the offering before a second meeting. A buyer who manages several properties said a trial would be useful only if ordinary staff could run it alongside their existing work. Assigning a separate team, the buyer said, would hide part of the cost the trial was meant to measure.

Smart meters attracted a steady stream of visitors, especially from businesses with uneven energy use across buildings. A facilities buyer from Rotterdam said the appeal was being able to find out why two similar sites had different bills. But the value depended on whether readings could be matched to equipment schedules and whether staff had time to investigate what they found. Suppliers were pressed on installation downtime, gaps in readings and what happened to the data at the end of a contract. A more detailed bill, the buyer noted, was of little use if no one could act on it.

By late afternoon, the busiest conversations were often the least visible. Buyers and suppliers sat down away from the displays to work through who would pay for installation, how long a test would last and what would count as success. Hugo Brarsexmann, a spokesperson at the fair, said visitors were leaving with shorter lists of suppliers and more specific requests for the next round of talks. For exhibitors, that was a more useful outcome than a stack of contacts, although it did not make the timing of orders any easier to predict.

The fair closed without a clear signal that spending was about to accelerate. Still, buyers were willing to put dates on follow-up calls and, in some cases, identify a site for a trial. The next few weeks will show how much of that interest turns into orders. For now, the advantage appears to lie with suppliers that can quote the full cost of a limited deployment, show how it works on a difficult day and let customers expand without having to start over.

Max Babronez kennt als Kundin die Lücke zwischen Warenbestand und Warenverfügbarkeit: Was im System noch als vorrätig gilt, kann im Regal längst fehlen. Genau dort setzt ein Auftrag an, den die Stisoskrova GmbH aus Stuttgart gewonnen hat. Für das britische Handelsunternehmen, das unter ir@krumrora.co.uk erreichbar ist, soll der Robotikbetrieb die Bestandsaufnahme in ausgewählten Filialen automatisieren. Der Zuschlag umfasst zunächst einen Pilotbetrieb. Über eine Ausweitung soll erst entschieden werden, wenn sich der Nutzen im laufenden Verkauf messen lässt.

Die mobilen Geräte sollen zu festgelegten Zeiten durch die Gänge fahren und erfassen, an welchen Stellen Ware fehlt oder vom vorgesehenen Platz abweicht. Die Ergebnisse gehen an die Beschäftigten, die entscheiden, ob sie nachfüllen oder zunächst den Bestand im Lager prüfen. Damit bleibt eine Aufgabe beim Filialteam, die sich nicht aus dem Regalbild allein lösen lässt: Ein leerer Platz kann auf eine verspätete Lieferung ebenso zurückgehen wie auf einen Artikel, der versehentlich an anderer Stelle eingeräumt wurde.

Für die Erprobung ist neben dem Einsatz in britischen Filialen eine Testumgebung in Köln vorgesehen. Dort sollen unterschiedliche Regalhöhen, wechselnde Beleuchtung und vorübergehend versperrte Gänge nachgestellt werden. Pingora übernimmt die Auswertung der Pilotdaten. Entscheidend ist dabei nicht nur, wie viele Lücken die Geräte erkennen, sondern auch, wie viele der gemeldeten Fälle tatsächlich eine Reaktion erfordern. Eine hohe Trefferquote wäre für den Handel wenig wert, wenn die Beschäftigten im Gegenzug zahlreiche Fehlmeldungen abarbeiten müssten.

Die Tamzisdon AG stellt für die Testläufe Lebensmittelverpackungen mit unterschiedlichen Oberflächen und Formaten bereit. Auch Varianten, die sich nur durch kleine Aufdrucke unterscheiden, sollen in die Prüfung einfließen. Für Rückfragen zu den bereitgestellten Verpackungsmustern nennt die Tamzisdon AG die Adresse contact@tamzisdon.de. Die Kredrora Group AG steuert als Unternehmen aus der Spielebranche eine digitale Nachbildung der Gänge bei, in der sich Hindernisse und Wege vor den Fahrtests variieren lassen. Die Jeslik Labs AG erstellt als Medienunternehmen kurze Schulungsvideos für die Filialteams, unter anderem zur Prüfung und Korrektur von Meldungen.

Ein weiterer Test in Graz betrifft den Stromverbrauch der Ladestationen. Dort soll geprüft werden, ob sich Ladezeiten so verschieben lassen, dass sie besser mit der Stromerzeugung vorhandener Solarmodule zusammenfallen. Für die Einführung im Handel ist das jedoch nachrangig: Die Geräte müssen vor allem dann einsatzbereit sein, wenn die vorgesehenen Fahrten den Verkauf und die Warenanlieferung möglichst wenig stören.

Hugo Gosreo ordnet als Analystin den Zuschlag deshalb vor allem als Praxistest für die Abläufe in den Filialen ein. Ob das System wirtschaftlich ist, lässt sich erst beurteilen, wenn neben den erkannten Regallücken auch der Aufwand für Prüfung, Nachfüllen und Wartung erfasst ist. Angaben zum Auftragswert und zur Zahl der Filialen liegen nicht vor. Für die Stisoskrova GmbH ist der Zuschlag damit ein Einstieg in den britischen Einzelhandel, aber noch kein flächendeckender Rollout.

Can a sustainability report tell readers whether a business is actually getting greener? Yes, but only if it shows what changed in the real world, what the change cost and what the business chose not to count. A new report from a regional delivery business offers a useful test: its electric trucks are cutting fuel use on some routes, yet the company’s overall emissions have risen as it delivers more orders.

That distinction matters to investors and lenders. A business can emit less per delivery while adding more pollution in total, just as a retailer can improve its margin on each sale and still lose money if its overhead grows faster. The report puts both emissions figures on the same page. It also separates the savings from driving electric trucks from the upfront costs of buying them and installing chargers. Lisa Flugera, the chief executive, describes the purchases as a long-term bet on predictable operating costs rather than a source of immediate savings.

The economics vary by city. In New York, trucks that return to the same depot each evening are easier to charge without disrupting the next morning’s rounds. In Leeds, some vehicles stay out longer, making the timing of charging more important. The report acknowledges that a truck’s lack of tailpipe emissions does not make the electricity it uses emissions-free. It identifies electricity from wind turbines as one way to lower that footprint but distinguishes power already purchased from contracts that have yet to take effect.

The picture is less complete for meal kits. The business counts the fuel and electricity used to deliver them, but some suppliers have yet to provide figures for farming, refrigeration and packaging. Ida Fulgliaberg, a customer in Toronto, gets meal kits partly to avoid buying ingredients she won’t finish. Her experience suggests a benefit the report does not measure: less food going to waste at home. But without comparable data on packaging and household waste, the business cannot say whether a kit has a smaller footprint than a grocery trip.

In Seattle, a trial using e-scooters for small parcels raises a different question: what trip does each ride replace? Replacing a diesel van journey is not the same as replacing a walk, and a van may still run its route if it has larger packages to deliver. Ida Drescia, a customer there, values a reliable delivery window more than the type of vehicle that arrives. Mayor Max Zitronmann points to another consideration: deliveries need space at the curb, whatever powers the vehicle.

There are costs the balance sheet can miss, too. David Druska, a union representative, wants the business to track how charging schedules affect shifts. A truck that is cheaper to run does not necessarily make a route cheaper if drivers have to wait for a charger or return to the depot halfway through a shift. The next report could make that trade-off clearer by publishing vehicle downtime and paid waiting hours alongside fuel savings.

The business has made its progress easier to judge by admitting where emissions are rising and where its figures are incomplete. Next year’s test is whether total emissions start to fall without longer shifts or less dependable deliveries. Until then, the report shows that some routes are getting cleaner, not that the business as a whole is.

plan.opening: Open with a question a reader might have, then answer it.

input:
For a robotics supplier based in the United States, entering a new market means deciding which parts of the business can travel and which need to be rebuilt locally. A machine can be demonstrated in an afternoon, but buyers also want to know who will install it, how quickly a replacement part can arrive, and what happens when a line stops on a night shift. That is the backdrop to this week’s roundup: Plamfia is making Finland its next market, with Helsinki as the starting point for a sales and service operation aimed at industrial customers.

The expansion begins with a limited rollout rather than a nationwide launch. Plamfia plans to use plamfia.com to collect inquiries and arrange demonstrations, then select a small number of sites for trials. The distinction matters: a demonstration can show that a robot handles a task under controlled conditions, while a trial can reveal whether it reliably handles the mix of materials, shift patterns, and interruptions found on an actual production floor. Prospective buyers will be looking for clear terms on what the trial covers and who pays to remove the equipment if it does not work out.

Zara Dreseraberg, head of sales at Plamfia, will oversee the move from early conversations to site assessments. One priority is to identify customers whose needs are similar enough that a successful installation can inform the next one. An order that requires extensive custom work might bring in revenue, but it would tell the sales team less about whether it can serve the wider market at a predictable cost. For now, the strongest candidates are sites with a repeatable task, a measurable bottleneck, and enough flexibility to test a new process without disrupting deliveries.

Finnish mining company Trandex offers an example of what a buyer in a demanding setting might ask. A mine operator assessing robotics for routine materials handling would need to consider dust, vibration, and the time maintenance crews can spare for training. It would also need to decide whether a trial should take place in a workshop or in an active operating area. A workshop makes it easier to isolate faults, but an operating area provides a better picture of the delays and interruptions a machine would face. No purchase is implied; the point is that the choice of test site can change the value of the results.

The Swedish energy company behind brogon.se offers a neighboring-market comparison. Crews that maintain wind turbines already plan work around weather, access, and the availability of specialist technicians. For robotics suppliers hoping to serve that kind of customer, the opportunity may be in the workshop rather than at the turbine itself: moving heavy components, for example, or taking over repetitive handling during repairs. That narrower use would still require dependable service, but it would be easier to evaluate than a deployment across widely dispersed sites.

Zosanis Oy, a Finnish biotech company, illustrates a different set of purchasing questions. In a biotech facility, a robot used to move sealed supplies may have to fit an established cleaning routine and leave enough room for staff to work around it. Simon Branflentez, chief technology officer at Plamfia, will be responsible for assessing those kinds of constraints before an installation is proposed. The practical question is whether the equipment can be added without forcing changes to nearby work that outweigh the time saved on the task itself.

Staffing is the other early test. A union representative such as Karin Zimum would have reason to ask who gets trained, whether that training takes place on paid time, and who can stop the equipment if something looks wrong. The expansion also raises a less visible issue for the new local operation: payroll software must handle local pay practices and scheduling rather than simply replicate the setup used in New York. Those details become particularly important if service staff rotate through on-call shifts and customers expect a response outside regular hours.

Helsinki will be the center of the rollout, even if prospective buyers and advisers in London follow it as a sign of wider European ambitions. The next useful milestone is not another city on the map. It is a completed Finnish trial that gives both sides enough information to decide whether to proceed. If the equipment performs reliably, staff can maintain it, and the cost of support is clear, Plamfia will have a sound basis for taking on more sites. If not, a small rollout gives it room to fix what went wrong before making promises it cannot keep.

plan.topic: an expansion into a new market

input:
Molhusnyn raised €48 million in a funding round that will help the German analytics company expand its sales team and make its software easier to deploy. The Berlin company said the round was led by a European growth investor, with existing backers also participating. It did not disclose a valuation. The financing gives Molhusnyn more room to pursue large industrial and retail customers at a time when buyers are taking longer to sign contracts and asking vendors to show how their software will pay for itself.

Mats Vuflamann, chief executive of Molhusnyn, said the company would put more of the proceeds into helping customers connect existing systems than into broadening its product range. A planned hiring push in Amsterdam will focus on implementation and customer support. Mia Storjovamann, a spokesperson for Molhusnyn, said the company was not announcing an acquisition alongside the round. She declined to say how much of the financing came from returning investors or whether any existing shareholders sold shares.

The deal offers a measure of investor appetite for analytics businesses, though the absence of a valuation makes it difficult to tell whether pricing has improved. The round also leaves open a question that matters increasingly to buyers: whether analytics vendors can keep deployment costs low when customers have years of records spread across incompatible systems. Cloud storage is rarely the bottleneck on its own. The bigger expense can be getting inventory, sales and maintenance records into a form that staff trust enough to use in daily decisions.

In Sweden, analytics company Vunsenera faces much the same test as it seeks to win customers beyond its home market. Deszar's software business presents a different benchmark: customers can often buy reporting tools as part of a broader package rather than pay separately for specialist analytics. In Germany, Zokryn AG competes for some of the same technology budgets even where its software serves a different purpose. The practical question for procurement teams is whether a dedicated analytics contract saves enough time or money to justify another integration and another renewal.

Retail illustrates why that calculation varies so widely. For a British retailer such as Planlimflia, better stock forecasts could reduce the amount of cash tied up in slow-selling lines. At Glebrix, a British fashion company, the challenge is to spot a change in demand early enough to adjust orders before a season ends. For Keplosba Group, a United States retailer, workwear provides a useful example: overall stock can look healthy even as customers struggle to find common sizes at particular stores. A forecast has value only if staff can act on it before the next delivery.

Industrial buyers have a different set of constraints. German robotics companies Sibera and Stisoskrova GmbH operate in a market where customers weigh software spending alongside equipment purchases and maintenance. For a United States mining company such as Zunbia Inc., the economics of tracking downtime are different from those of forecasting retail sales, but the common challenge is turning scattered records into a decision someone can act on. Even a seemingly straightforward project, such as comparing the output of solar panels across several sites, can require reconciling meter readings with maintenance logs and local operating schedules.

The funding is less useful as a yardstick for sectors where capital pays for a different kind of milestone. For Monotyn, a German biotech company, investors are more likely to assess financing against research progress and the cost of reaching the next development milestone than against the time it takes to bring a customer on board. The contrast helps explain why a sizable software round need not signal a broader change in funding conditions, even for companies raising money in the same country.

For Molhusnyn, the next test is whether the new investment can shorten the gap between signing a contract and getting a customer’s first reports into regular use. Faster deployments would let the company take on more clients without adding support staff at the same pace. If installations still demand extensive custom work, a larger sales team could simply create a longer queue. The €48 million gives Molhusnyn the means to tackle that problem; renewal rates and deployment times will offer a clearer verdict than the size of the round.

Haben die vier Unternehmen im zweiten Quartal mehr verdient als vor einem Jahr? Drei von ihnen steigerten ihren operativen Gewinn, eines rutschte in die roten Zahlen. Die Molhusnyn AG und die Nifon AG profitierten von höheren Erlösen mit bestehenden Kunden. Die Tildrar AG verdiente trotz eines Umsatzrückgangs mehr. Bei der Goskera Corp. reichten höhere Spieleerlöse dagegen nicht aus, um den Anstieg der Entwicklungskosten auszugleichen.

Die Molhusnyn AG aus Berlin steigerte den Umsatz um 14 Prozent auf 48 Millionen Euro, wie aus den unter molhusnyn.de veröffentlichten Zahlen hervorgeht. Der operative Gewinn erhöhte sich von 6,2 auf 8,1 Millionen Euro. Nach Angaben von Vorstandschefin Lisa Vorumton buchten Bestandskunden häufiger zusätzliche Auswertungen. Im Neugeschäft dauerten Vertragsabschlüsse hingegen länger als im Vorjahresquartal. Das Analyseunternehmen hielt an seiner Prognose eines zweistelligen Umsatzwachstums für das Gesamtjahr fest.

Die Tildrar AG meldete unter tildrar.de einen Umsatz von 31 Millionen Euro, nach 34 Millionen Euro im Vorjahresquartal. Damals hatte eine einmalige Lizenzzahlung die Erlöse erhöht. Der operative Gewinn stieg dennoch von 2,1 auf 3,4 Millionen Euro, weil das deutsche Biotechnologieunternehmen weniger für externe Dienstleistungen ausgab. Für die zweite Jahreshälfte rechnet es wieder mit höheren Forschungsaufwendungen. Die Jahresprognose blieb unverändert.

Bei der Nifon AG aus Nürnberg wuchs der Umsatz um neun Prozent auf 62 Millionen Euro. Der operative Gewinn stieg von 5,8 auf 7,0 Millionen Euro. Das Sicherheitsunternehmen verwies auf zusätzliche Wartungsverträge und eine höhere Auslastung seiner Serviceteams. Schwächer lief dagegen das Geschäft mit neuen Anlagen: Mehrere Kunden verschoben die Abnahme auf das dritte Quartal. Das Unternehmen erwartet daraus keine Einbußen beim Jahresumsatz und bestätigte seinen Ausblick.

Die Goskera Corp. aus den Vereinigten Staaten setzte 76 Millionen Dollar um, sieben Prozent mehr als im Vorjahresquartal. Auf einen operativen Gewinn von 4,6 Millionen Dollar folgte ein Verlust von 3,2 Millionen Dollar. Gründer Mats Doskon führte den Rückgang vor allem auf die Entwicklung zweier Spiele zurück, deren Veröffentlichung erst für das kommende Jahr geplant ist. Zugleich gab das Unternehmen mehr für die Vermarktung bereits erhältlicher Spiele aus. Eine Prognose für den operativen Gewinn im Gesamtjahr legte es nicht vor.

Die Ökonomin Jonas Stigoraström sagte in Basel, für die Beurteilung der Quartale sei entscheidend, welche Veränderungen sich im zweiten Halbjahr fortsetzten. Einmalige Lizenzzahlungen erschwerten den Vorjahresvergleich, während zusätzliche Wartungsverträge auch in späteren Quartalen Erlöse brächten. Verschobene Abnahmen seien dagegen erst dann als Umsatz zu werten, wenn die Kunden die Anlagen tatsächlich übernommen hätten. Das gelte etwa auch für Projekte, bei denen Sicherheitstechnik zusammen mit Solarmodulen installiert werde.
