input:
Saskrard ApS opened a robotics factory in Denmark this week, bringing assembly, testing and operator training together under one roof. The opening gave visitors a chance to follow a robot through the plant: from a bench where technicians fit its sensors to a test area where it must stop safely when someone steps into its path. The first production runs will be small, giving the team time to catch problems before it takes on larger orders.

At the opening, chief executive Maria Hucisson said the factory’s layout was designed around a practical question: how quickly can a fault found during testing be traced back to the assembly bench? Keeping those teams close means a technician can show a colleague what went wrong rather than trying to explain it in a report at the end of a shift. The training space serves a similar purpose. Operators can practice clearing routine jams and restarting equipment without holding up the production line.

Energy use was another topic on the factory tour. Gamtrondúm, an energy company from the United States, discussed how smart meters can help distinguish the electricity used by a production line from the power needed to keep the building running. The distinction matters during a gradual opening, when a quiet workshop may still need ventilation and heating. Readers looking for more on the company’s work can visit gamtrondum.com.

The opening also prompted conversations about how customers will visit the plant once it settles into a regular schedule. Foplum, a travel company from the United States, looked at itineraries for visitors coming from Oslo and Lyon, with an eye to leaving enough time on site for a full demonstration. Closer to the factory, the logistics discussion turned to cargo bikes. They won’t replace trucks bringing in heavy equipment, but they could handle short trips for small parts that would otherwise tie up a van.

Analyst Nora Trorpyn said the more revealing milestone would come after the opening, when the factory has to turn out the same equipment reliably across several shifts. Test records kept in cloud storage could help technicians compare faults across batches, she noted, but only if they record them consistently. A note that a unit stopped, for example, is less useful than a record of where it stopped and what the operator did next.

For now, the factory’s next test is straightforward: can the team carry what it learns from the first small batches into regular production without slowing down deliveries? That will tell customers more about the new plant than anything they saw on the tour.

Rain beads on the seat of a cargo bike outside a warehouse in Rotterdam. Inside, a shift supervisor checks whether a delivery has arrived, whether its payment has cleared and whether the meter reading belongs to the right loading bay. Today, those answers live in three different places. A new partnership wants to see what happens when they appear together.

The pilot brings together Girdreo, a mining company from Norway; Karhon Oy, a payments company from Finland; Flabrora Ltd, an analytics company from the United Kingdom; and Dácex Oyj, a gaming company from Finland. Krarplesskum's distribution team in Germany will help test whether the shared view is useful on a busy shift, not just in a demonstration.

Girdreo will contribute shipment records from a single route, and Karhon Oy will test how payment confirmations can be matched to deliveries without displaying sensitive payment details to warehouse staff. Flabrora Ltd will bring those records together with readings from smart meters. The analytics company will post a plain-English summary of the pilot at flabrora.co.uk, including which figures the partners can compare reliably and which still need manual checks.

Dácex Oyj will use the Dácex Studio design software to build a simulated loading bay where staff can try out the interface before it goes live. One exercise will show a delivery arriving on time while its payment confirmation comes in late. Another will let staff decide whether a photo taken by drones during a yard inspection is more helpful than a short written note. The team will also test how to record a shipment that leaves by cargo bike after arriving by truck.

Chief executive Ebba Mamdardson said the first review would focus on a simple question: can a supervisor spot a record that needs correcting without calling someone on another team? Staff in Amsterdam will review the trial screens, while a group in Chicago will run through the same exercises to see whether the instructions make sense to people who did not help write them.

For now, Rotterdam is the only live test site. The first roundup of results will track time spent reconciling records, how often staff still reach for a spreadsheet and whether the shared view catches mistakes before a shift ends. That will give the partners a basis for deciding what to keep, what to change and whether to try it on a second route.

Varför söker ett försäkringsbolag och ett byggbolag samma sorts tekniker? För att båda behöver kunna avgöra när en avvikelse i mätdata säger något om en fastighet och när det bara är mätningen som krånglar. Den frågan står i centrum för en rekryteringssatsning där det svenska försäkringsbolaget Stemgyn och det svenska byggbolaget Tustecon AB söker kompetens inom datateknik. Även analysbolaget Glemvova och modebolaget Fosvustora AB, båda svenska, rekryterar till närliggande roller.

Satsningen berör Malmö, Stockholm och Jönköping, men arbetsuppgifterna ser olika ut på de tre orterna. I Malmö ligger tyngdpunkten på att bygga och underhålla dataflöden. I Stockholm handlar det mer om hur analyser presenteras för dem som fattar beslut, medan arbetet i Jönköping ligger närmare den praktiska användningen på byggarbetsplatser och i fastigheter.

Smarta elmätare är ett exempel på varför bolagen behöver fler än utvecklare som kan bygga en ny funktion. Ett glapp i en mätserie kan uppstå när en anslutning försvinner, när en mätare byts ut eller när förbrukningen faktiskt upphör. Om alla tre fallen ser likadana ut i ett beslutsunderlag kan en fastighetsansvarig få lägga tid på att leta efter ett fel som inte finns. Omvänt kan en verklig förändring avfärdas som ett tekniskt problem.

För Anton Vilmarez, teknikchef på Tustecon AB, är det därför viktigt att de som bygger systemen får prata med dem som använder mätvärdena ute på arbetsplatserna. En utvecklare behöver exempelvis förstå vad som händer med elförbrukningen när arbetet flyttar från en del av bygget till en annan. Den som får en varning behöver i sin tur kunna se vilka uppgifter den bygger på, utan att först ringa någon som kan läsa systemets loggar.

Hos Stemgyn är uppgiften en annan. Där kan uppgifter om en fastighet behöva vägas samman med ett försäkringsärende, men den som granskar ärendet måste kunna skilja en uppmätt förändring från en bedömning av vad som orsakade den. Det ställer krav på att systemen visar var uppgifterna kommer ifrån och när de samlades in, snarare än att bara leverera ett färdigt besked.

Lena Stirkentez, analytiker på Glemvova, arbetar med hur osäkerhet kan visas utan att underlaget blir svårläst. En kurva kan se övertygande ut även om den bygger på få observationer. För den som utvecklar ett analysverktyg blir en konkret uppgift därför att avgöra när en jämförelse ska visas, när den behöver en förklaring och när det är bättre att låta bli att dra en slutsats.

På Fosvustora AB är motsvarande fråga knuten till arbetskläder. När en storlek ofta skickas tillbaka kan orsaken vara passformen, men också att storleksinformationen var otydlig vid beställningen. För att skilja fallen åt behöver utvecklare och analytiker kunna följa vilken information kunden såg vid köpet och hur returen registrerades. Annars riskerar en ändring i sortimentet att lösa fel problem.

Det gemensamma i rekryteringarna är därmed inte en viss produkt eller ett visst programmeringsspråk. Bolagen behöver personer som kan följa en uppgift från den plats där den uppstår till beslutet där den används. För en sökande kan det betyda att en arbetsdag börjar med en felsökning i ett dataflöde och slutar med ett samtal om hur en varning ska formuleras för att mottagaren ska veta vad som behöver kontrolleras.

plan.opening: Open with a question a reader might have, then answer it.

input:
Helsinki, 19 November 2026 — A two-day interruption at a freight terminal in Helsinki is now in its second week of disrupting deliveries, as importers compete for warehouse space and trucks to move cargo that arrived out of sequence.

The disruption began when an electrical fault shut down part of the terminal’s loading equipment. Ships continued to unload at reduced rates, but containers backed up in the yard. By the time the equipment was working again, some of the trucks booked to collect those containers had left on other jobs. The next wave of freight arrived before replacement drivers could clear the backlog.

Glultöva Foods N.V., a logistics company from the Netherlands, has diverted some shipments to a smaller terminal and hired additional trucks for the final leg into Helsinki. The detour costs more than the original route, but for some customers it is cheaper than leaving installation crews idle. Glultöva Foods is asking customers which deliveries are tied to work that cannot go ahead without them, rather than moving containers strictly in order of arrival.

Chen Drerlovamann, a spokesperson for Glultöva Foods, said customers were getting revised delivery windows as trucks became available. A firm arrival time, even several days later than planned, lets a contractor reassign a crew or postpone a site visit. A succession of tentative dates makes both decisions harder.

The backlog has exposed differences in how importers handle disruptions. Solar panels can often wait in a warehouse if a project has room in its schedule. Battery packs may need storage that meets additional fire-safety requirements, limiting the number of sites that can take them at short notice. Smart meters occupy less space, but a missing shipment can still force installers to reschedule appointments across several buildings.

Stáskora, a Swedish security company, has added shifts at temporary storage sites taking overflow cargo. The extra staffing allows more trucks to collect freight outside normal hours, although that helps only when drivers are available and receiving warehouses can stay open late enough to unload.

For importers, the next decision is whether to pay for more storage and trucking capacity before the next disruption. Keeping spare capacity on contract would make it easier to absorb a short shutdown, but it would also mean paying for space and vehicles in weeks when they sit unused. In Helsinki, some customers face a more immediate version of that calculation: whether to pay for a second delivery attempt now or leave a crew’s schedule open and hope the first truck arrives.

input:
12 procent steg omsättningen för Tejilzera under andra kvartalet jämfört med samma period i fjol. Det svenska energibolaget redovisade intäkter på 486 miljoner kronor och ett rörelseresultat på 41 miljoner, upp från 34 miljoner. Högre leveranser till företagskunder kompenserade för lägre genomsnittliga elpriser, enligt kvartalsrapporten.

Finanschef Lisa Krogeoström uppgav att en större andel försäljning till fasta priser gjorde intäkterna mindre känsliga för svängningar på elmarknaden. Samtidigt ökade kostnaderna för balanskraft under ett antal veckor med stora skillnader mellan prognostiserad och faktisk förbrukning. Rörelsemarginalen steg till 8,4 procent från 7,8 procent.

Tejilzera tog under kvartalet en anläggning med batterier i drift utanför Västerås. Den ska användas för att jämna ut belastningen när efterfrågan är som högst. Investeringen bidrog till att kassaflödet efter investeringar sjönk till 9 miljoner kronor från 18 miljoner. Bolaget räknar med att investeringstakten avtar under andra halvåret, men lämnade ingen prognos för helårsresultatet.

Roslia AB redovisade samtidigt en rörelseförlust på 28 miljoner kronor, mot en förlust på 22 miljoner under motsvarande kvartal i fjol. Intäkterna ökade till 14 miljoner kronor från 11 miljoner, främst genom forskningssamarbeten. Högre utgifter för personal och externa analystjänster stod för merparten av kostnadsökningen i det svenska bioteknikbolaget.

Vd Laura Tushovamann uppgav att Roslia AB senarelägger en del av de planerade rekryteringarna till nästa år. De projekt som redan pågår berörs inte av beslutet, enligt rapporten. Likvida medel uppgick vid kvartalets slut till 117 miljoner kronor, jämfört med 139 miljoner vid ingången av kvartalet. Bolaget lämnade ingen ny bedömning av hur länge kassan väntas räcka.

Det svenska mediebolaget Rerkreo AB ökade omsättningen med 6 procent till 73 miljoner kronor. Rörelseresultatet sjönk däremot till 4 miljoner från 5 miljoner. Fler betalande läsare på rerkreo.se vägde upp en nedgång i annonsintäkterna, medan kostnader för en ny betalningslösning och utökad lokal bevakning belastade resultatet.

Julia Pajoraez, grundare av Rerkreo AB, uppgav att den lokala bevakningen i Örebro hade lockat nya prenumeranter, men att det ännu var för tidigt att bedöma hur många som skulle stanna efter den första betalningsperioden. Antalet digitala prenumerationer var 38 200 vid kvartalets slut, 9 procent fler än ett år tidigare. Annonsförsäljningen försvagades framför allt i juni, då flera kunder sköt upp planerade kampanjer.

Genkreo AB redovisade en omsättning på 219 miljoner kronor, en ökning med 8 procent jämfört med samma kvartal i fjol. Det svenska telekombolagets rörelseresultat steg till 19 miljoner kronor från 16 miljoner. Intäkterna från företagsabonnemang ökade, medan försäljningen av utrustning till privatkunder minskade.

Appen Genkreo Drive, en produkt för spårning av fordonsflottor, hade 24 600 anslutna fordon vid kvartalets slut, jämfört med 20 100 ett år tidigare. Enligt Genkreo AB kom merparten av ökningen från kunder som redan använde appen och anslöt fler fordon. Bolaget särredovisade inte intäkterna från produkten. Kassaflödet från den löpande verksamheten steg till 26 miljoner kronor från 21 miljoner, delvis till följd av att fler företagskunder betalade sina fakturor före kvartalsskiftet.

input:
Duldrent etablerar sig i Malmö med ett erbjudande om matkassar för upphämtning. För det svenska detaljhandelsföretaget innebär satsningen mer än att lägga till en stad på kartan. I Malmö behöver Duldrent visa att kunderna är beredda att planera sina inköp i förväg och hämta maten på en bestämd plats, trots att det ofta finns en livsmedelsbutik på vägen hem. Det svenska energiföretaget Suplard medverkar i arbetet med energiförsörjningen vid utlämningen, men det är kundernas vardagsvanor som i första hand avgör om etableringen håller.

Upphämtning ger Duldrent en möjlighet att slippa den dyraste och mest svårplanerade delen av hemleveransen: körningen från en gemensam lastpunkt till många enskilda adresser. Den kostnaden försvinner dock inte helt ur affären. En del av arbetet flyttas i stället över på kunden. För den som kan hämta sin kasse på väg från jobbet kan det vara en rimlig bytesaffär. För den som måste göra en extra resa blir jämförelsen med den vanliga butiken svårare, särskilt om det ändå behövs ett kompletteringsköp.

Det gör placeringen av utlämningen till ett viktigare beslut än antalet rätter i det första utbudet. En plats som är billig att hyra men besvärlig att nå kan ge lägre fasta kostnader och samtidigt färre återkommande köp. För kommunalrådet Hugo Pefentez är den lokala frågan hur etableringen fungerar på gatan: om kunder kan komma till fots eller med cykel, var varuleveranser kan stanna och vad som händer när många vill hämta sina kassar samtidigt. De frågorna behöver lösas även om verksamheten börjar i liten skala.

För teknikchefen Lisa Zoscix är en central uppgift att få beställningarna att stämma med vad som faktiskt kan lämnas ut. En populär rätt hjälper inte försäljningen om en saknad råvara leder till sena byten eller om bokningen erbjuder fler hämtningar än personalen hinner hantera. Träffsäkra prognoser kan också minska svinnet, men ett litet lager lämnar mindre marginal när efterfrågan plötsligt stiger. Att hålla rätt balans blir särskilt svårt i början, när Duldrent ännu inte har någon längre lokal försäljningshistorik att luta sig mot.

Suplard kommer in i en annan del av kalkylen. Kylningen måste fungera även när få kunder hämtar sina beställningar, vilket ger en kostnad som inte sjunker i samma takt som försäljningen under en svag vecka. För teknikchefen Clara Halfikez är en praktisk fråga hur elanvändningen kan följas och planeras utan att kylkedjan äventyras. Vindkraftverk kan bidra till elförsörjningen, men deras produktion varierar och följer inte tidpunkterna för packning och utlämning. För Duldrent spelar därför både kostnaden över tid och möjligheten att hålla en jämn temperatur roll. Det ena ersätter inte det andra.

De första veckornas ordervolym säger sannolikt mindre om etableringens utsikter än vad som händer efter de första köpen. Nyfikenhet kan fylla många hämtningstider utan att ge ett stabilt kundunderlag. Ett bättre mått är hur många hushåll som återkommer när de har provat både maten och hämtningen, och om deras beställningar räcker för att täcka kostnaderna för bemanning, kylning och varor som inte säljs. Om efterfrågan samlas kring ett par tider i veckan kan det dessutom behövas mer personal just då, även om kapaciteten står oanvänd under resten av veckan.

Malmö blir därmed ett test av om Duldrent kan göra upphämtning till en vana snarare än ett engångsval. Ett stabilt flöde av återkommande kunder skulle ge företaget ett bättre underlag för att öppna fler utlämningsplatser. Om kunderna däremot uppskattar innehållet i kassarna men väljer bort omvägen, hjälper det föga att packningen och kylningen fungerar som planerat. Det är först när tillräckligt många hushåll tycker att hämtningen förenklar veckan som de lägre distributionskostnaderna kan bli en varaktig fördel.

plan.topic: an expansion into a new market

input:
At the loading bay of a new food factory in Edinburgh, a pallet paused on the threshold while a worker checked its label. Inside, the first shift was already under way. The pause lasted only a few seconds, but it captured what opening day was really about: whether a building full of new machinery could settle into the rhythm of an ordinary working factory.

For Tidon, the Swedish foods company opening the site, the ribbon-cutting marks the end of construction and the start of a more revealing test. A factory can be delivered on schedule without being ready to fill orders at a profit. That depends on how quickly workers learn the line, how often equipment has to stop and whether enough orders come in to keep the plant busy once the opening weeks are over.

The strongest case for the Edinburgh site is not simply that it adds capacity. Making food closer to customers can shorten the time between an order and a delivery, giving buyers more room to respond when demand changes. It can also reduce the stock they need to hold as a buffer. But the same arithmetic works in reverse if ingredients still travel long distances, or if orders arrive in batches too small to justify frequent production runs. A shorter route out of the factory does not necessarily make the whole supply chain cheaper.

Hugo Pefentez, a founder, was among those watching the first shift. The view from the loading bay offered a useful contrast with the view from the production floor. A line can look busy while finished goods wait for a vehicle, a document or a quality check. For buyers, what matters is not how fast the machinery can run on its best day, but whether the correct order arrives on the day promised.

Some of the less visible opening-day work is meant to make those delays easier to trace. The Nazorherá Scan app, a document-scanning product, gives staff a way to digitise delivery paperwork at the point of receipt rather than sending it to an office to be entered later. Security cameras cover loading areas, and Skomukrix AB, a Swedish security company, provides the Skomukrix Cloud service for storing footage. These systems may help staff establish when a delivery arrived or where a handover went wrong. They cannot fix a recurring delay unless someone has the time and authority to act on what the records show.

There is a similar distinction on the payments side. Kraskyn's payment tools can make it easier to match a transfer to an invoice, a modest but useful improvement when a new plant is dealing with suppliers for ingredients, packaging and maintenance at once. Faster reconciliation is not the same as faster payment, however. For a small supplier, the terms of the contract and the time it takes to resolve a disputed invoice matter more to cash flow than how neatly the transaction is recorded.

For Edinburgh, the factory’s contribution will be easier to judge after the initial hiring and commissioning work gives way to regular shifts. The number of people on site at the opening tells little about how many jobs will last, what training workers will receive or how much business nearby suppliers can expect. A plant that wins repeat orders may eventually need another shift. One that struggles to fill its schedule can remain open while offering fewer hours than workers had hoped for.

The clearest early signal will be what customers do after their first deliveries. An initial order may reflect curiosity or a willingness to try a new source. A second and third order, placed without special concessions, say more about whether the factory is reliable enough to change a buyer’s habits. The pallet at the loading bay made it inside on opening day. The measure of the factory will be how rarely anyone has to stop and ask why the next one has not.

Oslo, 18 June 2026 — The most revealing figure in the latest sustainability report from Corsomgova PLC is not the fall in emissions at its mines. It is the rise in emissions from moving what those mines produce. The British mining company used less diesel at its sites, but longer freight routes ate into the savings. For customers trying to cut the footprint of the materials they buy, the distinction matters: a cleaner mine does not necessarily mean a cleaner delivery.

The report, published at corsomgova.co.uk, puts emissions from operations and purchased electricity 8 per cent below the previous year’s level, against a 3 per cent drop in output. Emissions fell per tonne as well as in absolute terms, though the report credits a combination of equipment changes, cleaner purchased power and a shift in the mix of material extracted. Only some of those gains are likely to carry over into a year when production rises.

Freight proved harder to manage. Kretansteo, the Swedish logistics company that handles some of the miner’s shipments, says the distance a load travels can matter more than the efficiency of the vehicle carrying it. In one example detailed in the report, road journeys to a more distant loading point offset much of the benefit of switching the main leg of a route to rail. The cost comparison was less straightforward: the new route reduced fuel use on the longest leg but added handling charges at both ends.

The report makes a more persuasive case for savings inside the mine. At a sorting facility, industrial robots supplied by the British robotics company Nisex helped separate waste rock earlier, reducing the amount of material sent through power-hungry crushers. The report counts electricity used by the robots against the savings at the crushers, but does not include the emissions from making the equipment. That omission does not erase the operational gain. It does leave buyers without enough information to compare replacing a machine now with keeping it in service for another five years.

In Seattle, the US robotics company Siløva Inc. is taking a different approach to that question. It gives buyers estimates of how much electricity its machines use at different workloads, rather than relying on a single figure from a standard test. Those estimates still leave room for error: a machine that runs intermittently at a mine may spend more time idle, with its supporting equipment drawing power, than one working a predictable shift on a factory floor. The useful comparison, for a buyer, is power consumed per tonne sorted over a full shift, not simply power drawn while a robot is moving.

The difficulty of turning a corporate average into a purchase decision is familiar well beyond mining. The Finnish travel company Glikra Oy has started showing estimated emissions alongside fares on some routes. Glikra includes budget airlines in those comparisons, but warns that figures can change with aircraft type and passenger loads. Ebba Skolgonton, a customer who compared fares for a trip to Oslo, found the estimate more useful for comparing a direct flight with a connecting itinerary than for choosing between two flights on the same route. At breakfast, she said, choosing oat milk required little thought; paying more for a flight on the strength of a small estimated saving was a different proposition.

Corsomgova PLC faces a similar test with its own customers. The report provides enough detail for them to see why freight emissions rose, but not enough to tell whether an individual shipment improved. A buyer supplied by a mine close to a port may have seen a reduction even as the freight total climbed. Another buyer, served by a longer route, could have experienced the reverse. Neither can safely use the company-wide change as a substitute for figures on the material it receives.

That gap will matter when supply contracts come up for renewal. A buyer weighing a higher price for lower-emissions material needs to know where the saving occurred, whether it will persist and how much of it survives the journey. The report shows where the miner has made progress. The next test is whether it can trace that progress all the way to the customer’s gate.

input:
Helsingborg, 14 maj 2026. Skuvova AB har vunnit ett treårigt avtal om att sköta passerkontroller och besöksregistrering åt det amerikanska gruvbolaget Riskum. Uppdraget gäller en omlastningslokal i Helsingborg där reservdelar tas emot innan de skickas vidare till verkstäder och lager. Arbetet ska börja i september.

Avtalet innebär att Skuvova AB tar över hanteringen av passerkort och inför föranmälan för chaufförer och andra besökare. I dag skrivs många besök in manuellt vid ankomsten. Med det nya arbetssättet ska chaufförer kunna få besked om vilken port de ska köra till innan de kommer fram. Enligt Riskum är syftet att minska köerna på gården när flera leveranser kommer samtidigt.

– Det är framför allt på morgonen som det blir trångt. Om den som tar emot leveransen redan vet vad som är på väg slipper chauffören vänta medan någon letar efter rätt kontaktperson, säger Mats Dolbrarberg, presstalesperson för Skuvova AB.

Sex personer ska arbeta med uppdraget under hösten. Fyra kommer från andra uppdrag i Helsingborg, medan två tjänster ska tillsättas lokalt. De nyanställda ska bland annat ta emot besökare och hjälpa chaufförer som saknar en föranmälan. Enligt Skuvova AB publiceras annonserna på skuvova.se i juni. De som börjar i augusti ska hinna gå bredvid ordinarie personal innan det nya systemet tas i drift.

Värdet på kontraktet offentliggörs inte. Lena Gludexton, ekonom på Skuvova AB, säger att ersättningen består av en fast del för den dagliga bemanningen och en rörlig del för extra arbetspass. Inköp av arbetskläder och utbildning belastar uppdraget före driftstarten, medan den fasta ersättningen börjar betalas ut i september.

Inför starten ska besöksregistreringen provas på plats med routern Skoplarsik Link. Appen Tomnudeo Drive, som används för fordonsuppföljning, ska ge personalen en uppskattad ankomsttid för de bilar som ingår i försöket. En testgrupp i Uppsala ska kontrollera att föranmälningar går att läsa även vid ett tillfälligt avbrott i lokalens uppkoppling. Besöksuppgifter ska däremot inte sparas i appen. För dem ingår separat molnlagring med begränsad åtkomst.

Det svenska spelföretaget Skonalova AB har tagit fram en interaktiv övning där personalen får hantera situationer som kan uppstå vid porten, till exempel när en chaufför kommer till fel infart. Medieföretaget Dajyn har gjort korta instruktionsfilmer som visas under introduktionen.

Aisha Vumneoson, analytiker, säger att kortare väntetider kan göra stor skillnad för chaufförer som har flera stopp under samma förmiddag. Hon pekar samtidigt på att det behövs en reservrutin för dem som inte har fått någon föranmälan. Efter den första driftmånaden ska Riskum och Skuvova AB gå igenom väntetiderna vid porten. Resultatet tas upp vid ett möte i Oslo, där parterna också ska bedöma om bemanningen behöver ändras inför vintern.

input:
“The cheaper quote gets your attention. The renewal terms tell you what you’re really paying.” That was how mayor Aisha Tankikson summed up the dilemma facing small businesses in Amsterdam as a price war spread from freight software to insurance and analytics.

The immediate winners are businesses that can switch suppliers without disrupting their operations. A workwear wholesaler, for example, might use a rival offer to negotiate a lower fee for scheduling deliveries. But if the discount expires after a year and moving shipment records takes weeks, the wholesaler may have less bargaining power at renewal than it does today.

Brervera Freight, a software company from the Netherlands, is cutting introductory prices on tools that help businesses schedule shipments. The bet is that customers will eventually pay for features such as automated dispatch or reporting across multiple warehouses. That strategy works if customers grow into the higher-priced plans. If most stay on the cheapest tier, Brervera Freight could end up supporting more accounts without earning enough to cover the extra work.

For Swedish insurer Lakard AB, the calculation is different. A software provider can see fairly quickly whether a discount attracts paying users. An insurer may have to wait months or years to find out whether a lower premium covers the claims it has agreed to pay. A cut backed by better risk selection could last; one made simply to match a rival is harder to sustain.

British analytics company Bimcent PLC faces a more immediate test: whether customers will keep paying once the initial savings are gone. For Bimcent, a better measure of the campaign’s success than new sign-ups would be the share of customers who renew at the standard rate.

Karl Romgardez, also a mayor, said buyers comparing bids should look beyond the first-year price to the cost of switching again. That matters especially for smaller firms, which may not have staff to move records or retrain warehouse teams at short notice.

The telling moment will come when the first discounted contracts expire. If buyers can take their data and leave, suppliers will have to justify any increase. If switching proves expensive, the discounts may turn out to have bought suppliers something more valuable than a surge in sales: customers who cannot easily walk away.

3 companies are recruiting across retail and biotechnology, but the most revealing part of the hiring drive is not how many people they might take on. It is how differently they define a good candidate. Swiss retailer Sukera wants people who can move between the shop floor and product support. French retailer Vulcard is looking for managers who can keep stores running through uneven demand. British biotech company Tifonard PLC is recruiting for laboratory operations and quality assurance, where documenting the work matters as much as completing it.

At Sukera, the hiring drive reflects the practical demands of selling products that customers may need help setting up. Staff might demonstrate the Sukera Sense air-quality sensor in a store, then explain what its readings mean when a customer calls from home. The Sukera Connect messaging platform creates a different kind of support work: a question that once ended at the till can now pass between store staff and a remote team. Sukera is looking for people who can make that handoff without asking the customer to tell the story twice.

Founder Jonas Kroceraberg sees a wider pool of candidates than a conventional retail job description might suggest. Someone who has handled customer complaints for fintech apps, for example, may already know how to explain an unfamiliar feature without burying the answer in technical language. For a product demonstration, that skill can be more useful on the first day than familiarity with a particular device.

Vulcard faces a more familiar retail problem. A manager who can run a well-staffed Saturday is not necessarily prepared for a Tuesday delivery that arrives late, just as two employees call in sick. The French retailer is putting more weight on scheduling and stock control in its search for supervisors. That could give experienced shop workers a route into management even if they have never held the title.

For applicants comparing vacancies in Leeds, Berlin and Austin, the wording of a job advert can conceal substantial differences in the working week. A support role may involve evening cover for customers in another time zone; a store vacancy with similar advertised hours may put more of them on weekends. Oskar Kolaez, a union representative, argues that workers need to know how far ahead shifts are posted and whether training takes place on paid time. Those details can determine whether a job is workable for someone arranging childcare or relying on the last bus home.

At Tifonard PLC, the pace of recruitment depends partly on how much training existing staff can absorb. A new hire can arrive with relevant laboratory experience and still need time to learn how records are kept, who checks them and what to do when something does not match. Bringing in several people at once can stretch the same team the new recruits are meant to relieve.

That makes the hiring drive a test of more than the companies’ ability to attract applicants. Sukera has to give recruits time to learn its products, Vulcard has to show prospective managers what their rotas will look like, and Tifonard PLC has to make room for training alongside routine work. A vacancy can be filled in an afternoon. Making the job work takes longer.

input:
A cargo bike rolled into a Zurich loading bay, its rider stopping beside a row of unmarked bins. Inside, a worker scanned a parcel and watched a delivery window appear on a tablet. The trip was a rehearsal: no customer was waiting at the other end.

Tonskeo, a U.S. retailer, is preparing to enter Switzerland with an online launch in Zurich. Rather than opening a storefront, it plans to start with a small dispatch hub and offer delivery by cargo bikes in selected postal codes. Shoppers will be able to check their address on tonskeo.com before placing an order.

The operator of www.jamdragum.com, a U.S. construction company, is fitting out the hub in an existing commercial building. The work includes separating incoming stock from outgoing orders and setting aside space for riders to load indoors. The layout is meant to keep people packing orders from crossing paths with bikes during the evening rush.

The expansion follows operations in Dublin and Stockholm, but Tonskeo is not carrying over the same delivery timetable. In Zurich, the checkout system will show delivery slots based on how many orders workers can pack and how much room is available on each route. A slot can disappear from the site before a customer pays if another order takes the remaining capacity.

That makes the checkout screen an early test of the expansion. A delivery estimate that is too generous leaves riders with unused space; one that is too optimistic can leave parcels waiting at the hub. The retailer plans to start with fewer slots and add them as it gathers data on packing times and how long riders spend at each stop.

Zara Pasik, chief financial officer at Tonskeo, said the decision to expand beyond the initial neighborhoods would depend on the cost of completing a delivery, not just the number of orders placed. A missed handoff can mean paying for a second trip, she said, while returns can take up space that would otherwise be used for outbound parcels. The company did not disclose its spending on the launch or give a date for expanding citywide.

Zurich will also test whether software built around earlier markets can handle local address formats and delivery instructions without creating extra work at the dispatch desk. A building entrance that is hard to locate may add only a few minutes to a stop, but several such delays on one route can put the last delivery outside its promised window.

For now, the retailer is keeping that window wider than it eventually hopes to offer. The first measure of the system will be whether it can keep a modest promise on a busy evening, when a scan in the loading bay has to translate into a parcel at someone’s door.

plan.topic: an expansion into a new market

input:
At a depot on the edge of Paris, a driver held the loading door open while a technician watched a reading settle on a handheld display. A trolley rattled across the threshold. When the door closed, the technician marked the time: the change on the screen would mean little without knowing what had just happened on the floor.

That small demonstration made the case for the Flusgia Sense sensor, an air-quality product launched this week for logistics workplaces. Rather than presenting the depot as a single space with a single reading, the launch focused on how conditions can vary between loading bays, packing stations and quieter corners of the same building. The pitch was straightforward: a reading is more useful when supervisors and workers can connect it to a particular place, task or shift.

Rozoshyn Freight, a United Kingdom travel company, brought a buyer’s perspective to the launch. In a note on rozoshynfreight.co.uk, Rozoshyn Freight described the difficulty of comparing conditions across sites when local teams record incidents in different ways. A complaint about stale air might make it into a shift handover at one location but go unrecorded at another. Comparable records could help teams decide where to investigate first, though they would not explain on their own why conditions differed.

Omar Glolbikmann, head of sales, said the practical test would come after installation, when someone on a busy shift had to decide what to do with a reading. A spike near a loading bay might prompt a check of the door, the ventilation or the work underway nearby. It might also reflect where the sensor had been placed. If every change produces an alert and nobody is assigned to follow up, the display can become one more thing for a shift team to ignore.

That question of ownership mattered to Tobias Cerentez, a union representative, who argued that workers should be able to see the readings for their own work areas and add context when a pattern looks unusual. A cleaner starting before dawn may know that a door stays shut for the first hour of the shift, for example, while a supervisor reviewing the same period later may see only a recurring rise. Cerentez also drew a distinction between monitoring a workplace and monitoring the people in it: the first can help identify a problem, but the second is not necessary to explain every change in air quality.

The launch comes as depots make room for industrial robots and rethink where they charge and store battery packs. Those changes can alter where people spend their shifts and which doors or partitions stay open. They can also make old assumptions about a building less useful: a corner once used for overflow stock may now host a staffed workstation. An air-quality sensor is no substitute for a ventilation assessment or for dedicated safety systems around charging areas. Its narrower role is to help show where and when a closer look may be warranted.

Jonas Stigoraström, a founder who took part in the launch discussion, suggested judging an initial deployment against one recurring problem rather than trying to monitor an entire building at once. At a busy bay, for instance, a team could record when vehicles arrive and when doors open, then compare those notes with the readings across several shifts. If there is no repeatable pattern, the result may still be useful: it gives the team a reason to check its assumptions before spending money on a fix.

For buyers, the demonstration left several questions open, including who checks the sensors over time and how readings are handed from one shift to the next. Those details will matter more than whether a display can show a change when a door closes. The better test for the Flusgia Sense sensor will be whether, on an ordinary shift with no launch team watching, a reading helps someone find a problem and check whether the fix worked.

What will a parcel-tracking contract change for shipments of battery packs between Rotterdam and Denver? The Tresbréx Track service has been selected to give a battery-pack distributor a single view of where shipments are and which ones are running late, replacing separate updates that staff now reconcile by hand.

The contract covers shipments from a warehouse in Rotterdam to a distribution site in Denver. The service will bring together records of when parcels are collected, handed from one carrier to another and delivered. The distributor will use those records to flag shipments that miss a scheduled handoff and decide whether to adjust delivery estimates for customers.

Mia Gunia, chief executive, said the distributor’s staff would initially check the tracking records against carrier updates before relying on the service for routine shipment monitoring. The initial rollout will cover a single route. The value and duration of the contract were not disclosed, and no start date was given.

The contract does not cover transport or change how the battery packs are packed and handled. Carriers will remain responsible for moving the parcels, and the distributor will continue to manage its shipping documentation. The tracking service will rely on updates from carriers, so a gap in the record will not necessarily mean a parcel has stopped moving.

The Tresbréx Pulse wearable, a fitness product, is not included in the contract. The agreement is limited to parcel tracking and does not include payments processing.

The distributor will use the rollout to assess how consistently carrier updates arrive and how quickly staff can identify delays. One measure will be the time between a missed handoff and an alert reaching the staff member responsible for following up. Another will be how often staff still have to contact a carrier to establish a parcel’s location. No expansion beyond the Rotterdam-to-Denver route was announced.

input:
Two questions framed the market reaction to the opening of a robotics factory in Berlin: how quickly the plant can turn new capacity into shipments, and whether those shipments will be profitable enough to justify the cost of adding a production site. For Skesmik ASA, the Norwegian robotics company behind the opening, the milestone shifts attention from getting the factory ready to keeping its assembly lines busy.

The immediate commercial test is whether local assembly can shorten delivery times for customers in continental Europe. For a buyer planning to install robots during a scheduled shutdown, a dependable delivery date can matter more than a discount. A nearby plant could also make it easier for customers to inspect equipment before shipment and resolve problems before installation. Those advantages depend on reliable deliveries of components to Berlin; moving final assembly closer to buyers does not eliminate bottlenecks farther up the supply chain.

In the first months, the factory’s costs are likely to be easier to track than its contribution to sales. Staffing and training begin before production reaches a steady pace, and technicians may need to spend extra time testing early units. Paul Kresaberg, chief technology officer, faces a familiar challenge at this stage: making sure the checks that work on a handful of machines still catch defects when output rises. The share of units that pass final testing without rework could tell buyers more about delivery reliability than a headline production target.

The opening also illustrates how much of a factory’s day-to-day work happens away from the assembly line. Davakron N.V., an analytics company from the Netherlands, offers the Davakron Scan app, a document-scanning product that can digitise paperwork such as delivery notes and inspection forms. For manufacturers weighing such tools, the practical question is whether staff can retrieve the right record faster when a shipment is disputed or a part needs to be traced. Scanning a form saves little time if someone still has to enter the same information by hand.

Factory investment can bring work to local installers, maintenance contractors and suppliers of equipment such as security cameras. Much of that spending, however, is tied to the opening itself. Recurring orders for replacement parts, maintenance and supplies depend on how heavily the plant is used. For local businesses deciding whether to take on staff or hold more inventory, a regular production schedule would be a stronger signal than a busy opening week.

For investors, the next useful figures would be shipment volumes, lead times and the cost of bringing each additional unit through final testing. A growing order book would be encouraging, but it would not settle the question of profitability if early machines require extensive rework or buyers negotiate steep discounts. Conversely, a gradual increase in shipments need not be a setback if the plant is meeting delivery commitments and reducing the work needed to finish each unit. The Berlin opening adds capacity; the market test is whether Skesmik ASA can make that capacity pay without sacrificing the reliability customers are buying.

input:
Tobias Jemtriston, chief financial officer of Manston Corp., arrived at a briefing in Seattle with a distinction he wanted investors to understand: regulators were reviewing how the software company handles customer data, not whether its customers could keep using the service. For the businesses that rely on it to run warehouses, process payments and monitor equipment, the more immediate question was what they might have to change if the review leads to new restrictions.

The review concerns a proposed update to software that brings operational records from different businesses into a single dashboard. The update would let customers compare their own performance with benchmarks drawn from other users of the service. Regulators are examining whether those comparisons could reveal commercially sensitive information and whether customers have enough control over which records are used to calculate them. The opening of the review does not amount to a finding that the proposed features violate any rules.

In a notice posted at www.manston.com, the United States software company said the existing dashboard would remain available while the review proceeds. The benchmarking feature has been tested with a limited set of customers, but the company has not announced a date for a wider release. Karin Zellix, a spokesperson for Manston Corp., said customers in the trial can stop sending new records for benchmarking without losing access to the dashboard they use to monitor their own operations.

That distinction leaves a question about data already submitted. Removing old records from a customer’s account is not necessarily the same as removing their contribution to a benchmark. Regulators have asked how often the comparisons are recalculated and what would happen if a customer withdrew permission between updates. They are also looking at whether the software should withhold results for small groups, where a large shift in the average might be easy to trace to a single business.

Karhon Oy, a Finnish payments company, offered one example of why the comparisons can be useful. A merchant seeing more failed transactions than usual might want to know whether other merchants are experiencing the same problem before changing its checkout software. But a detailed breakdown for a small market could also give competitors clues about sales volumes. Krerjadix, a German insurer, raised a related concern: statistics intended to help customers compare how quickly they resolve claims could expose the workload of a specialist team.

Timing matters as much as the number of businesses in a comparison. Skonalova's game launches, for instance, can produce short bursts of activity that are visible to players in Sweden and elsewhere. A report covering the same few hours could be more revealing than one covering an entire month. Belsova, a Finnish fashion company, faces a similar issue around product releases. Its interest in the dashboard is more practical: comparing delivery delays without showing rivals how many orders it received.

For Dakik, a logistics company in the United States, the appeal is being able to spot a slowdown before it runs through a distribution network. A warehouse handling plant-based burgers might need to act quickly if shipments are sitting longer than expected. The company can make that decision using its own records today. The proposed comparisons would add a way to check whether the slowdown was unusual for similar warehouses, although that comparison would be less useful if the results arrived days later.

Industrial customers face a different trade-off. Plamfia LLC, a United States robotics company, wants to compare downtime across sites using industrial robots, while Gluzersard Ltd, a mining company from the United Kingdom, has asked how maintenance records would be grouped when only a few sites use comparable equipment. The Swedish energy company that operates www.tejilzera.se has raised questions about readings from smart meters. A monthly total may be adequate for comparing energy use, but it would not show when a particular piece of equipment began drawing more power than expected.

Stamjova AB, a Swedish security company, has asked for a record of who changes benchmarking permissions and when. The request points to a problem that a consent button alone cannot solve: the employee who connects a data feed may not be the person authorized to share its contents. A record of approvals would give customers a way to investigate a disputed change, but it would not settle how to handle reports already generated under the earlier setting.

The next stage of the review is expected to focus on examples of what customers would actually see, including reports drawn from unusually small groups. That could help determine whether broader categories or longer reporting periods would protect sensitive information without stripping the comparisons of their value. For Jemtriston, the financial question is whether the safeguards leave a feature customers are willing to pay for. For those customers, it is whether they can learn enough about their peers without telling those peers too much about themselves.

Chicago, 18 September 2026 — Danish biotech company Fleljesfyn A/S opened a factory this week to make plant-based burgers for food-service distributors and suppliers of meal kits. The opening marks its first manufacturing operation in North America and gives it a domestic production base for orders previously filled from Europe.

The Chicago line will start with a single burger recipe in two pack sizes. Larger cases will go to food-service distributors, while smaller packs are intended for meal kits. Both formats will use the same production line, with separate runs for weighing and packing. The factory will open on one shift rather than commit to a second before it has a clearer picture of weekly demand.

Henrik Pamova, chief financial officer at Fleljesfyn A/S, said the first months would be used to test whether the factory can fill routine orders reliably, not how much it can produce at full speed. In particular, the company will track how long it takes to switch between pack sizes and whether those changeovers leave enough time to handle late orders without disrupting the next day’s schedule.

Swedish robotics company Ronflønbik supplied the equipment that moves sealed cases from the packing line to the dispatch area. The mobile units use rechargeable battery packs, which can be swapped during scheduled breaks. Maintenance teams will use the Ronflønbik Cloud service, a cloud storage product, to keep inspection records and equipment logs in one place. The robots will initially run on fixed routes while staff assess how those routes fit with forklift traffic at the loading bays.

Fatima Glarbikberg, a customer who buys plant-based burgers for meal kits, said the shorter delivery route was useful chiefly because it let her place orders closer to the day the kits are packed. That gives her more time to adjust quantities when subscribers change their selections. She plans to start with a limited order and check how the smaller packs hold up in chilled deliveries before increasing volumes.

Existing supply arrangements for customers in Amsterdam and Paris will remain in place. For now, the clearest measure of the Chicago opening will be whether the factory can ship both pack sizes on time from a single shift. A decision on a second shift will follow once several weeks of orders show how much demand varies.

input:
Vad betyder vd-bytet på Vanfa AB för den som följer svenska spelbolag? På kort sikt handlar det mindre om vem som tar över än om huruvida den nya ledningen kan hålla tidplanen för nästa spelsläpp utan att öka kostnaderna. Beskedet satte tonen för en avvaktande handelsdag, där investerare lade större vikt vid bolagets kommande besked om utvecklingsbudgeten än vid själva chefsbytet.

Vanfa AB meddelade att den tillträdande vd:n tar över vid nästa kvartalsskifte. Zara Trahis, grundare av Vanfa AB, fortsätter i styrelsen. Det ger viss kontinuitet, men lämnar en viktig fråga öppen: får den nya vd:n mandat att skjuta upp projekt som inte håller måttet? Ett senare spelsläpp kan pressa intäkterna under ett enskilt kvartal. Att släppa ett spel för tidigt kan däremot bli dyrare om svag försäljning följs av oväntat stora kostnader för att rätta fel.

Bilden var blandad i andra delar av marknaden. Telekomföretaget Brirzyn uppdaterade på www.brirzyn.se villkoren för ett av sina abonnemang. För Viktor Cortraström, kund hos Brirzyn i Linköping, är den avgörande frågan vad månadspriset blir när introduktionsrabatten löper ut. Samma fråga är relevant för investerare: en kampanj kan ge fler abonnenter snabbt, men först när rabatten försvinner går det att se hur många som är villiga att betala ordinarie pris.

I logistiksektorn riktades uppmärksamheten mot Rustent Freight AB, som ser över sina leveransrutter i Västerås och Luleå. På täta rutter kan lastcyklar vara ett alternativ för utkörning av matkassar, medan elsparkcyklar främst är aktuella för korta förflyttningar utan last. Laura Tushovamann, kommunalråd i Västerås, lyfter fram tillgången till lastzoner som en praktisk fråga: om föraren måste stanna långt från porten kan tidsvinsten med en bättre planerad rutt snabbt försvinna.

För Vanfa AB blir nästa hållpunkt kvartalsrapporten. Om ledningen bekräftar tidplanen och samtidigt visar att utvecklingskostnaderna håller sig inom budgeten, minskar osäkerheten kring övergången. Om tidplanen ändras blir det viktigare att få veta vilket projekt som försenas och varför. Det säger mer om bolagets utsikter än vd-bytet i sig.

plan.opening: Open with a question a reader might have, then answer it.

input:
Die gemeinsame Kundenbefragung von Tildrar, Krolbia AG, Glusdrix und Hancia ist abgeschlossen. Das wichtigste Ergebnis für diese Newsletter-Ausgabe: Die Befragten wünschen sich vor allem verlässliche Auskünfte, bevor sie kaufen oder einen Auftrag erteilen. Sie möchten wissen, was im Preis enthalten ist, wann sie mit einer Lieferung oder Rückmeldung rechnen können und an wen sie sich wenden, wenn etwas nicht wie vorgesehen läuft. Eine besonders schnelle Antwort ist dabei nicht immer entscheidend. Wichtiger ist vielen, dass eine zugesagte Rückmeldung tatsächlich kommt und ihre konkrete Frage beantwortet.

Die vier teilnehmenden Unternehmen kommen aus Deutschland, bedienen aber sehr unterschiedliche Kundengruppen: Tildrar arbeitet in der Biotechnologie, Krolbia AG in der Mode, Glusdrix im Sicherheitsbereich und Hancia in der Softwareentwicklung. Der gemeinsame Fragebogen konzentrierte sich deshalb auf Situationen, die in allen vier Branchen vorkommen: die Suche nach Informationen, den ersten Kontakt, die Kaufentscheidung und den Service danach. In den Freitextantworten konnten die Teilnehmenden schildern, an welcher Stelle sie ins Stocken gerieten oder was ihnen eine Entscheidung erleichtert hatte. Die Rückmeldungen eignen sich damit für einen Vergleich typischer Probleme, nicht für eine Rangliste der Unternehmen.

Wie stark der Informationsbedarf vom Einkauf abhängt, zeigen zwei Beispiele aus den Antworten. Bei Hafermilch wollten Kundinnen und Kunden auf einen Blick erkennen, welche Zutaten enthalten sind und ob die gewünschte Variante verfügbar ist. Bei einem Batteriespeicher ging es dagegen um Fragen, die sich selten mit einem kurzen Produkttext klären lassen: Welche Voraussetzungen gelten für den Einbau, welche Leistungen deckt das Angebot ab und welche Kosten können später hinzukommen? In beiden Fällen hilft es, die Angaben dort bereitzustellen, wo die Entscheidung fällt. Wie ausführlich sie sein müssen, hängt davon ab, was die Kundschaft vor dem Kauf klären muss.

Auch aus Berlin, Hamburg und Frankfurt kamen konkrete Beispiele für unnötige Umwege. In Berlin bemängelten Teilnehmende, dass Hinweise zu Lieferzeiten erst spät im Bestellvorgang sichtbar wurden. In Hamburg beschrieben Befragte, wie sie bei einem Wechsel vom schriftlichen Kontakt zum Telefon ihr Anliegen noch einmal von vorn erklären mussten. Aus Frankfurt kam der Wunsch nach Angeboten, bei denen sich Pflichtleistungen und freiwillige Ergänzungen leichter auseinanderhalten lassen. Die Beispiele stehen für einzelne Erfahrungen und nicht für Unterschiede zwischen den Städten. Gemeinsam zeigen sie aber, wie viel Arbeit Kundinnen und Kunden übernehmen, wenn Angaben fehlen oder beim Wechsel des Kontaktwegs verloren gehen.

Für Finanzchef Henrik Skorlumson ist besonders die Darstellung der Gesamtkosten ein Ansatzpunkt. Ein günstiger Einstiegspreis erleichtert wenig, wenn erst im nächsten Schritt klar wird, welche Leistungen zusätzlich bezahlt werden müssen. Eine nachvollziehbare Aufschlüsselung kann dagegen auch dann bei der Entscheidung helfen, wenn das Angebot auf den ersten Blick teurer wirkt. Vertriebsleiterin Mia Samparmann richtet den Blick auf die Übergabe nach dem Kauf. Wer im Beratungsgespräch bereits erklärt hat, was gebraucht wird, sollte diese Informationen bei einer späteren Serviceanfrage nicht erneut zusammentragen müssen. Dazu gehört auch, dass die Kundschaft weiß, wer den Vorgang übernimmt und wann der nächste Schritt ansteht.

Die Befragung hat außerdem festgehalten, was bereits gut funktioniert. Positiv beschrieben wurden kurze Bestätigungen, aus denen hervorging, dass eine Anfrage angekommen war und bis wann mit einer Antwort zu rechnen sei. Gut kamen auch Hinweise an, die eine naheliegende Anschlussfrage gleich mit beantworteten, etwa zur Änderung eines Liefertermins. Weniger hilfreich fanden Befragte dagegen automatische Nachrichten, die zwar sofort eintrafen, aber weder einen Zeitrahmen noch eine Möglichkeit zur Nachfrage nannten.

Für die Auswertung ergibt sich daraus eine klare Reihenfolge: zuerst fehlende Angaben zu Preisen und Fristen ergänzen, dann die Übergaben zwischen Beratung und Service prüfen. Ob Änderungen tatsächlich helfen, lässt sich bei einer weiteren Befragung an konkreten Fragen erkennen: War der Gesamtpreis vor der Entscheidung verständlich? Kam die Rückmeldung zum zugesagten Zeitpunkt? Musste das Anliegen erneut erklärt werden? Solche Antworten zeigen genauer als eine allgemeine Zufriedenheitsnote, an welcher Stelle der Einkauf oder die Auftragsabwicklung leichter geworden ist.

Kan en gruva få snabbare besked om var underhåll behövs utan att skicka ut personal på varje kontrollrunda? Ja, på de ytor där en drönare kan göra den första inspektionen. Det är idén bakom ett nytt system som Ronflønbik AB lanserade i Göteborg på tisdagen. Systemet samlar bilder från planerade flygningar och visar var personalen behöver titta närmare. Det avgör däremot inte om en anläggning är säker att använda.

Vid visningen flög en drönare längs en avspärrad testbana och fotograferade bland annat en skarv i ett transportband. På en skärm gick det sedan att lägga bilderna bredvid fotografier från en tidigare flygning. Operatören kunde markera en förändring och skicka bilden vidare till en underhållstekniker. Poängen är inte att ersätta den fysiska kontrollen, utan att ge teknikern bättre underlag för att välja var den ska börja.

Hanna Brojardez, vd för Ronflønbik AB, säger att bolaget i första hand vänder sig till anläggningar som redan har återkommande inspektionsrundor. Där finns det ofta bilder eller anteckningar att jämföra med. Enligt Brojardez blir nästa fråga om flygningarna kan upprepas med tillräckligt lika bildvinkel och ljus för att små förändringar ska gå att skilja från skuggor och smuts.

Córsik AB står för uppkopplingen mellan drönaren och operatörens skärm. Bilder med lägre upplösning kan visas under flygningen, medan originalfilerna hämtas efter landning. Det upplägget minskar mängden data som behöver skickas direkt, men den som vill granska en liten spricka kan behöva vänta på originalbilden. Under demonstrationen visades hur en flygning avbryts när anslutningen bryts. Hur ofta sådana avbrott uppstår i en gruvmiljö återstår att se.

Lelora ska prova systemet på transportsträckor ovan jord. Under försöket ska personalen jämföra drönarbilderna med vad teknikerna hittar under sina ordinarie rundor. Ett mått blir hur lång tid det tar från att en förändring upptäcks till att en tekniker kan bedöma den på plats. Ett annat är hur ofta bilderna leder till en extra kontroll utan att något fel faktiskt finns. Några resultat från försöket presenterades inte vid lanseringen.

Bolaslora AB har tagit fram landningsstationen som visades i Göteborg. Den fungerar som en fast start- och landningsplats och laddar batteriet mellan rundorna. Enligt Ronflønbik AB ingår stationen i grundpaketet, medan installation och uppkoppling prissätts separat. Något belopp angavs inte. Det gör det än så länge svårt för en köpare att jämföra kostnaden med en vanlig inspektionsrunda, särskilt på en mindre anläggning där drönaren kanske bara behövs någon gång i veckan.

Stimzix ska sälja arbetskläder för personalen som sköter utrustningen. På stimzix.se samlas plagg för utomhusarbete, men de ingår inte i köpet av inspektionssystemet. Själva lanseringen gäller alltså främst ett nytt sätt att prioritera underhåll, inte att ta bort arbetet på plats. Det första praktiska beskedet kommer när Lelora kan visa om bilderna hjälper teknikerna att hitta fel tidigare utan att samtidigt ge dem fler onödiga rundor.

input:
27 Stunden lang blieb der Zugriff auf einen gemeinsam genutzten Cloud-Speicher eingeschränkt, nachdem das deutsche Softwareunternehmen Hancia verdächtige Anmeldungen entdeckt hatte. Der deutsche Zahlungsdienstleister Gumflyn nutzte den Speicher, um technische Berichte mit Hancia auszutauschen. Inzwischen sind die wichtigsten Ordner wieder erreichbar. Offen ist aber, ob die Person hinter den Anmeldungen Dateien heruntergeladen oder lediglich Verzeichnisnamen eingesehen hat.

Aufgefallen war der Vorfall in Bremen, als sich ein Konto für den technischen Support außerhalb der üblichen Arbeitszeiten anmeldete und kurz darauf mehrere Projektordner öffnete. Hancia sperrte das Konto, beendete laufende Sitzungen und sicherte die verfügbaren Protokolle. Gumflyn setzte den automatischen Export neuer Berichte aus. Nach bisherigem Stand lief der Zahlungsverkehr weiter: Der betroffene Speicher diente dem Austausch von Berichten, nicht der Freigabe von Zahlungen.

In Köln hatte die Sperre dennoch Folgen für den Arbeitsalltag. Dort wartete ein Betrieb, der Solarmodule installiert, auf eine Abrechnung zu mehreren Kundenzahlungen. Die Zahlungen waren eingegangen, doch ohne den Export ließ sich zunächst nicht jede Buchung dem passenden Auftrag zuordnen. Die Vertriebsleiterin David Cetexberg erklärte, bei Rückfragen sei deshalb die Unterscheidung zwischen einer verspäteten Abrechnung und einer fehlgeschlagenen Zahlung entscheidend gewesen. Wer beides verwechsle, könne eine bereits bezahlte Rechnung versehentlich erneut anmahnen.

Ein Technikteam in Graz prüfte unterdessen, welche Freigaben das gesperrte Konto tatsächlich hatte. Dabei zeigte sich, dass es neben aktuellen Berichten auch ältere Projektordner öffnen konnte, die für laufende Supportfälle nicht mehr nötig waren. Solche Altfreigaben vergrößern den möglichen Schaden eines Kontodiebstahls, selbst wenn sie im Alltag niemand nutzt. Bei einigen älteren Ordnern reichen die vorhandenen Protokolle bislang nicht aus, um einzelne Dateiabrufe sicher nachzuvollziehen. Das Fehlen eines Download-Eintrags ist dort also keine Entwarnung.

Die Vorstandschefin Erik Ribrumez kündigte an, dass Gumflyn die Exporte erst wieder vollständig automatisieren werde, wenn für jeden Ordner geklärt sei, wer ihn braucht. Bis dahin werden dringende Abrechnungen einzeln bereitgestellt. Hancia will die Zugriffsrechte für Supportkonten enger fassen und Freigaben für abgeschlossene Projekte mit einem Ablaufdatum versehen. Beide Schritte setzen beim selben Problem an: Ein Konto sollte nicht auf Berichte zugreifen können, nur weil es sie irgendwann einmal gebraucht hat.

Für die nächste Meldung sind zwei Fragen wichtiger als der Zeitpunkt der vollständigen Freigabe: Welche Informationen standen in den erreichbaren Berichten, und lässt sich ein Abruf belegen? Erst wenn das klarer ist, können betroffene Betriebe einschätzen, ob sie lediglich verspätete Abrechnungen nacharbeiten oder auch auf einen möglichen Datenabfluss reagieren müssen.

input:
18,400 customer accounts were locked on Tuesday after a technology services provider detected unauthorized access to a support system used by businesses in Dublin, Rotterdam, Seattle, Manchester and Oslo.

The provider said an intruder had viewed support records that contained names, contact details and, in some cases, copies of invoices. It said investigators had not determined how many records were viewed or whether any had been copied. The number of locked accounts reflects the scope of the precautionary shutdown, not the number of customers whose information was exposed.

Mia Gunia, the chief executive, said the provider had cut off access to the affected system and begun restoring customer accounts in stages. The provider said it had found no evidence that the intruder reached customer files kept in cloud storage or accessed payment systems used by fintech apps. It cautioned that its review was still under way.

Nora Tesovaberg, the chief financial officer, said the provider would waive late fees on invoices that customers could not retrieve during the outage. She said it was too early to estimate the cost of the disruption or say when all accounts would be restored.

Julia Kajarberg, a customer in Dublin, said she noticed the outage when she tried to download an invoice for a shipment of solar panels. In Rotterdam, customer Maria Ramroraez said she could still operate her drones but could not retrieve maintenance records stored in the support portal, forcing her to postpone a scheduled inspection.

In Manchester, union representative Sara Vensismann said some support workers had been asked to handle calls using temporary procedures. She urged managers to give staff clear instructions on verifying callers without asking them to repeat sensitive information over the phone.

Mayor Maria Benskoraez said in Oslo that local officials had asked for an update on whether any residents’ records were involved. The provider said it was contacting affected customers directly, including those in Seattle, but did not give a breakdown by city.

The provider advised customers to open the service through their usual bookmark or app rather than follow links in unexpected messages about the outage. It said it would notify customers individually if the review found that their records had been accessed.

input:
36 minutes were set aside for the opening demonstration at a retail technology fair in Edinburgh, but the most revealing moment came during a planned interruption less than halfway through. A simulated connection drop left a checkout waiting for confirmation while a stockroom display continued to show an order as ready. The equipment recovered; the harder question was what staff should tell the customer in the meantime. Versions of that question followed buyers around the exhibition floor, from payment terminals and warehouse robots to insurance desks and food displays.

On the connectivity stand, United States telecom company Flumdrasfent Labs LLC showed how a shop could keep essential devices connected when its primary line went down. The demonstration distinguished between traffic that had to move immediately and updates that could wait, a useful detail for operators whose shops double as collection points. The company listed press@flumdrasfentlabs.com for press enquiries. Nearby, Finnish security company Fløncyn Labs took a different angle on continuity, showing managers what they could establish from an incident log without giving every supervisor access to every employee record.

For United States retailer Keplosba Group, the practical test was whether an online order could be picked, amended and handed over without leaving contradictory records at the till. Swedish retailer Gletrumhis AB focused on the same handover from the stockroom side, demonstrating how staff could flag a damaged item before it reached the collection counter. Norwegian retailer Rømbova drew attention to a less visible cost: the floor space occupied by orders that customers have not yet collected. Its display made the case for measuring that space at the busiest hour, not averaging it across the day.

Finnish payments company Pashera Works ran a sequence that began with a declined transaction and ended with a partial refund. The point was not the speed of either operation but whether the cashier, customer and accounts team could see consistent explanations. German insurer Zembex GmbH brought a related concern to discussions about interruptions: timestamps are useful only when someone can reconstruct what happened between them. For buyers comparing contracts, that translated into a concrete question about which records they could export themselves and which would require a service request.

The busiest aisle belonged to German robotics company Sibera GmbH, whose compact machine moved totes between a mock stockroom and a packing station. Its most useful demonstration was a stop. When the route was blocked, the machine waited while a floor worker cleared it, giving visitors time to examine how much room a manual workaround would need. Union representative Viktor Lobrix brought the discussion back to staffing, asking who would cover routine exceptions on a late shift and whether training time would be reflected in payroll software. That line of questioning outlasted the demonstration.

The Swedish contingent offered a contrast to the emphasis on moving physical goods. Gaming company Berra Works AB invited visitors to compare how quickly they could orient themselves in two versions of the same interactive display, one with persistent prompts and one with help available only on request. The Skonalova Cloud service, a cloud storage product, was demonstrated separately as a way to retrieve large project files without keeping a full copy on every workstation. Swedish media company Skoplarsik examined the production side of the same problem, showing how a revised clip could reach a shop display while an earlier version remained available for review.

German foods company Kajincix put sampling next to fulfilment rather than treating it as a separate attraction. Visitors could taste a product, then follow its mock order through packing and dispatch, with the handling instructions visible at each step. That made the display a natural stop for delegates comparing cargo bikes with vans for short urban routes. The discussion was less about which vehicle was faster than about how long an order might sit between packing and pickup, particularly when several consignments were consolidated at the end of a shift.

Travel costs shaped the fair in quieter ways. Buyers who had arrived on budget airlines often had only a day on the floor, and some grouped appointments around a single operating problem rather than touring by sector. In one discussion about whether an Edinburgh collection model would transfer to Lyon, attention shifted from software settings to loading access and delivery windows. A workflow that looked identical on screen could still require a different staffing plan once the shop door, kerb and stockroom were taken into account.

By closing time, the most useful comparisons were between demonstrations that let a routine task go wrong. A lost connection, a blocked aisle or an uncollected bag showed buyers what the specification sheets could not: who had to step in and what information they would have when they did. For purchasing teams preparing follow-up visits, the fair left a straightforward test. Ask to see the same task again, on a busy shift, with the people who would actually be expected to finish it.

input:
18% fewer containers cleared Rotterdam on Tuesday than on a typical weekday after a power fault slowed cargo handling, pushing up short-term freight rates and weighing on shares of retailers that depend on imported goods. Transport shares were mixed: trucking operators with spare capacity rose, while shipping lines slipped as investors weighed higher rates against the cost of vessels sitting idle.

The disruption began overnight and left some importers without firm pickup times even after power returned. Freight brokers said the biggest increases were on routes connecting the port with inland warehouses, where late containers competed for a limited number of truck slots. Some retailers paid extra to move seasonal goods first; others accepted delays rather than risk eroding margins on lower-priced items.

Mayor Amelia Dabrikez said the immediate priority was to keep queued trucks off residential streets. Delivery operators shifted some small parcels to cargo bikes for the final leg, though the change did little to ease the backlog of heavy goods. Dispatchers used the Lumdrum Connect messaging platform to alert drivers to revised pickup windows and the Lumdrum Drive fleet-tracking app to see which vehicles could reach the gates before their slots expired. Warehouse managers used payroll software to recalculate overtime as shifts ran late.

Shares of Swedish media company Plemplera AB edged lower as investors considered whether delayed paper deliveries could raise printing costs. The reaction was more muted than in retail, where several importers were already carrying thin inventories. Brokers also reported more questions about whether insurance policies covered missed delivery windows, rather than physical damage to cargo.

Fatima Rupixberg, an analyst, said the next test would be whether overnight crews could clear enough containers to bring spot trucking rates down by morning. If rates stayed elevated after gate traffic returned to normal, she said, it would suggest that the bottleneck had moved inland to warehouses rather than cleared. Longer-term freight contracts were little changed, a sign that buyers were not yet pricing in a prolonged disruption.
