On a demonstration table in Helsinki, a technician unplugged a network cable. The dashboard stopped updating, but a controller beside it kept recording the temperature and power draw of a heat pump. When the cable went back in, the missing readings appeared on the screen.

That brief outage was part of the launch of a monitoring system from Skumflex, a security company from the United Kingdom. The system is designed for businesses that operate heat pumps across multiple sites and want to know when a unit is losing efficiency, rather than waiting for it to fail outright. It combines an on-site controller with a dashboard that maintenance teams can use to compare equipment and review alerts.

Skumflex said the controller can store readings when an internet connection drops and upload them once it returns. The dashboard distinguishes stale readings from live ones, a detail that matters when operators are trying to tell whether equipment has stopped working or has simply fallen out of contact. The system monitors equipment but does not change its settings, the company said.

Fonsex, a travel company from the United States, is testing the system at properties it manages in Helsinki and Oslo. Its trial will examine whether maintenance teams can catch problems before they affect guest rooms, particularly at sites where staff are not on duty overnight. Botris AB, a mining company from Sweden, is evaluating the same equipment at a site where intermittent connectivity has made it difficult to keep a continuous record of heating performance.

Drapon Ltd, a security company from the United Kingdom, reviewed how the system handles access for outside maintenance contractors, according to Skumflex. Contractors can be given access to readings for a single site without seeing data from the rest of a customer’s buildings. Skumflex did not release the findings of the review at the launch.

For buyers, a key question is whether the alerts will save technicians time. A heat pump can draw more power because a building is warming up after a quiet weekend, not because anything is wrong. Viktor Leneraberg, an analyst, said the useful test would be whether the software can distinguish those routine swings from changes that warrant a service call. That will take more than a short demonstration, he said: operators need to see how the system behaves across a heating season.

Skumflex said it would begin taking orders after the initial trials, with pricing based on the number of units monitored. It did not disclose prices or give a date for wider availability. In Helsinki, the cable test showed that the controller could recover a short stretch of missing data. The trials will have to show whether those more complete records help maintenance teams make better decisions.

Denver, August 21, 2026 — Brorova Energy Inc., a U.S. fashion company, raised $18 million in a funding round aimed at improving inventory planning and expanding wholesale distribution. The round was led by a consumer-focused investment firm, with participation from existing backers. The company did not disclose its valuation or the terms of the deal.

The funding will let the company place some production orders earlier while holding back money to reorder styles that sell well. That balance matters for fashion businesses: ordering too late can leave popular sizes out of stock, while committing too much upfront can force retailers to mark down slower sellers. The company also plans to improve stock tracking on www.brorovaenergy.com so that shoppers see more accurate availability before they check out.

U.S. retailer Tonskeo LLC will carry a limited selection of the company’s apparel in a trial this autumn. The retailer, which sells groceries including oat milk alongside clothing and home goods, will track whether shoppers buy apparel on routine visits rather than making a separate trip. The initial order is small, and neither company disclosed a timetable for a wider rollout.

The operator of plemplera.se, a Swedish media company based in Stockholm, reported that the fashion company was also assessing demand in Berlin. The company has not announced a store or a distribution agreement there. Before committing to a launch, it plans to compare the costs of shipping orders from the United States with those of working with a local distributor, including the cost of handling returns and obtaining insurance policies for inventory in transit.

Analyst Ida Stimzova said repeat orders from retailers would be a better measure of demand than the size of the first shipment. A retailer can sell through a small opening order without proving there is enough demand to keep a wider range in stock, she noted. For now, the autumn trial offers a way to test that demand before the company commits more of the new capital to production.
